true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize silently overrides the width/height variant

The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the later definition wins, so any existing caller that passes width and height separately (the signature kept at line 145 implies such callers exist, e.g. avatar/import paths) will actually hit the second method: `dimensions` receives the width and `opts` receives the height (an Integer). Inside `optimize`, `opts[:allow_animation]` is then called on an Integer, which raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer`, breaking every width/height-style downsize call at runtime. The first definition is dead code and the width/height calling convention is broken; either remove the old method and update all callers, or give the dimensions variant a different name.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hard-coded 10MB client limit ignores max_image_size_kb and max_attachment_size_kb site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously enforced `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, i.e. the admin-configured per-type limit (images vs attachments). It now always allows 10MB. For attachments there is no server-side downsizing, so on sites where `max_attachment_size_kb` is set below 10MB the client-side guard no longer rejects oversized files with the friendly size message; the upload is sent in full and then fails server-side with a generic error. It also ignores admins who raised limits above 10MB. Only image downsizing was added server-side; the attachment check should keep reading the site setting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
413 error message always claims the limit is 10 MB

`displayErrorForUpload` reports a hard-coded "10 MB" maximum when the server returns 413, but the actual limit is `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb`, which the admin can set to anything. On sites with a different limit the message shown to users is factually wrong and confusing. The previous code read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` here.

API URL download cap hard-coded to 10MB regresses sites with higher max_image_size_kb

The remote-download size limit for API uploads was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hard-coded `10.megabytes`. Sites that configured `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer pull images via URL larger than 10MB (they now silently fail with `rescue nil`, producing a confusing `tempfile`-nil path), while the client-facing intent of the PR is to allow large images that are then downsized. The cap should be derived from the setting (or at least max(setting, 10MB)).

Animated GIFs are flattened to a single frame when downsized because the extension check never matches tempfile paths

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) pipeline only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the paths passed from `create_upload` are Rack multipart tempfiles or `FileHelper.download` tempfiles, whose names have no `.gif` extension. Consequently any animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is processed by ImageMagick `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame: the user's animated upload is silently converted to a still image even when `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation-detection should be based on the original filename/content, not the tempfile path.

Downsizing loop runs up to 5 full ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload and can still not converge

Each iteration applies `-resize 80%`, which reduces area to ~64%, so five iterations shrink the image at most ~10x; an image far above the limit (e.g. 50MB against a 1MB setting) still exceeds it after the loop and then fails in `Upload.create_for` with a generic error. Additionally, when `downsize` returns false (convert failure), the return value is ignored, so the loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing on the same file. Each pass also invokes ImageOptim, making this expensive CPU work on the request path for synchronous API uploads. The loop should stop early on failure and compute a resize percentage that reaches the target in one pass.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update/destroy raise NoMethodError (500) when the host id doesn't exist or params are missing

In `update` and `destroy`, `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns nil for an unknown id; `save_host(nil)` then does `host.host = ...` on nil, and `destroy` calls `nil.destroy`, both producing a 500 instead of a 404. Similarly, `save_host` dereferences `params[:embeddable_host][:host]` without checking the param exists, and if `host` is assigned nil the model's `before_validation` block (`self.host.sub!`) raises NoMethodError instead of returning a validation error. Stale ids (e.g. the record deleted in another tab) will surface as server errors rather than a clean error response.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated host values are inserted verbatim (no scheme/path stripping) and interpolated raw into SQL

The migration takes each line of the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting and inserts it directly via raw SQL. The old setting accepted values like `http://discourse.org` or `https://example.com/1234` (the PR's own controller spec fabricates exactly such values), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` matches with `lower(host) = uri.host` (e.g. 'discourse.org'). Because the INSERT bypasses the model's `before_validation` callbacks that strip the scheme and path, any migrated host containing a protocol prefix or path will never match a referer, silently breaking embedding for those sites after upgrade. Additionally, the value is interpolated into the SQL string with `#{h}`; a value containing a single quote (possible in the free-text setting) breaks the SQL statement. The migration should normalize each host the same way the model does and use quoted/parameterized values.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Category and embeddable_host fabricator contents are swapped between files

This PR puts the `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` definition into `spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` (whose entire category content was deleted) and moves all the category fabricators (`:category`, `:diff_category`, `:happy_category`, `:private_category`) into the newly added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb`. Tests still pass because Fabricator loads all files, but the file names no longer reflect their contents at all; anyone adding or editing a category fabricator will look in the wrong file, and this is clearly an accidental file mix-up rather than an intentional move. The contents should be swapped back so each fabricator lives in its matching file.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.

The migration takes each line of the old `embeddable_hosts` site setting and inserts it directly via raw SQL. The old setting accepted values like `http://discourse.org` or `https://example.com/1234` (the PR's own controller spec fabricates exactly such values), but `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` matches with `lower(host) = uri.host` (e.g. 'discourse.org'). Additionally, the value is interpolated into the SQL string with `#{h}`; a value containing a single quote (possible in the free-text setting) breaks the SQL statement. The migration should normalize each host the same way the model does and use quoted/parameterized values.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes with NoMethodError when embed_category is unset or doesn't match a category

The migration looks up the old `embed_category` site setting via `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id'].to_i`. On any install where the `embed_category` setting is empty (its default is '') or its value doesn't match a category name, the query returns zero rows, so `[0]` is nil and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration. The `if category_id == 0` fallback on line 14 was clearly meant to handle the 'not found' case, but it is unreachable because the code crashes before it. The lookup must tolerate an empty result set (e.g. `rows[0].try(:[], 'id').to_i`) before the fallback can work.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

false_positives.candidate:
EmbeddingController#update is a no-op that reports success without saving anything

The `update` action (routed via `put "customize/embedding"`) fetches the embedding data and re-renders it, but never applies any submitted attributes. The admin controller's `saveChanges` action calls `this.get('embedding').update({})` against this endpoint, so a client saving changes gets a 200 with the unchanged payload while any data is silently discarded. Either the action should process and persist the submitted parameters, or the route/action and the client `saveChanges` code should be removed so nobody is led to believe saving works.

New admin controllers have no behavioral tests (create/update/destroy, validation, permissions)

Both `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` and `Admin::EmbeddingController` specs only assert that the class is a subclass of `Admin::AdminController`. There is no test covering create/update/destroy of embeddable hosts, the host normalization/validation rules, the category_id fallback to uncategorized, error rendering for invalid hosts, or access control (e.g. that a non-admin is rejected). Given this controller writes data that gates which external sites can embed content, at least CRUD and authorization request specs should be added; as written, the nil-id and bad-param failures described elsewhere would not be caught.

create_table uses force: true in a production migration

`create_table :embeddable_hosts, force: true` will drop the table (and all host/category data) if it already exists when the migration runs. Using `force: true` is appropriate in schema definitions for test convenience, not in a shipped migration; if the table pre-exists on any install (e.g. from a partially applied migration or a plugin), this migration silently destroys the data instead of failing loudly.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe action crashes when the user has no TopicUser record

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil, and the next line immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. A TopicUser row is only created once a user has visited/interacted with a topic, yet the unsubscribe link is included in every notification email — e.g. a user who was mentioned or invited to a topic but never opened it will have no row. Clicking the emailed 'stop receiving notifications' link then raises NoMethodError on nil and returns a 500 instead of unsubscribing them. The code should fall back to TopicUser.change(...)/create the row with the desired level.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
Email copy promises to stop notifications but the endpoint only downgrades to regular

The new unsubscribe_link text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here', but TopicsController#unsubscribe only sets watching/tracking users to `regular` — a level that still emails the user when someone replies to them or @mentions them. A user who clicks the link believing they will no longer receive emails for that topic will keep getting reply/mention notifications, which is a trust/warranty problem for the feature. Either the endpoint should set the level to muted, or the message should accurately describe what will still be received.

No request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The TopicsController#unsubscribe action introduces new routing, access control (ensure_logged_in), a toggle rule based on the current notification level, and a 301 redirect for slug mismatch, but no controller/request specs were added for it — the only test change in the PR is unrelated (adding unsubscribe_url to a message_builder spec). Notably, the nil-TopicUser case and the watching->regular vs regular->muted toggle behavior are completely untested, which is how the nil crash above ships unnoticed.

Notification state is mutated by an unauthenticated-CSRF-able GET request, and refresh re-toggles it The `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route is a GET that flips the user's notification_level (watching/tracking -> regular, regular/muted -> muted) with no CSRF token or confirmation. Because it is a plain GET with session cookies, any logged-in user can have their topic notification settings silently changed just by loading a URL — e.g. an attacker can embed `` in a post or external page and the victim's browser will hit the endpoint and mute/unwatch the topic. Additionally, since the same GET both performs the toggle and renders the unsubscribe page, every page refresh or link re-visit toggles the level again (watching -> regular -> muted), so the user's final state depends on how many times the URL was loaded. State changes should not happen on GET (or should be idempotent, e.g. always mute).

Unsubscribe link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} and raises for callers that don't supply it

The `unsubscribe_link` locale now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, and both `html_part` (line 67) and `body` (line 90) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`. I18n raises `MissingInterpolationArgument` when an interpolation key in the translation has no value, so any caller that builds an email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now fail to render and the email send will blow up. The only in-repo caller was updated (and the message_builder spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url`), but MessageBuilder is a reusable API used by plugins and mailers that set `add_unsubscribe_link` on its own; the builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. to the user preferences URL) or use `I18n.t(..., unsubscribe_url: ... )` with a fallback so missing values degrade gracefully.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write inside model validation and double-counts attempts

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation. In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` is called at line 168 and then `user.save` runs the same validations again, so every blocked signup attempt increments match_count twice (or more if valid? is called elsewhere, e.g. change_username also calls valid?). Side-effectful writes during validation are also surprising: any code calling valid? on a user with a changed email mutates the blocked_emails table. The statistics update should happen once, outside the validation path (e.g. in the controller when the error is actually returned), or use a guard so it only runs once per attempt.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with the raw email string, and there is a unique index on the email column as-is. User emails are not normalized to lowercase on assignment (UsersController#create passes params[:email] straight into the model, and mixed-case emails can exist since email uniqueness is also case-sensitive here). A user whose address was blocked as 'spammer@example.com' can register as 'Spammer@Example.com' and the lookup returns no row, completely bypassing the block. The lookup (and the unique index) should compare downcased emails.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
Any server-side email error permanently marks the email invalid with the wrong message

On a failed account creation, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into rejectedEmails whenever the response contains any `errors.email` key. That includes errors unrelated to the email being unacceptable, e.g. 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist 'not allowed' error. The emailValidation computed property then shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') ('invalid email address') for that address, which is misleading for a taken or blocked address (the server message is 'is not allowed.' / 'has already been taken'). The client should key off the specific error type, or at least surface a message matching the server's reason. The email also stays rejected for the lifetime of the controller even if the underlying condition changes.

Read-modify-write race on match_count loses increments under concurrency

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the counter in Ruby and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same value and both write value+1, losing one increment (and clobbering last_match_at updates with a stale AR object). Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` instead.

Validator spec stubs out the behavior under test; no integration coverage for users or the controller contract

The only spec for EmailValidator stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the actual model wiring (User's `validates :email, email: true`, the migration, and the BlockedEmail lookup) is never exercised end-to-end: nothing proves that a user with a blocked email fails validation and cannot be created. There is also no spec for the new UsersController#create failure payload (`errors` hash and `values` hash) that the new frontend code in create_account_controller.js depends on, so a rename or shape change of that JSON would not be caught. Add a spec that fabricates a blocked email, builds/creates a User with it, and asserts the validation error, plus a controller spec asserting the errors/values keys on failed create.

change_email flow bypasses the blocked-email check entirely

The new EmailValidator only runs on the User model when `email_changed?`. The change_email action never assigns user.email; it creates an email_token with the new address (`user.email_tokens.create(email: lower_email)`) and the address is later attached to the user when the token is confirmed (EmailToken.confirm), which typically uses update_attribute/save paths that skip validations. As a result, an existing user can switch their account email to any blocked address and receive mail there, defeating the purpose of the blocked-email feature. The blocked/whitelist/blacklist check must also be applied in change_email (and at token creation/confirmation), not only in the model's email-changed validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check via `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` is a weak substring match

The postMessage handler validates the sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it accepts any message whose origin string appears anywhere in the configured discourseUrl. Because it is a substring (not prefix/exact) match, an origin that happens to be contained in the URL string passes; e.g. a discourseUrl of `http://discourse.example.com` accepts an event from origin `http://d` (host `d`) or any origin that is a substring of the URL. The consequence is limited to setting the iframe height today, but the correct check is an exact/parsed comparison (e.g. compare `e.origin` against the URL's `protocol + '//' + host`), since future message types would inherit the flaw.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer-based authorization is trivially spoofable, allowing unbounded job enqueueing and forced fetching

Access control for /embed/best relies solely on the Referer header matching SiteSetting.embeddable_host. Any non-browser client can set an arbitrary Referer header, so anyone on the internet can hit the endpoint and cause `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` for arbitrary embed_url values. The TopicRetriever throttle is only 60 seconds per exact URL string, so an attacker can vary the URL (query strings, paths) to enqueue an unbounded number of jobs, each of which causes the Discourse server to make an HTTP request to the embeddable host (a limited but real SSRF/abuse vector) and, when feed polling is enabled, synchronously executes the entire Jobs::PollFeed run inside the job. Rate limiting at the controller level and/or a global cap on retrieve jobs is needed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: URL interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute in the 'imported from' footer `contents << "...#{url}..."` interpolates the embed URL directly into HTML that is later stored via the raw_html cook method and rendered with `raw`. The `^https?://` regex check on line 11 does not exclude single quotes, `>` or other markup characters that can appear in a URL's path/query (e.g. `http://embeddable-host/?x='>`). This allows attribute breakout and markup injection into the stored post. The URL should be HTML-escaped (and the href properly quoted) before interpolation.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view fails to render

Line 6 closes the header if/else with `<%- end if %>`, which ERB compiles to the Ruby fragment `end if ` — a modifier `if` with no condition, a syntax error. Every render of the embed view (the success path when a topic exists) will raise ActionView::Template::Error / SyntaxError and return a 500 to the embedding site, making the whole feature non-functional in the topic-found case. It should be `<%- end %>`. The controller specs don't catch this because `TopicView` is stubbed with a mock, so the template never renders against a real topic view.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil `i.content` (or a feed error) crashes the whole poll, and retry is disabled

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has `content`; RSS feeds that only provide `description` (or ATOM entries with only a summary) will raise NoMethodError on nil, aborting the entire `poll_feed` run partway through — items after the offending one are never imported. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until the next hourly run, which will fail at the same item. `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is likewise unguarded, so a transient network error kills the run. Guard for missing content (fall back to `i.description`) and rescue per-item/feed-level errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript allows XSS on the Discourse origin

The embed layout renders `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` with the raw Referer header inserted into a JavaScript string literal without escape_javascript/html escaping. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter only validates that the referer's *host* equals SiteSetting.embeddable_host, so an attacker making a direct HTTP request (where the Referer header is fully attacker-controlled, e.g. `http://<embeddable_host>/', alert(document.cookie), '`) can break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary script in a page served from the Discourse origin. This is a reflected XSS; the value must be escaped with `j()`/escape_javascript before interpolation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

false_positives.candidate:
Discussion replies rendered with `raw post.cooked` include any HTML users managed to post

The embed view renders each post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. While normal posts go through the cooking/sanitization pipeline, this view bypasses all of the markup filtering Discourse normally applies when displaying cooked content (e.g., the whitelist applied elsewhere), so any HTML that survives into `cooked` for any post in the topic — including raw_html posts created by other import paths or plugins — is executed verbatim in a frame that is served from the Discourse origin with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL`. Combined with the raw_html import path this widens the XSS surface; cooked output should be passed through the same sanitization used by the main topic renderer.

Imported RSS content is stored as raw HTML with skip_validations and rendered with `raw`, enabling stored XSS

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`, which makes `Post#cook` return the raw content verbatim (no markdown/sanitization pipeline). The RSS path in `Jobs::PollFeed` passes `i.content` (fully controlled by whatever the feed at feed_polling_url contains) straight into import — unlike `import_remote`, which at least runs the content through ruby-readability's tag/attribute whitelist. `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` then renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. A compromised or malicious feed entry containing `<script>` or `onerror=` handlers is stored and executed on the Discourse forum and on every page that embeds the comments iframe. The feed content needs sanitization (e.g., Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw HTML.

Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can leave the throttle key without a TTL, permanently blocking retrieval

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key exists with no TTL and never expires, so that embed_url is throttled forever — the topic is never retrieved and the embed shows the loading page indefinitely. Use a single atomic command (e.g., `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` available via the redis gem, or a Lua script) so the expiry is always set.

PostCreator jobs are enqueued inside the wrapping transaction, before the TopicEmbed row commits

`TopicEmbed.import` wraps `creator.create` in `Topic.transaction` and only creates the `TopicEmbed` record *after* the post is created. PostCreator's `enqueue_jobs` (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs while still inside this outer transaction. If the subsequent `TopicEmbed.create!` fails — most plausibly in the race where two concurrent retrieve jobs for the same embed_url both pass the `where(embed_url: url).first` check and the second hits the unique index — the whole transaction rolls back, but the already-enqueued Sidekiq jobs referencing the rolled-back post/topic are not un-enqueued, and `TopicTrackingState.publish_new` messages have already been published on MessageBus for a topic that never committed. As it stands every poll re-parses and re-imports the full feed each hour.

This PR modifies the existing CreateTopTopics migration (2013-12-23) to add `force: true`, which makes `create_table` DROP the table if it exists. For any database that already ran this migration and then re-runs it (e.g., `rake db:migrate:redo`, or environments that replay migrations), all top_topics data would be destroyed. Editing historical migrations also means schema state diverges between deployments that ran the old version and the new one. The `force: true` should be reverted here (it belongs only in brand-new migrations, if anywhere).

When the Fallbacks backend resolves a miss by looking up the key in the default locale or :en, those locales' YAML files are never loaded by that code path. The PR compensates for this by calling I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale, but that before_filter only runs for web requests. In background jobs and mailers (e.g. user-targeted emails where I18n.locale is set to the recipient's locale), the fallback locale files are not loaded, so fallback lookups will miss and produce 'translation missing' strings (or the raw missing-translation marker) instead of falling back to the default/English text. The preloading should happen wherever locale is switched, or the accelerator should load the fallback locales for config.locale inside translate/load_locale.

By moving fallback configuration into config/initializers/i18n.rb, fallbacks to the site default locale and English are now active in every environment, including the test suite. This means tests and development rendering that used to fail loudly on incomplete locale files will now silently render English, hiding locale-file regressions (missing/renamed keys) until production-like behavior differs from what was validated. If global fallbacks are intended, consider keeping a way (e.g. raising on missing translations in test) to detect incomplete locale files.

This PR introduces a nontrivial behavior: a custom FallbackLocaleList whose [] computes [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] on every lookup, a per-request ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale, and interaction between fallbacks and the caching/lazy-loading translate accelerator. None of this is covered by tests. At minimum there should be specs verifying that (a) a key missing in the user's locale is served from the site default locale and then :en, (b) the fallback order is correct when locales coincide, and (c) the accelerator still caches correctly across locales. Without these, regressions in translation resolution (e.g. from future i18n gem upgrades or changes to the accelerator) will ship silently.

SiteSetting.default_locale is a runtime-changeable setting (admins can change it from the site settings UI without a restart or I18n.reload!), so after such a change, requests for a key missing in the user's locale will keep serving the previously cached string from the OLD default locale until the cache is cleared. The cache key (or the cache invalidation) needs to account for the fallback list.

false_positives.candidate:
Admin-gated 'advanced features' flag is security theater with a misleading safety comment

The gating `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` combined with the comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" implies the advanced path exposes something extra that permissions must guard. It does not: pagination offsets never bypass queryset filters, and the only 'advanced' capability (negative offsets) is an error path in the ORM. Meanwhile, the flag does create a real inconsistency: a superuser and a regular owner hitting the same URL with the same cursor get different paginator semantics (and, per the other findings, a 500 vs. working results). If there is no concrete capability being gated, remove the flag and the misleading comments rather than implying there is a privileged pagination mode.

BasePaginator change claims to support negative offsets but still crashes for is_prev cursors, and silently changes behavior otherwise

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for forward cursors; for previous-page cursors a negative client-supplied offset still flows into queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises Django's "Negative indexing is not supported" AssertionError, contradicting the comment that negative offsets are now allowed. For forward cursors, the clamp silently changes existing behavior: a malformed cursor like "0:-50:0" that previously errored now returns the first page, and the unclamped negative offset is still passed into build_cursor via the original cursor object, so the generated next/prev cursors can carry bogus negative offsets forward. Either validate the offset (reject negatives) or handle both directions consistently.

Client-toggled paginator class breaks cursor portability between requests

The paginator implementation now depends on a per-request query parameter (optimized_pagination) plus who is calling, so the same endpoint issues cursors with different semantics depending on the request. A cursor produced by DateTimePaginator encodes a ms-epoch value that DateTimePaginator converts back to a datetime for its WHERE clause; if the same cursor is replayed against OptimizedCursorPaginator (same user toggles the flag, or a superuser shares a link with a non-superuser), the raw integer is compared against the timestamp column and the request errors or returns wrong rows. Pagination cursors are supposed to be opaque tokens valid for the endpoint; making their interpretation depend on a mutable flag violates that contract and will produce intermittent 500s/incorrect pages for clients.

Comment-only change documents behavior that does not exist

The only change in cursors.py is a comment asserting "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`. The line of code is unchanged — Cursor has always accepted any int, and nothing in this file enables or handles negative offsets. Worse, downstream consumers (build_cursor's _build_next_values/_build_prev_values) compute new offsets via `offset + limit` / `offset - limit` with no lower bound, so negative offsets propagate into emitted cursors. The comment misleads readers into thinking negative-offset support was added and validated here; it should be removed or replaced with a note that offsets are unvalidated.

No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by many endpoints, and adds a new request-parameter-driven branch on a production endpoint, but includes no tests. At minimum it needs: (1) a regression test that BasePaginator.get_result behavior is unchanged for existing cursors (including the new max(0, offset) clamp), (2) tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator covering forward/prev cursors, which would have immediately caught the datetime TypeError and the Django negative-slicing AssertionError, and (3) endpoint tests covering the optimized_pagination flag for both authorized and unauthorized users.

OptimizedCursorPaginator's non-negative path is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result and provides no performance benefit

Apart from the broken negative-offset branch, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result line for line (same build_queryset, same slicing, same cursor building). The PR is titled 'Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs', but for every working request the query plan and workload are identical to the existing DateTimePaginator path — no index hints, no query reduction, nothing. The class adds ~100 lines of duplicated pagination logic (which will drift from the base implementation, as it already has with the misleading comments) with no measurable gain, while the only genuinely new behavior (negative offsets) is a guaranteed exception. The feature should either be justified with a real optimization or removed.

Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError

When `enable_advanced_features` is on and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative indices ("AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported"), so this path raises instead of paginating. The inline comments ("The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") are factually wrong: negative slicing does not work on querysets, and permissions have nothing to do with slicing. The advertised core feature of this paginator cannot function as written.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime sort keys

OptimizedCursorPaginator copies Paginator.get_item_key, which does `int(math.floor(value))` on the item's sort-key attribute. The only caller of this class (organization_auditlogs.py) paginates with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes to epoch-ms; the optimized class also lacks DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor's ms-to-datetime conversion, so a page-2 cursor would compare a timestamp column against a raw float in SQL. Net effect: any request with `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 (page 1 in get_item_key via build_cursor, page 2+ in the where clause).

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds ~100 lines of new paginator code (OptimizedCursorPaginator), modifies BasePaginator.get_result's offset handling for every existing paginator, and adds a new request-driven code path to the audit logs endpoint, yet includes zero tests: no unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator (including its negative-offset branch), no tests that BasePaginator behavior is unchanged for existing paginators, and no endpoint tests for the `optimized_pagination` parameter (including the authorization gate). Any of the crash modes described in the other findings would have been caught by a single basic test invoking the new code path.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, splitting deep segments

The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a trace's redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:*` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop now exits without resolving the root, `set_span_id` stays at the 1000th intermediate node, and the span is buffered under a partial key — silently splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments. This is a 10x reduction in the supported chain depth with no accompanying metric, log, or test, so the failure mode is invisible in production.

Unrelated audit-log pagination feature mixed into a span-buffer PR with no rationale

This PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and its description is just "Test 2", yet roughly half the diff introduces an unrelated, undocumented API behavior (`optimized_pagination=true` query param enabling a different paginator for superusers/global-access members) to the audit logs endpoint. This makes the change unreviewable as a unit and unrollbackable independently: a revert of the span-buffer work would either take the API change with it or require manual surgery. The audit-log changes should be split into their own PR with a real description, and if kept, the new query param should be documented/validated rather than read ad-hoc from request.GET.

enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`, but `Endpoint.paginate` in sentry/api/base.py has a fixed keyword signature (paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, max_limit, desc, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits) and constructs the paginator with only those arguments — it does not forward arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`. Unless the base method was also changed (it is not in this PR), this call raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, 500-ing every request that passes `optimized_pagination=true` with the required privileges. Even if the intent is for the flag to reach the paginator, `BasePaginator.__init__` would then need to receive it.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit

The Python-side enforcement of `max_segment_spans` (the check in `_load_segment_data` with its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log) was removed in favor of eviction inside the Lua script, but the `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` constructor parameter was left in place and is now never read. Meanwhile the Lua script hardcodes its own limit of 1000. Consequence: any deployment that configures `max_segment_spans` via options gets silently ignored behavior, and the off-by-one (1001 vs 1000) plus the dead parameter will confuse future readers. The limit should be passed to the script (e.g., as an ARGV) or the parameter removed.

zpopmin eviction can drop the root span, producing segments with no is_segment span

Eviction removes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. Nothing protects the root/segment span from eviction: if the root span's end timestamp is among the 1000 smallest (possible for out-of-order or async spans), its payload is popped while the `span-buf:hrs:*` flag is still set and the segment is still flushed under the root's key. The flushed segment then contains no span with `is_segment=true`, and every remaining span is stamped with a `segment_id` referring to a span that isn't in the payload — breaking the segment contract for downstream consumers. Evicted spans are also silently dropped with no metric, so the data loss is unobservable.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows all errors and drops client_sample_rate of 0

The new factory helper wraps its logic in two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks, so any structural problem with `contexts` (or an invalid sample rate value) is silently ignored and the event is stored without a sample rate, making downstream upsampled-count assertions pass or fail for the wrong reason. Upsampling eligibility is computed against the closure `dataset` and original request query, not the scoped dataset/query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer `dataset` variable and the raw `request.GET["query"]`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments. When the outer dataset is e.g. metrics_enhanced_performance, or the original query string lacks `event.type:error`, the transform is skipped even though the executed query is an error-only discover query that should be upsampled — dashboards on allowlisted projects will show under-sampled counts. false_positives.candidate:
Endpoint tests don't isolate the 60s eligibility cache, making them order-dependent

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches its result under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds in the shared cache, and nothing in the new test class clears it. Django test transactions roll back org/project id sequences, so consecutive test methods in this class reuse the same org id and project ids. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches `True` for that key; if `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` (which mocks a partial allowlist and asserts un-upsampled counts of 1) runs afterwards in the same process with a real (non-dummy) cache backend, it reads the cached `True`, applies upsampling, and asserts against counts of 10 — failing. setUp should delete the cache keys (or the helper should be patched), and there are no tests at all for `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself, its caching, or `invalidate_upsampling_cache`.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites y-axis columns; `equations=self.get_equation_list(organization, request)` is passed through untouched. A widget using yAxis `count()` plus an equation such as `equation(count() / count_unique(user))` on an allowlisted error query will get an upsampled `count()` series next to an equation computed from the raw sampled `count()`, producing internally inconsistent numbers (e.g. an "events per user" ratio computed from a count 10x smaller than the displayed count). Either rewrite count() inside equations or reject/skip upsampling when equations are present.

Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` filters as error-focused queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A discover query like `!event.type:error` (excluding errors, i.e. returning transactions/other events) contains the substring, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True and `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. For non-error events `sample_weight` is not populated (the helper itself documents that sample_weight doesn't exist for transactions), so the returned count will be wrong (typically 0) instead of the real event count. The check needs to parse the query's filter conditions rather than substring-match, or at least reject negated terms.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code — nothing calls it when the allowlist option changes

The docstring of `invalidate_upsampling_cache` says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but no code in this PR (option update handler, signal, or task) invokes it. In practice the only consistency mechanism is the 60-second TTL, so the function is misleading dead code; either wire it into the option-change path or remove it and document that only the TTL bounds staleness.

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to DiscoverDataset's function_converter, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in error_upsampling.py returns True whenever the request's dataset is `sentry.snuba.errors`, causing `_get_event_stats` to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` for errors-dataset requests. Either register the function in the errors dataset's converter as well, or restrict the transform to datasets where the function is actually defined. This path is also untested — all new endpoint tests exercise the default (discover) dataset.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore results via zip on dict values

In fetch_error_details, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id, and the code builds ErrorEvent objects with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. Dict values are not guaranteed to be in the same order as the requested node ids, and any node that is missing (deleted/expired event) is simply absent from the dict, which shifts every subsequent pairing. The result is that error titles, messages, and timestamps can be attributed to the wrong event id (the `id` field of ErrorEvent), and the filtering `if data is not None` does not fix the offset. The code should look up each event by its node id (e.g. `events.get(node_id)`) instead of zipping positional lists.

Error event timestamps read from nodestore are ISO strings, causing TypeError when compared with float breadcrumb timestamps

fetch_error_details builds ErrorEvent objects with `timestamp=data.get("timestamp", 0.0)` from raw nodestore event data. Nodestore event payloads store `timestamp` as an ISO-8601 string (and the 0.0 fallback is a float), while breadcrumb events from replay segments carry float timestamps. Downstream, `get_request_data` sorts error_events by timestamp (`error_events.sort(key=lambda x: x["timestamp"])`) and `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`, which mixes str and float operands and raises TypeError in Python 3 (both in the sort when a defaulted 0.0 is present, and in every comparison against a float breadcrumb timestamp). This will make the summarize-breadcrumbs endpoint raise a 500 for any replay that has associated error events. Timestamps should be parsed to floats (e.g. via `datetime.fromisoformat` / `Event.timestamp`) before use.

`tooFewFeedbacks` is computed as `data.numFeedbacksUsed === 0 && !data.success`, so when the summary generation fails with feedbacks present (numFeedbacksUsed > 0, success: false, summary: null), the hook reports tooFewFeedbacks=false and isError=false. FeedbackSummary then falls through to rendering the 'Feedback Summary' box with `summary` of null, showing users a permanently empty summary card rather than hiding it or surfacing an error state. The success/failure distinction should be based on `data.success` (or the summary being non-null), not just on the feedback count.

In `ourlogs.query`, when orderby is `[-timestamp]` or `[timestamp]`, the function appends `tags[sentry.timestamp_precise,number]` to `selected_columns` directly. This mutates the list passed in by the caller, so the hidden tie-breaking column leaks into any downstream use of that same list (response meta/fields, caching of the field list, or repeated calls that would append the column again on the same list). true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison is case- and whitespace-sensitive, but codes are lowercase hex

Backup codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` (lowercase a-f0-9), and verification does `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` with no lowercasing or trimming (same in apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts line 61). Codes can contain the letters a–f, so a user who types or saves the code in uppercase (the UI placeholder "XXXXX-XXXXX" actively suggests uppercase), or pastes it with leading/trailing whitespace, will be told the code is incorrect even though it is valid. Given each failed attempt is a dead end for the user, the input should be normalized (trim + toLowerCase) before comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write; codes can be replayed or burned

The backup code is consumed by reading `user.backupCodes`, decrypting, nulling the matched index, and writing the whole array back with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction or conditional update, so two concurrent login requests presenting the same code can both pass `indexOf` and both succeed — the code is effectively reusable within the race window. Additionally, the code is burned inside authorize() before the rest of the sign-in pipeline completes; if anything fails downstream or the client never receives the success response (network drop), the user's code is permanently consumed and their retry with the same code returns IncorrectBackupCode. Consumption should be atomic (e.g. a conditional update filtered on the code being present, or a transaction with a re-check) and ideally only committed once sign-in is assured.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
"Generate backup codes in your settings" is impossible — no regeneration path exists, and pre-PR 2FA users have none

The new `missing_backup_codes` message says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no endpoint or UI to generate/regenerate backup codes — they are only created once, during initial 2FA setup (setup.ts), and only shown once. Users who enabled 2FA before this PR have `backupCodes = null`, so if they lose their authenticator the "Lost access" flow is a dead end, and users who dismiss the backup-codes dialog without saving can never retrieve their codes again. The error message instructs them to do something that cannot be done, on both the login page and the disable-2FA modal.

Backup codes stored with reversible encryption instead of a one-way hash

Backup codes are persisted as AES-encrypted plaintext (`symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))`) using the shared CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and returned in plaintext in the API response. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be recoverable to validate codes), backup codes can be validated by hashing the user input and comparing digests, which is the industry standard (GitHub, Google, etc.). As stored, anyone with database access plus the encryption key — a key already used for many other secrets — recovers all unused backup codes, which per the finding above can even be replayed as a standalone credential.

No test covers actually using a backup code to log in or disable 2FA

The PR's headline feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The updated e2e tests only exercise the backup-codes screen's download/copy/close buttons; the TODO at the top of the file ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") acknowledges this. Neither the happy path (correct code logs in and is consumed), nor wrong-code rejection, nor code-single-use behavior is verified anywhere, leaving the new authorize() and disable.ts branches untested.

Users on the external TOTP login path (totpEmail) have no way to use a backup code

When a user arrives at /auth/login via a `totp` JWT (SSO/Google users with 2FA who were redirected by loginWithTotp), the footer rendered is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers a "cancel" button — the "Lost access" button that switches to the BackupCode input exists only in TwoFactorFooter. Such users have backup codes generated by this feature but no UI to enter them, so if they lose their authenticator they are locked out despite the feature existing. The lost-access toggle should also be offered in the external TOTP flow.

Valid backup code alone can authenticate without the account password

In the credentials authorize() the password check is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), i.e. the password is skipped whenever any non-empty totpCode is supplied. The new backup-code branch at line 131 then runs when `credentials.backupCode` is set, without ever verifying the password. So a request containing email, an arbitrary junk totpCode (e.g. "000000"), and a valid backupCode signs the user in with no password knowledge. Backup codes are single-use 40-bit hex strings typically saved in plaintext files or on paper; they are intended as a second factor, not a password substitute. The server should require a verified password (or otherwise ensure the first-factor step actually happened) before accepting a backup code.

onEnable is only fired from the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog via X/Escape skips it and resetState

The prop contract says onEnable is "Called when the user enables two-factor auth", and previously it was invoked as soon as enable succeeded. Now it is only called from the backup-codes "Close" button click handler. If the user dismisses the dialog through the built-in close affordances (X button, Escape key, overlay click — all routed to onOpenChange), onEnable never fires, so any parent that refreshes its state in onEnable (e.g. the two-factor switch on the security settings page) will keep showing 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled. resetState is also skipped, leaving the modal on the DisplayBackupCodes step with the codes still in memory if reopened.

resetState() does not clear the totpCode form field, leaving stale code from a previous setup

resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step, but never resets the react-hook-form `totpCode` field. After a completed (or abandoned) setup, the form still holds the previously entered 6-digit code. When the user later re-opens the modal and reaches the EnterTotpCode step, the registered hidden `totpCode` input still contains the old value while the digit boxes render empty; submitting (or any change that retriggers the auto-submit effect watching `totpCode`) can send the stale, now-invalid code, producing a confusing "code is incorrect" error before the user has typed anything. resetState should also call form.setValue("totpCode", "").

tabIndex={-1} on the password visibility toggle removes keyboard access

The change adds `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button inside PasswordField. This makes the toggle unreachable via keyboard (Tab/Synth events), so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reveal their password on the login page, the 2FA setup modal, or anywhere else PasswordField is used. If this was added to keep e2e selectors stable, it should be scoped differently rather than disabling focus for all users.

Breaking change to webhook payload destinationCalendar shape

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The core change — destinationCalendar becoming an array, per-credential calendar selection in EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents, Google's find-by-credentialId, and the collective push of team calendars — is only covered by an updated e2e assertion for BOOKING_REJECTED. Office365 (`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []`), Lark (packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:128) and the CalDAV BaseCalendarService (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts:156) all read only the first element of the now-array `destinationCalendar`. Since EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination with each host's own credential, for a collective event with multiple hosts on these providers the second host's credential is used against the first host's `externalId`, creating the event in the wrong calendar or failing with an auth/404 error. minimumTokenResponseSchema is broken and strips fields, corrupting stored credentials

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", so the 'any numeric property is the expiry' and 'allow other properties' intent is not implemented. Worse, z.object() strips unknown keys by default and this helper returns `safeParse(...).data`, so when credential sync is enabled every caller receives only `{access_token}` plus the injected `refresh_token: "refresh_token"` placeholder (line 26). The schema needs `.passthrough()` and a real expiry field, and the fake refresh_token should not be persisted into the credential.

So the refresh has no effect on the connection actually used, and expired credentials stay broken. Additionally there is no expiry check, so this token refresh + DB write happens on every single `getClient` call (every booking), which is both a performance problem and a rate-limit risk against Salesforce's token endpoint.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Webhook handler: no method check and unhandled parse/decrypt errors return 500s

The handler never checks `req.method` (a GET with no body will run the logic), and it uses `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (throws ZodError on malformed input) plus `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (throws on wrong encryption key or non-JSON plaintext). All of these are unhandled, so invalid requests produce opaque 500 errors instead of 400s. Use `safeParse`, wrap decryption, and gate on POST.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential sync does not reset the `invalid` flag on update

When updating an existing credential the handler only sets `key`. If the credential was previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. by the invalid_grant handling in Google/Zoom/Webex), pushing fresh valid keys through the webhook will not re-enable it — the app stays broken for that user even though the sync succeeded. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

HubSpot refresh stores garbage credentials in sync mode

`refreshOAuthTokens` in sync mode returns a `fetch` Response, but the code treats it as a HubspotToken: `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken` is undefined (so `setAccessToken(undefined)` is called) and `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` is undefined, making `expiryDate = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` = NaN. That NaN expiryDate and the empty token are then persisted to the credential via prisma.update, silently corrupting the stored credential and breaking subsequent HubSpot operations.

Lark refresh incompatible with sync response shape

The refresh result is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`, which expects Lark's envelope `{code: 0, data: {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`. The credential-sync endpoint returns a plain `{access_token, expiry}` body with no `code`, so `handleLarkError` will treat it as an error (or `data.data.*` will be undefined), making Lark token refresh fail — or worse, persist credentials with undefined refresh_token/refresh_expires_date — whenever sync is enabled.

MS Teams credential key replaced wholesale, dropping refresh_token and email

In `refreshAccessToken`, `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: responseBody } })` replaces the entire stored key with the refresh response. In sync mode the response only contains access token + expiry, so the persisted credential loses `refresh_token` and `email`. Even though the parent app is the source of truth while sync is enabled, the local credential is silently destroyed: turning sync off, or any code path that hits the local refresh (e.g. a team credential where userId is null and `refreshOAuthTokens` falls back to the local refresh function) will then fail because the refresh token is gone.

No tests for the webhook or the sync-mode refresh paths

The PR adds a new externally-callable endpoint that writes OAuth credentials and rewires token refresh for ~10 apps behind an env flag, with zero automated tests (the checklist explicitly says no tests were added). At minimum: webhook auth/validation/404/200 paths, and refresh behavior for each adapted app with sync both enabled and disabled. Given the number of adapters that break in sync mode (Google, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Zoom), tests would have caught most of these regressions before merge.

Outbound credential sync request carries no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` — no shared secret, signature, or header of any kind. The endpoint's response contains the user's third-party access token, so unless the self-hoster independently protects that URL, anyone who can reach it and guess/enumerate a user id can retrieve arbitrary users' OAuth access tokens. The webhook flow in the other direction is authenticated with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET; this direction should send a comparable secret (e.g. the same webhook secret as a header).

Webex refresh always fails in sync mode: full schema validated against sync response

Unlike Zoom/Office365, the Webex adapter wraps its refresh in `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the response with the full `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires scope (exact literal), token_type, and refresh_token — none of which the credential-sync endpoint returns (it only returns access token + expiry). Every Webex token refresh under sync mode will reject with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". It should use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` like the other adapted apps, or the schema needs to differ per mode.

Webhook secret compared with plain string inequality

`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is not constant-time. For a shared-secret check on an endpoint that can write OAuth credentials, use a timing-safe comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can measure response times.

Zoho CRM refresh throws TypeError in sync mode: fetch Response has no `.data`

In sync mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a `fetch` Response, but the code immediately accesses `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`. A fetch Response has no `.data` property, so this is a TypeError (cannot read properties of undefined) on every Zoho CRM token refresh when credential sync is enabled — the adapter was only adapted for the axios response shape.

prisma is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService

The new token-refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)` (line 96) and the file's import list contains no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a compile-time failure (type-check/build breaks) and, if it somehow ran, a runtime ReferenceError. The newly added refresh flow can never work as shipped.

Attendees are persisted before the calendar update, leaving unrecoverable partial state on failure

This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

retryCount deletion filter is not scoped to SMS and deletes reminders of any method

The deleteMany at the top of the handler now includes an OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` without a `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` condition (the first branch has it, this one does not). Any WorkflowReminder row whose retryCount exceeds 1 is deleted, regardless of whether it is an EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminder. Today only this SMS cron increments retryCount, but any future code path (or a WhatsApp/email retry implementation) that bumps retryCount on a non-SMS reminder will have its rows silently destroyed by the SMS cron job, cancelling reminders that were never related to SMS. The branch should be `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` (and ideally also `scheduled: false`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Comment no longer matches what the deleteMany does

The comment on line 28 says "delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date", but the query now also deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1 regardless of scheduled date or method. A maintainer reading the comment will misunderstand the destructive scope of this query; update the comment to reflect both conditions.

Database update inside the catch block can itself throw, aborting the entire cron run

The new code in the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` before the console.log. If that update throws (e.g., the reminder was concurrently deleted by the deleteMany of an overlapping cron run, or a transient DB error), the exception propagates out of the catch and out of the for-loop, so the handler never sends a response (the caller gets a 500) and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are not processed in this run. Previously the catch only logged, so one bad reminder could not break the loop. The update inside the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or the whole per-reminder processing should be isolated) so a single failure cannot abort the batch.

New retryCount predicate in deleteMany cannot use any existing index

The existing indexes on WorkflowReminder are on bookingUid, workflowStepId, seatReferenceId, [method, scheduled, scheduledDate] and [cancelled, scheduledDate]. The added `retryCount > 1` OR-branch matches none of these, so the periodic deleteMany will degrade to a sequential scan over the WorkflowReminder table on every cron invocation. As this table accumulates rows over time this adds avoidable load; consider adding an index on retryCount or combining the conditions so the method/scheduledDate index applies.

Reminders dropped after two failures with no logging or record of the loss

When the deleteMany removes reminders because retryCount > 1, nothing is logged and no record is kept of which bookings lost their reminders. The per-attempt failures only `console.log` the raw error with no reminder id, so after the row is deleted there is no way to audit that an attendee stopped receiving an SMS reminder. Since two consecutive failures can be caused by a transient Twilio outage (the cron may run every few minutes, so both retries can happen during one incident), reminders can be permanently and silently dropped. At minimum, log the ids/count of deleted retry-exhausted reminders.

Caching tests deleted instead of converted

Public findMany method removed with no caller updates in this PR

Any existing code that constructs `InsightsBookingService` and calls `findMany({ select, ... })` will fail to compile (or fail at runtime in untyped usage), and every caller now has to write its own `$queryRaw` with select/pagination/ordering logic, moving query construction out of the service. Before merging, verify there are zero callers of `findMany` (and of the old constructor option type) across the repo, or update them in this PR.

The PR description explicitly states the tests were never executed ('I encountered test runner configuration issues, so please verify the tests actually pass'). This PR rewrites the authorization logic of an insights service from Prisma where-inputs to hand-built raw SQL fragments (the highest-risk kind of change: security scoping for user/team/org data), and every assertion in this file was changed, yet none of them have been run. Notably, the new assertions compare `Prisma.Sql` objects with `toEqual`, which depends on Prisma's internal representation (own `_strings`/`values` properties), and the final test queries the `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` table, whose population path for bookings created directly via `prisma.booking.create` is unverified. The tests must be executed and confirmed passing before merge rather than delegating verification to the human reviewer checklist.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

The `sed -i ''` form (empty suffix as separate argument) only works on BSD/macOS sed; on GNU/Linux sed (used by most CI and dev containers) it fails with 'can't read : No such file or directory' because the empty string is treated as a filename. true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws generic Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential lookup fails, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In a tRPC procedure this surfaces to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with the message potentially logged as an unexpected server error, rather than a typed TRPCError (e.g. UNAUTHORIZED/NOT_FOUND) like the other handlers in this router use. The client cannot distinguish authorization failure from a real server fault, and the message conflates two different conditions ('not found' vs 'access denied').
