true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale

The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)` instead of the user's locale. The component already calls `useLocale()`; every other localized string in the dropdown respects the user's language, but the date will always render in US English format (e.g. '12/25/2025, 3:00 PM') for all users, which is wrong for non-US locales and inconsistent with the rest of the UI.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status includes expired cache rows

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups CalendarCache rows by credentialId with no `expiresAt` filter. `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows where `expiresAt >= now`, so a cache that expired over a month ago (and is no longer used for availability lookups) will still report a `updatedAt` value. The UI will then show a 'Cache Status' with a stale 'Last updated' time and a 'Delete cached data' action for data that is effectively already gone, telling the user they have an active cache when they don't. The where clause should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to match what the cache actually serves.

Cache status never resolves for delegated (in-memory) credentials

The cache status is looked up with `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connectedCalendars.map(cal => cal.credentialId))`, but for delegated Google Calendar connections the connectedCalendar.credentialId is a synthetic negative in-memory id (see `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` in the cache repository, and the userId+key based lookup in `getCachedAvailability`). CalendarCache rows for delegated users are stored/retrieved keyed by userId, not by that credentialId, so the groupBy on these ids returns nothing and `cacheUpdatedAt` will always be null. Since calendar cache is primarily a team/organization (delegation) feature, the new cache status and delete-cache UI will silently never appear for the main audience of this feature. The status query needs a userId-based path (mirroring `getCachedAvailability`) to cover delegated credentials.

No tests for the new cache-status and delete-cache code paths

This PR adds a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), a new repository method (`updateManyByCredentialId`), a Prisma schema change, and a new UI component, but includes no tests at all: no test for the authorization check in `deleteCacheHandler` (e.g. that a user cannot delete another user's cache by passing an arbitrary credentialId), no test that `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the max updatedAt per credential, and no test for `updateManyByCredentialId`. The PR description itself notes end-to-end verification could not be performed locally, making the missing automated coverage more significant.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status

After a successful `trpc.viewer.calendars.deleteCache` call, only `onSuccess?.()` (the parent's `onChanged`) is invoked. Unlike the sibling `disconnectMutation`, which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`, the deleteCache mutation never invalidates that query. `onChanged` in `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` is the caller's callback and does not refetch the tRPC `connectedCalendars` query, so after deleting the cache the 'Cache Status' row and 'Last updated' timestamp remain visible until a manual page refresh, contradicting the success toast.

dev:cron now depends on unpinned 'npx tsx' that is not a declared dependency

The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not present in devDependencies (only `ts-node` is). With npx, tsx will be fetched/ad-hoc resolved at run time (requiring network access and giving an unpinned version), or fail in offline/restricted environments. If tsx is the intended runner it should be added to devDependencies with a pinned version; also this change is unrelated to the calendar cache feature and shouldn't ride along in this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget; the 'cancelled' DB update can be lost

In handleCancelBooking, the loop `updatedBookings.forEach((booking) => { booking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { ... deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); ... }) })` calls async functions without awaiting them, and the resulting promises are not added to `prismaPromises` (the old code collected the reminder deletes and awaited them via `Promise.all`). `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` now performs a Prisma `update` setting `cancelled: true` (or a `delete` when there is no referenceId), and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` performs a Twilio call plus a DB delete. If the request handler returns before these complete (which is a real risk on serverless), those writes never happen, the reminder stays `scheduled: true` with `cancelled` unset, the cron never picks it up, and the email is sent for the cancelled booking — exactly the bug this PR is meant to fix. The cancellation calls should be collected and awaited before responding.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path has no retry and reintroduces the 100 pending-cancellation limit

`deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminderId, referenceId, immediateDelete=true)` (used on reschedule in handleNewBooking, workflow deletion, and step deletion/edit) immediately POSTs a cancellation to SendGrid and returns without deleting the row or marking it `cancelled: true`. Two problems: (1) if the SendGrid request fails — including failure caused by SendGrid's cap of 100 pending cancellations, which is the very issue this PR is meant to solve, since these immediate cancels can be for emails scheduled up to 72 hours out — the error is only console.logged, the DB row keeps `scheduled: true` and `cancelled` unset, and the cron in scheduleEmailReminders will never retry the cancellation, so the email is sent anyway. (2) Even on success, the workflowReminder row is left in the DB (neither deleted nor marked cancelled), relying on the cron's past-dated `deleteMany` for cleanup. A failure here should at minimum fall back to marking the reminder `cancelled: true` so the cron retries.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellations are deferred to the next cron run, so reminders sending within ~15 minutes are still sent

When a booking is cancelled, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only sets `cancelled: true` and relies on this cron (running every 15 minutes) to actually cancel the SendGrid batch, and only for reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. If a reminder's `scheduledDate` (the SendGrid `send_at`) falls within the window between the cancellation request and the next cron execution (up to 15 minutes later), the cron runs after the email has already been sent, and the SendGrid cancel arrives too late. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` should cancel immediately when `scheduledDate` is within the cron interval (or within the hour, matching the cron's own lookahead) instead of always deferring to the cron.

No tests cover the new cancellation lifecycle

This PR changes the core cancellation semantics of workflow reminders (new `cancelled` flag, deferred cancellation via cron, changed signatures of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now taking `reminderId` and nullable `referenceId`), but adds no unit or integration tests. The reworked paths include several edge cases that are easy to regress: reminders with `referenceId === null`, the `immediateDelete` flag, SendGrid failure handling, and the cron's cancel-then-delete ordering. At minimum, tests for `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`'s three branches and the cron's cancellation query/loop would guard the fix for the issue this PR addresses.

One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole cancellation loop and skips all DB deletes

In the new cancellation block of the cron, the `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop awaits `client.request(...)` inside a single outer try/catch. If any single SendGrid cancellation request throws (invalid batch id, rate limit, network error), the loop aborts immediately: none of the remaining cancelled reminders are cancelled in SendGrid, and — because Prisma query builders are lazy and only execute when awaited — none of the already-collected `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` calls in `workflowRemindersToDelete` execute either. Since the failing reminder stays in the result set every run, it can permanently block cancellation of all reminders that come after it, causing their emails to be sent for cancelled bookings. Wrap the SendGrid request and the corresponding delete in a per-reminder try/catch.

Reschedule reminder cancellation is unawaited and the surrounding try/catch is dead code

In the reschedule branch of handleNewBooking, `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true); ... })` fires async operations (SendGrid cancel request via `client.request`, Twilio cancel, Prisma delete) without awaiting any of them. The surrounding `try { ... } catch (error) { log.error(...) }` can never catch anything because no promise is awaited inside it. If the handler responds before these complete (serverless), the old booking's scheduled email/SMS is never cancelled in SendGrid/Twilio, and the reminder rows are never removed, so reminders for the superseded booking are still delivered. Await the promises (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`) and let the try/catch actually guard them.

Workflow update fires reminder cancellations in unawaited forEach callbacks

In the `update` mutation, `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` (and the same pattern at the removed-event-types loop around line 376 and the deleted-step loop around line 519) never awaits the async callbacks. These calls now perform DB writes (setting `cancelled: true`, deleting rows) and network calls (SendGrid/Twilio), so their outcome is nondeterministic relative to the rest of the mutation and the HTTP response; on serverless the pending work may be terminated before executing. This means reminders for edited steps / disabled event types can remain scheduled and still be sent. Collect and await the promises.

requestReschedule cancels reminders without awaiting the async delete calls

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingToReschedule.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId); ... })` invokes async functions whose promises are discarded. The old code gathered the DB deletes and awaited them with `Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. Now the Prisma write that marks the email reminder `cancelled: true` (or deletes the row when unscheduled) and the Twilio/DB work in `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` may not complete before the mutation returns; on serverless the work can be killed entirely, leaving the reminder active so the attendee still receives a reminder for a booking that was cancelled pending reschedule.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach discards deletion promises; reschedule completes before calendar/video events are deleted

This PR changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})`. `Array.forEach` ignores the returned promises, so nothing waits for the `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls. Consequences: (1) `Reschedule` returns `true` and the reschedule email is sent before the external calendar events and video meetings are actually deleted; on a serverless platform the execution context can be frozen after the response, so the deletions may never run and stale events remain on users' calendars; (2) the surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from these async callbacks, so any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => ...))` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Eager import() calls mean all apps load at import time and failed chunks become unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal evaluates `import("./x")` for every app as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so all ~29 app chunks start loading immediately on any code path that touches appStore — the intended deferral is not achieved for cold starts. Worse, each of these promises is created without a rejection handler: if any app chunk fails to load (a common case on Next.js/Vercel when in-flight requests reference chunks invalidated by a new deploy), the promise for that app rejects before anything awaits it. Since Node 15+, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default, so one app's failed chunk can take down the whole server even though no request ever used that app. To be genuinely lazy and safe, the store should use getters (e.g. `get stripepayment() { return import("./stripepayment"); }`) so the import (and its promise) is only created when actually requested.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests accompany the async conversion of booking create/cancel/reschedule flows

This PR changes the timing semantics of core booking flows: getCalendar/getVideoAdappers/deleteMeeting became async, appStore lookups are now awaited dynamic imports, and several loops became async forEach. None of these paths (calendar event creation/update/deletion, booking cancellation, reschedule request, payment refund) have accompanying tests added or updated in the PR. Given the fire-and-forget issues this conversion introduces (deletion promises not awaited), at minimum regression tests for cancel/reschedule asserting that external deletions are awaited before the handler resolves should be added before merging.

Recurring-cancellation branch pushes into apiDeletes after awaits, racing the final Promise.all

In the recurring-event cancellation branch (lines 458-470), the PR adds `await getCalendar(credential)` inside a `forEach(async (credential) => {...})` that pushes results into `apiDeletes`. Because forEach does not await the callbacks, the handler continues to line 652 (`await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`) while the forEach callbacks are still suspended at their awaits; the Promise.all therefore snapshots a `apiDeletes` array that may be empty or partial, and the cancellation API response is returned before the calendar deletion calls have even been started. The attendee/bookingReference DB deletes then complete while external calendar events are still pending, so a subsequent process freeze or crash leaves external calendars with events that no longer exist in Cal.com. Convert the forEach to an awaited `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` and push the deletion promises before awaiting them.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not a promise, in the paid-booking branch

In the paid-booking cancellation path, line 617 does `await apiDeletes;`. `apiDeletes` is an array of promises (populated by `deleteMeeting`/`calendar?.deleteEvent` calls which this PR makes asynchronous), not a promise itself, so awaiting it resolves immediately without waiting for any of the contained deletions. The comment says the code deliberately deletes booking references, but the external calendar/video deletions should still be awaited before returning, e.g. `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)`. Since this PR touches the surrounding async deletion logic, this is the place to fix it.

getCalendarCredentials creates getCalendar promises that are never awaited for non-calendar variants

`getCalendarCredentials` now stores the un-awaited `getCalendar(credential)` promise in the returned objects, and only `getConnectedCalendars` awaits `item.calendar`. Two problems: (1) `getCalendar(credential)` is called for every app credential before the `app.variant === "calendar"` filter, so for non-calendar variants a promise is created and immediately discarded — if the app's dynamic import rejects, this is an unhandled rejection (fatal by default on Node 15+); (2) the exported return type of `getCalendarCredentials` silently changed from `calendar: Calendar | null` to `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>`, a breaking contract change for any caller outside this file that accesses `.calendar` directly (they will now hold a Promise where they expect a service instance). Await the promise inside this function or only construct it for calendar-variant apps, and document/verify all callers.

requestReschedule fires-and-forgets calendar/video deletions via async forEach

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, this PR changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => ...)` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)`. forEach does not await the async callbacks, so the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule-request email and webhooks and returns the response while the old calendar events (`calendar?.deleteEvent`) and video meetings (`deleteMeeting`) are still being — or have not yet begun to be — processed. There is also no try/catch or `.catch()` on these promises, so any deletion failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. In a serverless environment the function can be suspended after the response, leaving the old calendar events permanently in place. Collect the promises with `.map()` and `await Promise.all(...)` before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is a duplicate of `start`, so slots overrunning the host's working hours are not rejected

In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start` and never accounts for the event length (it should be derived from slotEndTime). As a result the condition `end > workingHour.endTime` only rejects slots that *start* after the working hours end; a slot that starts before closing but extends past it (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 30 minutes before the fixed host's end of day) passes the check and is offered even though the host is not available for the full duration. This is precisely the class of bug (fixed hosts bookable when unavailable in round-robin) that this PR claims to fix, so the fix is undermined for end-of-day slots.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === , so the equal-start/end override branch is dead code

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two Dayjs object references, which is always false regardless of the underlying times. The intended check — detecting overrides where start equals end (the "unavailable" full-day marker) — never executes, and such overrides instead fall through to the window comparisons, where a slot starting exactly at the override timestamp is returned as available. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `.valueOf()`/`.getTime()`.

false_positives.candidate:
No test for the headline fix: round-robin with a fixed host having a date override

The PR description states the primary fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected in round-robin events (issue #8207), but no test covers that scenario: all team-event tests use empty `hosts` or non-fixed configurations, and the only new test added is the timezone variant of a single-user personal event (which also only differs by 30 minutes of offset, both on the same side of the override window). Additionally, there is no test combining a date override with an existing booking, which is exactly the interaction that the new `dateOverrideExist` short-circuit in checkIfIsAvailable gets wrong (slots inside an override are never checked against busy times). Both scenarios should be covered before merging.

Optional override.timeZone silently falls back to the server's local timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` uses the new optional `timeZone` field of TimeRange. If a caller supplies date overrides without `timeZone` (the type explicitly allows this), `dayjs.tz(..., undefined)` falls back to the server's local timezone, and the computed organizer UTC offset — and therefore every converted override start/end — will be wrong with no error. getSlots already receives `organizerTimeZone` as a parameter; that should be the fallback (or the field should be required) so a missing value cannot silently corrupt slot times.

Override date is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared against a UTC date

The date gate compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` (UTC mode), but `dayjs(date.start)` is in the server's local timezone, so its `.format()` renders the date in the server's timezone. On any deployment where the process timezone is not UTC, the two dates disagree for times near midnight, causing date overrides to fail to match (slots wrongly unavailable via the fall-through, or wrongly available). The left side should be built with `dayjs.utc(date.start)` so both dates are rendered in UTC.

Overrides shifted across midnight by the timezone conversion are applied to the wrong invitee day

activeOverrides is selected by checking `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (the raw stored wall-clock-UTC value) against the invitee's day window, but the override times are then converted to invitee-local minutes-of-day. When the offset shift moves the override across a midnight boundary, those minutes belong to a different calendar day than the one being built. Example: an organizer in UTC+13 with an override stored at 23:00–23:30 UTC and an invitee in UTC-11 yields an offset of -1440 minutes; the invitee-local times are 23:00–23:30 on the *previous* day, but the filter attaches the override to the invitee day containing the stored 23:00 UTC, so availability is added on the wrong day (and the user's normal working hours for the wrong day are removed).

Slots inside a date override bypass the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot's date matches a date override and the slot falls inside the override window, the code hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` and returns before evaluating the `busy` array. That means for any host that has a date override on a given day, existing ACCEPTED bookings and external calendar events that fall inside the override window are completely ignored, and those slots are returned as available. An attendee can then book over an existing booking (double booking / data integrity). The busy check must still run for slots that lie within a date override; only the working-hours check should be skipped for override days.

Working-hours check treats days outside the host's schedule as available

The new working-hours filter uses `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { if (workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())) { ... } })`. If the slot's weekday is not included in any of the host's working-hours entries (e.g. a Saturday slot for a Mon-Fri host), the callback returns undefined for every entry, `find` returns undefined, and the code falls through to the busy-only check — i.e. the slot is considered available. For round-robin events the aggregate availability is the union of hosts, so slots generated from another host's Saturday availability will pass this fixed-host check even though the fixed host never works that day. A day with no matching working-hours entry must be treated as unavailable, not available.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth 'state' is a static per-provider value, so the CSRF/state check provides no real protection

OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` and validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic value derived from the pipeline/provider name (the tests hard-code the same state, `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, across different users, organizations, and sessions), so it is identical for every user of the deployment. Any user who starts their own GitHub install flow sees this value in the authorize redirect URL and can therefore forge a valid callback for any other user's pipeline. Concretely: an attacker obtains their own OAuth `code` (authenticating as themselves), then gets a victim's browser to hit the setup URL with that code plus the known state; the token exchange succeeds in the victim's pipeline and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, after which the installer-identity check passes and the integration is linked. The state must be a per-pipeline/per-session random nonce (stored in pipeline state and compared on callback), not a shared constant, for the check described in the PR description to be meaningful.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata

GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. However, `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is set, so Integrations can legitimately exist without a "sender" key (e.g. created through the pipeline when the installation webhook never supplied a sender, or legacy rows). For such installations this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. The lookup should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Installer verification is skipped when the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration

The new user-identity check (comparing `github_authenticated_user` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs on the branch where the Integration row already exists. That row is created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; if the webhook is delayed or lost, `Integration.objects.get` raises DoesNotExist and dispatch calls `pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all, and `build_integration` later creates the Integration without a sender. This means the security control this PR is meant to add can be bypassed by simply racing the webhook (or by webhook delivery failure), which is a common condition in practice. The verification (or an explicit 'installation not yet registered, retry' failure) should also apply on the DoesNotExist path, or the pipeline should wait/retry until the webhook-created Integration is visible.

Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info and token exchange produce a 500 instead of the error page

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP call to GitHub's /user endpoint and raises ApiError on any non-2xx response (e.g. revoked token, GitHub 5xx, secondary rate limit); `safe_urlopen` for the token exchange can likewise raise on connection errors. These exceptions propagate out of the pipeline view and result in an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page shown for the other failure modes. The calls should be inside the try/except (or a separate one) that falls back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 / 'installation could not be found' path

The test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, i.e. that build_integration's IntegrationError on a GitHub 404 is surfaced. After the change it asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` because the second request uses a state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the flow fails at the state check and the `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for `/app/installations/<id>` is never exercised. The renamed test now effectively duplicates a state-mismatch test, and the 'installation could not be found' regression path (IntegrationError raised in build_integration on GitHub 404) has no coverage. A separate test with a valid state and a 404 stub should be added, along with a dedicated test for the state-mismatch case.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time, not per instance

The task `sync_assignee_outbound` now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, and the abstract method `sync_status_outbound` in the same class was explicitly updated to declare `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires

In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring says "one process per shard" but the shipped default is one process total

The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the new --flusher-processes CLI option in sentry/consumers/__init__.py defaults to 1, so the default (and typical) deployment runs a single process handling all shards in round-robin groups. The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

Per-process restart counters are never reset, so lifetime restarts eventually crash the consumer

self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

Redis memory usage is summed across per-shard-group buffers, potentially double-counting clusters

submit() now computes Redis backpressure by extending memory_infos from every buffer in self.buffers and summing used/available across all entries. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources

In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

_create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code

The method _create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere; restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive() -> _create_process_for_shards() directly. Dead code with a misleading name that suggests per-shard restarts exist; it should be removed to avoid confusion.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
A sentry_sdk transaction is started per message in each worker, nested inside ResultProcessor's own transaction

OrderedQueueWorker.run() wraps every single work item in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). This creates one Sentry transaction per consumed message (per worker), which at uptime-results throughput means a very large transaction ingestion volume and per-message tracing overhead. It is also redundant: ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 48) already starts its own transaction per result, so every message now produces nested/duplicate transactions. Existing modes (serial/parallel) only instrument the processor, not one transaction per message. The per-item transaction should be removed or sampled.

Claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is false: failures are still marked complete and committed

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 254) guarantees offsets are only committed after successful processing, but OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises (lines 144-149), and ResultProcessor.__call__ additionally swallows all exceptions itself. A message whose processing fails is therefore treated as done, its offset becomes committable, and after the commit it is permanently skipped — a silent drop of failed messages with no retry and no DLQ. This is the opposite of what the docstring (and the PR's own error-handling test, see separate finding) states. Either the guarantee should be implemented (e.g. don't complete the offset, or route to a DLQ/retry) or the docstring must be corrected to state that failed messages are skipped.

Code requires Python 3.13+ (queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown) with no guard

The implementation uses queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception, both of which were only added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError (breaking close()/terminate() and therefore consumer shutdown), and queue.ShutDown does not exist so the except clauses in the worker would themselves fail. If the repository still supports Python < 3.13 in CI or deployment targets, this breaks at runtime; if 3.13 is now the minimum, this is fine, but it's worth confirming since nothing in the PR documents or enforces the requirement.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued messages are abandoned

In shutdown(), worker.shutdown = True is set for all workers before q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker that is mid-item will check `while not self.shutdown` after finishing and exit, leaving any remaining items in its queue unprocessed; queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not block until the queue is drained in this construction (and task_done() is never called anyway). The docstring says 'Gracefully shutdown all workers', but in-flight backlog is discarded. Because those offsets were added but never completed they won't be committed, so the messages are replayed on restart (at-least-once), but the shutdown is not actually graceful: to drain, only the queue shutdown should signal termination and workers should keep processing until get() raises ShutDown.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit under backlog

FixedQueuePool creates each queue via queue.Queue() with no maxsize, so submit() never blocks. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately to Arroyo, which keeps polling and handing over messages, so if the worker threads fall behind, both the in-memory queues and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound (offsets can't be pruned until they're committed, and commits can't advance past the backlog). This is a memory leak / OOM risk exactly in the slow-consumer scenario this PR is meant to address. It also contradicts the class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') — no backpressure exists. Pass maxsize to queue.Queue (or bound the number of in-flight messages) so put() blocks the Arroyo thread when queues fill.

Strategy close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, causing silent message loss after any Kafka rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and shuts down every queue.Queue. But the FixedQueuePool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. Arroyo's StreamProcessor rebuilds the processing strategy on every rebalance (it calls close() on the old strategy, then create_with_partitions again on the same factory). After the first rebalance, the new strategy is constructed around the already-shut-down pool: queue_pool.submit() calls work_queue.put() which raises queue.ShutDown, that exception is caught by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325), which marks the offset as completed. The commit loop then advances the committed offsets past those messages. Result: after any routine consumer-group rebalance (deploys, consumer joins/leaves), every subsequent message on that consumer is silently dropped while offsets are committed as if processed. The strategy must not tear down factory-scoped resources (e.g. the pool shutdown should only happen from ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or the pool should be recreated per strategy).

queue_depth gauge is missing a worker/queue tag, so workers overwrite each other's values

OrderedQueueWorker emits metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize()) with only an 'identifier' tag — no worker_id or queue index. Every worker reports the same metric name and tags with a different value (its own queue's depth), so the last writer wins and the gauge reflects an arbitrary single queue rather than per-queue depths. Since it's emitted after every processed item, the value is also effectively random. Add a worker_id/queue tag or drop this gauge in favor of the aggregate total_queued gauge emitted in poll().

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, racing the workers

The test submits 10 items and immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. The three worker threads can process all items within microseconds (the result processor just appends to a list), so by the time get_stats() is called the queues may already be empty, making the assertion flaky. The assertion should either be removed, or the pool should be paused/verified deterministically (e.g. block the result processor on an event until stats are captured).

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behavior and only passes by racing the 1s commit loop

The test asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that no commit happens after a processing failure. But the implementation completes offsets even when result_processor raises (the worker's finally block), so once both messages finish the commit loop will commit offset 102 for the partition on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it breaks out of its wait loop as soon as queues are empty (within ~0.3s) and asserts before the commit thread's 1.0s wait elapses; on a slow CI machine or if the commit interval fires earlier, the assertion fails. The test should either assert the real behavior (failed messages' offsets are committed) or the implementation should be changed to match the intended behavior.

This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
