) present in the English source yields an empty message list. Without such a passing-case test, a regression in the normalization/unescaping pipeline that makes the checker flag every file with HTML (e.g. the "" stripping or the unescapeHtml4 round-trip) would not be caught by the suite.

error-invalid-multivalued-size changed to Java ChoiceFormat syntax in the admin console JS message bundle

The keycloak.v2 admin messages bundle is loaded by the admin console's JS i18n layer (i18next), not by Java MessageFormat. Replacing "value(s)" with "{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}" means the admin UI cannot render this validation message: the choice expression will be displayed literally to administrators, and single-brace {0}/{1}/{2} placeholders are not interpolated by i18next's default {{...}} syntax. The MessageFormat variant should only live in the server-side theme bundles (themes/src/main/resources/theme/base/admin/messages and themes/src/main/resources-community/...), not in this JS resource.

error-invalid-multivalued-size now uses single-brace placeholders and Java ChoiceFormat in an i18next-consumed bundle

This file is consumed by the React account console via i18next, which is why every other entry uses double-brace interpolation (e.g. "error-username-invalid-character='{{0}}' contains invalid character." on line 14) and <0>-style Trans component tags (line 13). The new value "Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}." uses single braces, which i18next does not interpolate, and Java MessageFormat choice syntax, which i18next cannot evaluate. If this key is rendered in the account UI, users will see the literal text "{0}", "{1}" and "{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}" instead of a formatted message. The Java-side MessageFormat version belongs in themes/src/main/resources-community/theme/base/account/messages (where {0} is correct), not in the keycloak.v3 JS bundle.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor null-checks grantType twice; rawTokenId is never null-checked

In the `AccessTokenContext` constructor, `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` is invoked twice (lines 72 and 73) and the second one is mislabeled "Null rawTokenId not allowed". The intended check for `rawTokenId` is missing, so an AccessTokenContext with a null rawTokenId can be constructed and will only fail later (e.g., NPE during string concatenation in `encodeTokenId`). Fix the second requireNonNull to check `rawTokenId`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and wrong substring index, so it never validates the grant shortcut

The new `isAccessTokenId` matcher contains `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — two bugs. First, the condition is inverted: it returns false (no match) when the shortcut *equals* the expected value, so even with a correct index the matcher would reject valid tokens and accept wrong-grant tokens. Second, the index is wrong: the grant shortcut occupies characters 4-6 of the 6-char prefix (session type 0-2, token type 2-4, grant type 4-6), so it should be `substring(4, 6)`, not `substring(3, 5)` which extracts e.g. "ta" from "onrtac". Because of the wrong index, the equality check essentially never fires for real tokens, so `expectCodeToToken`, `expectRefresh`, `expectDeviceCodeToToken` and `expectAuthReqIdToToken` only assert that the ID has two colon-separated parts and the second is a UUID — the grant-type encoding added by this PR is completely unverified by the testsuite. Any regression in the token ID encoding would go unnoticed. Additionally, `items[0].substring(3, 5)` can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException for IDs with a shorter prefix instead of returning false.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Decoder assumes fixed 2-character shortcuts but the SPI javadoc invites longer shortcuts, producing undecodable token IDs

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` hard-requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 chars each for session type, token type and grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. However, `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` is documented as "usually like 3-letters shortcut" with no length constraint, and third parties can implement it. A custom grant whose shortcut is not exactly 2 characters will encode fine (`encodeTokenId` just concatenates), but the resulting token ID (e.g., 7-char prefix) will be rejected by `getTokenContextFromTokenId` with an exception — tokens minted by Keycloak itself become undecodable. Either enforce/validate the 2-char length when populating the factory maps in `postInit`, or make the decoding format length-agnostic (e.g., split on fixed delimiters as in the original longer `st.on_tt.rt_gt.ac:` format).

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType catches bare RuntimeException and never asserts the exception type

`testIncorrectGrantType` wraps the call in `try { ... } catch (RuntimeException iae) { }`, so the test passes for *any* runtime failure — including a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` or NPE from an unrelated bug in the parsing code — not just the intended `IllegalArgumentException` about the unknown grant shortcut. It should assert the exception type (and ideally the message), e.g., `Assert.fail` in try and `catch (IllegalArgumentException e)` specifically. Also note the test relies on the 'ac' shortcut being absent from the hand-built maps, which makes it sensitive to map-setup drift rather than testing the real factory wiring; there is no test that exercises `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit` against the actual grant providers, nor any test of `getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`.

false_positives.candidate:
Duplicate-shortcut validation only runs at startup; late-registered grants can silently corrupt the shortcut maps

`postInit` validates shortcut/ID uniqueness once by comparing map sizes, and `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` later add entries for grant factories not present at startup (comment: "in case new grant type was deployed") without re-checking for collisions. If a hot-deployed grant uses a shortcut (or ID) already mapped, `grantsByShortcuts.put(...)` silently overwrites the existing entry, so two distinct grant types map to the same shortcut and previously issued token IDs are misinterpreted (wrong grant type returned from `getTokenContextFromTokenId`). At minimum the lazy-population paths should detect the collision (e.g., refuse to overwrite an existing different mapping) instead of silently clobbering.

New abstract method getShortcut() on the pluggable OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI breaks existing custom grant implementations

`getShortcut()` was added as an abstract (non-default) method to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` interface in `server-spi-private`. OAuth 2.0 grant types are a deployable extension point (factories are registered via META-INF/services), so any existing third-party grant-type provider will fail to load/compile after upgrade with "does not define getShortcut()". To preserve compatibility, the method should have a sensible `default` implementation (e.g., deriving from the ID or returning a marker that the encoder maps to the UNKNOWN shortcut) instead of forcing every existing implementation to be updated.

Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) was removed

The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` of the public static class `OAuth2GrantType.Context` was deleted as part of this change. This class lives in the `server-spi-private` grants package that custom grant-type implementations compile against; any external code that used the copy constructor will break at compile time on upgrade. The removal is not required by the rest of the change (the new `grantType` field could be copied along), so it should either be kept (also copying `grantType`, which would arguably be more correct than re-reading form params) or the break should be explicitly acknowledged.

getTokenContextFromTokenId throws on any colon-containing but malformed/unknown prefix instead of degrading to UNKNOWN

The decoder is lenient for legacy IDs without ':' (returns UNKNOWN context) but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for IDs that contain ':' with an unknown or wrong-length prefix. Since the token ID (`jti`) originates from externally presented tokens — e.g., tokens issued by another Keycloak deployment with a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider` (the SPI explicitly exists to allow alternate encodings), a future format change, or foreign IDPs whose `jti` happens to contain a colon — any consumer of this method (introspection, userInfo, the planned session-lookup optimization from #37662) can be made to fail with a runtime exception by presenting an otherwise perfectly valid, signature-verified token. Decoding of a descriptive prefix should degrade gracefully to UNKNOWN (as already done for the no-colon case) rather than throw, since the encoded info is an optimization hint, not a security invariant.

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Optional.get() without presence check now depends on user-storage getCredentials() consistency

The bean still calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` unconditionally, but the Optional now comes from `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()`, which requires the user storage to (a) implement `CredentialLookupProvider.getCredentials` and (b) return credential data in the exact `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` JSON schema. A storage that reports `isConfiguredFor(recovery-authn-codes) == true` (which is all `configuredFor()` checks) but returns no/foreign-format credential from `getCredentials()` — e.g. the raw code JSON that `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential` stores in `credentialData` — will cause a `NoSuchElementException` or a Jackson parse failure while rendering the login page, turning a misconfigured storage into a 500 error. Handle the absent/malformed case explicitly instead of `.get()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
removeStoredCredentialById() is called with a user-storage credential ID it cannot delete

After successful validation, when `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` returns a federated credential and `allCodesUsed()` is true, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. That ID belongs to the user storage, not Keycloak's local credential store (for the test provider it is even regenerated fresh on every `getCredentials()` call via `createFromValues`, and may be null), and `CredentialInputUpdater` offers no delete-by-id for storages (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.disableCredentialType` ignores recovery-authn-codes entirely). Consequence: an exhausted federated recovery-code credential is never removed, the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-added on every login while the dead credential keeps `configuredFor` true, and passing an unresolvable/null ID risks an exception from the credential store inside the authentication flow.

false_positives.candidate:
Extending the frozen 4.8.3 backwards-compatibility provider undermines the test's purpose

The class javadoc states this provider was created with Keycloak 4.8.3 and that "Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider" — its whole point is to verify current Keycloak against an unchanged, old provider. This PR substantially modifies it (adds recovery-authn-codes support to supportsCredentialType/updateCredential/isValid/isConfiguredFor, adds getCredentials), so the suite no longer exercises a genuinely legacy provider. Also, `getCredentials()` can NPE via `getMyUser(user)` returning null (the sibling methods `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `isConfiguredFor` guard against this), and on deserialization failure it silently drops the credential from the stream, making `getCredentials()` and `isConfiguredFor()` inconsistent for the same user.

Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and can be reused indefinitely

When the recovery-authn-codes credential lives in a user storage (the scenario this PR enables), `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...)` delegates to the storage provider's `CredentialInputValidator.isValid`. Unlike the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`, whose isValid() marks the matched code as used, there is no framework path that tells the storage to invalidate the used code, and the reference implementation added in this PR (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid`, which does a plain `anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`) demonstrates that the same recovery code passes validation again on every login. One-time use is a core security property of recovery codes. Either the framework needs a consumption/update callback for storages, or the storage SPI contract (and the test provider plus a reuse-rejection test) must require storages to invalidate used codes; as merged, a federated user's recovery code is effectively a permanent credential.

Regenerating recovery codes does not remove a pre-existing credential in the other store

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` either stores the new codes in the user storage (`userStorageCreated == true`) or in Keycloak's local DB, but never removes an existing recovery-authn-codes credential from the store it did not write to. A user who previously had recovery codes in the local DB (e.g. created before federation or while the storage did not support the type) keeps that old credential fully valid after regenerating: `credentialManager().isValid()` can still accept the old local codes, so regeneration fails to invalidate the previous code set. Additionally `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` prefers the federated credential while validation may succeed against the local one, so the UI can prompt with a code number from a different credential than the one actually consumed. Both stores should be reconciled (old credential deleted) when new codes are created.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null for a deleted group, inconsistent with the adapter's contract elsewhere

When the underlying group has been deleted concurrently, `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns null instead of throwing. Every other path in GroupAdapter that fails to load the delegate (`getDelegateForUpdate()` at line 61 and `isUpdated()` at line 74) throws `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`, so this change introduces a third, silent behavior for the same condition. Returning a null Long is risky: GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() is not documented to return null, and any caller that unboxes it (e.g. `== 0` comparisons) will now get an NPE at a distance from the real cause. In GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount it results in `representation.setSubGroupCount(null)`, leaking a null count into the admin REST response rather than signaling the group is gone. Returning 0L or throwing the same IllegalStateException used by the rest of the class would keep the contract consistent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the race being tested can be missed or exceptions lost

In `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti`, after `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty, without joining the reader thread. Two consequences: (1) an HTTP request that is in flight when the flag is set can still fail after the assertion has already run, so a real regression can pass the test; (2) the thread is left running (it is not a daemon thread), leaking it and its admin-client connections for the remainder of the JVM/test-suite run. The test should signal completion, then `thread.join()` (with a timeout) before asserting. Additionally, since the thread is only started and never synchronized before deletions begin, it may not execute at all before all groups are deleted, in which case the test passes vacuously without ever exercising the concurrent read/delete path it was written to cover.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE on concurrent group deletion still possible in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The PR fixes the NPE only in `getSubGroupsCount()`, but the sibling methods at lines 256, 262, and 268 (`getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer)`, `getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer)`, `getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer)`) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier` wraps `getGroupModel()`, which returns null when the group has been deleted, so the exact same concurrent-delete scenario that produced issue #40368 (a cached group being read while another thread removes it) will still produce an NPE on these paths. The fix should apply the same null handling (whatever is chosen for getSubGroupsCount) to all delegating methods that dereference `modelSupplier.get()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Metric tag typo: wait_produce timer uses "shards" while sibling metrics use "shard"

The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` in the same function use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the test's own monkeypatch

test_basic monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a lambda returning None at the top of the test, which patches the time module globally. The later `time.sleep(0.1)` added "to give flusher threads time to process after drift change" therefore sleeps for zero time, so the comment is wrong and the intended wait never happens. The assertion `(msg,) = messages` still depends on a race: the flusher thread must observe the new current_drift and complete producing before step.join() sets the stopped flag and the thread exits its `while not stopped.value` loop. The test can flake or silently stop covering the flush path; it should use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr` scoped to the flusher module, or a real sleep via a saved reference).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to return immediately, making the subsequent `time.sleep(0.1)` call a no-op instead of actually waiting.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires

In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires causes the code to skip calling `terminate()` on the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources

In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

Redis memory usage is summed across per-shard-group buffers, potentially double-counting clusters

submit() now computes Redis backpressure by extending memory_infos from every buffer in self.buffers and summing used/available across all entries. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

Per-process restart counters are never reset, so lifetime restarts eventually crash the consumer

self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

_create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code

The method _create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere; restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive() -> _create_process_for_shards() directly. Dead code with a misleading name that suggests per-shard restarts exist; it should be removed to avoid confusion.

Docstring says "one process per shard" but the shipped default is one process total

The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the new --flusher-processes CLI option in sentry/consumers/__init__.py defaults to 1, so the default (and typical) deployment runs a single process handling all shards in round-robin groups. The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

fetch_error_details misaligns error IDs with nodestore results via zip on dict values

In fetch_error_details, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id, and the code builds ErrorEvent objects with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. The result is that error titles, messages, and timestamps can be attributed to the wrong event id (the `id` field of ErrorEvent), and the filtering `if data is not None` does not fix the offset. Downstream, `get_request_data` sorts error_events by timestamp (`error_events.sort(key=lambda x: x["timestamp"])`) and `gen_request_data` compares `error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] < event.get("timestamp", 0)`, which mixes str and float operands and raises TypeError in Python 3 (both in the sort when a defaulted 0.0 is present, and in every comparison against a float breadcrumb timestamp). This will make the summarize-breadcrumbs endpoint raise a 500 for any replay that has associated error events. Timestamps should be parsed to floats (e.g. via `datetime.fromisoformat` / `Event.timestamp`) before use.

The success/failure distinction should be based on `data.success` (or the summary being non-null), not just on the feedback count.

OAuth 2.0 grant types are a deployable extension point (factories are registered via META-INF/services), so any existing third-party grant-type provider will fail to load/compile after upgrade with "does not define getShortcut()". To preserve compatibility, the method should have a sensible `default` implementation (e.g., deriving from the ID or returning a marker that the encoder maps to the UNKNOWN shortcut) instead of forcing every existing implementation to be updated.

Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) was removed

The removal is not required by the rest of the change (the new `grantType` field could be copied along), so it should either be kept (also copying `grantType`, which would arguably be more correct than re-reading form params) or the break should be explicitly acknowledged.

getTokenContextFromTokenId throws on any colon-containing but malformed/unknown prefix instead of degrading to UNKNOWN

The decoder is lenient for legacy IDs without ':' (returns UNKNOWN context) but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for IDs that contain ':' with an unknown or wrong-length prefix. Since the token ID (`jti`) originates from externally presented tokens — e.g., tokens issued by another Keycloak deployment with a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider` (the SPI explicitly exists to allow alternate encodings), a future format change, or foreign IDPs whose `jti` happens to contain a colon — any consumer of this method (introspection, userInfo, the planned session-lookup optimization from #37662) can be made to fail with a runtime exception by presenting an otherwise perfectly valid, signature-verified token. Decoding of a descriptive prefix should degrade gracefully to UNKNOWN (as already done for the no-colon case) rather than throw, since the encoded info is an optimization hint, not a security invariant.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError; the 'advanced feature' can never work

The negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 877-882) slices the queryset as queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — the ORM raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" — so this branch always errors instead of returning results. The code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Since the cursor string ("value:offset:is_prev") is client-controlled and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets, any client hitting this endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a crafted cursor such as "0:-5:0" triggers an unhandled exception / 500. There is no valid input for which this feature works.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` attempts to slice a Django queryset with negative offsets, which is not supported by Django and raises an `AssertionError`.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the endpoint's datetime sort key and will 500

The endpoint orders by "-datetime" but OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits Paginator's key handling: get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838-840) computes int(math.floor(value)) on a datetime, which raises TypeError, and value_from_cursor (line 842) returns the raw millisecond integer from the cursor and passes it into a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to a bigint ("datetime <= 1234567890123"), which Postgres rejects with an operator-does-not-exist error. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class never converts between datetimes and the ms-epoch cursor representation. Consequently, any request with optimized_pagination=true from a superuser or globally-access member against a non-empty audit log will raise an unhandled exception and return a 500 instead of a page of results.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `get_item_key` in the paginator attempts to call `math.floor` on a `datetime` object (due to `order_by=-datetime` in the audit logs endpoint), which raises a `TypeError`.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change claims to support negative offsets but still crashes for is_prev cursors, and silently changes behavior otherwise

The new line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for forward cursors; for previous-page cursors a negative client-supplied offset still flows into queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises Django's "Negative indexing is not supported" AssertionError, contradicting the comment that negative offsets are now allowed. For forward cursors, the clamp silently changes existing behavior: a malformed cursor like "0:-50:0" that previously errored now returns the first page, and the unclamped negative offset is still passed into build_cursor via the original cursor object, so the generated next/prev cursors can carry bogus negative offsets forward. Either validate the offset (reject negatives) or handle both directions consistently.

Client-toggled paginator class breaks cursor portability between requests

The paginator implementation now depends on a per-request query parameter (optimized_pagination) plus who is calling, so the same endpoint issues cursors with different semantics depending on the request. A cursor produced by DateTimePaginator encodes a ms-epoch value that DateTimePaginator converts back to a datetime for its WHERE clause; if the same cursor is replayed against OptimizedCursorPaginator (same user toggles the flag, or a superuser shares a link with a non-superuser), the raw integer is compared against the timestamp column and the request errors or returns wrong rows. Pagination cursors are supposed to be opaque tokens valid for the endpoint; making their interpretation depend on a mutable flag violates that contract and will produce intermittent 500s/incorrect pages for clients.

OptimizedCursorPaginator's non-negative path is a verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result and provides no performance benefit

Apart from the broken negative-offset branch, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates BasePaginator.get_result line for line (same build_queryset, same slicing, same cursor building). The PR is titled 'Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs', but for every working request the query plan and workload are identical to the existing DateTimePaginator path — no index hints, no query reduction, nothing. The class adds ~100 lines of duplicated pagination logic (which will drift from the base implementation, as it already has with the misleading comments) with no measurable gain, while the only genuinely new behavior (negative offsets) is a guaranteed exception. The feature should either be justified with a real optimization or removed.

Admin-gated 'advanced features' flag is security theater with a misleading safety comment

The gating `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` combined with the comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" implies the advanced path exposes something extra that permissions must guard. It does not: pagination offsets never bypass queryset filters, and the only 'advanced' capability (negative offsets) is an error path in the ORM. Meanwhile, the flag does create a real inconsistency: a superuser and a regular owner hitting the same URL with the same cursor get different paginator semantics (and, per the other findings, a 500 vs. working results). If there is no concrete capability being gated, remove the flag and the misleading comments rather than implying there is a privileged pagination mode.

No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds a new paginator class, modifies the shared BasePaginator.get_result used by many endpoints, and adds a new request-parameter-driven branch on a production endpoint, but includes no tests. At minimum it needs: (1) a regression test that BasePaginator.get_result behavior is unchanged for existing cursors (including the new max(0, offset) clamp), (2) tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator covering forward/prev cursors, which would have immediately caught the datetime TypeError and the Django negative-slicing AssertionError, and (3) endpoint tests covering the optimized_pagination flag for both authorized and unauthorized users.

Comment-only change documents behavior that does not exist

The only change in cursors.py is a comment asserting "Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios" above `self.offset = int(offset)`. The line of code is unchanged — Cursor has always accepted any int, and nothing in this file enables or handles negative offsets. Worse, downstream consumers (build_cursor's _build_next_values/_build_prev_values) compute new offsets via `offset + limit` / `offset - limit` with no lower bound, so negative offsets propagate into emitted cursors. The comment misleads readers into thinking negative-offset support was added and validated here; it should be removed or replaced with a note that offsets are unvalidated.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the coarse BuildIndex lock allows concurrent duplicate builds of the same index key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the whole function, which (accidentally) serialized builds. Now the lock only guards the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write, but the caller-side check in searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go, which its own TODO admits has no per-key dedup) is a check-then-act: two concurrent callers (e.g. a gRPC Search request and the watch-event goroutine in handleEvent, or two simultaneous Search requests for a cold namespace) both get nil from GetIndex and both run a full build. The last writer wins in the cache, so the losing bleveIndex becomes orphaned while the watch goroutine may still be writing documents into it - searches then run against a different index instance and silently miss those updates. It also double-counts IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds, and for disk-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) two concurrent bleve.New calls on the same directory will make one fail with 'path already exists'. A per-key singleflight or keyed mutex is needed to preserve the old serialization semantics for the same key while allowing different keys to build in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same race condition in `BuildIndex` caused by moving `b.cacheMu` to only guard the final cache write, allowing concurrent duplicate builds for the same key.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed across init errgroup workers

In searchSupport.init, each group.Go closure assigns to the function-scoped `err` variable (`_, _, err = s.build(...)`) and increments `totalBatchesIndexed` from multiple worker goroutines with no synchronization. With WorkerThreads > 1 this is a data race (caught by -race) and makes both the error value observed by `return err` and the `namespaced_indexed` span attribute unreliable. Each goroutine should use its own local error variable and the counter should be atomic (or aggregated from group results). This function is the direct target of this PR's concurrency changes, so the race is worth fixing alongside them.

Search event goroutine panics when the storage watch channel is closed

The goroutine started in init does `v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)` with no ok-check. The SQL backend's poller closes the stream channel when the backend is stopped (backend.Stop -> b.cancel() -> poller returns -> close(stream)), e.g. during server shutdown. After close, the receive returns nil immediately in a hot loop, and handleEvent dereferences evt.Type on the nil event, panicking and crashing the process. It should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }` (and ideally also honor a cancellable context). Since this PR makes init run unconditionally at construction, every server with search configured now runs this goroutine and will hit the panic on shutdown.

Trace propagation fix was missed in bleve BuildIndex

The PR's stated goal is to fix trace propagation by keeping the span context (done in search.go init/build and sql/backend.go GetResourceStats), but bleveBackend.BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`, discarding the child span context. The builder callback and everything it calls (storage.ListIterator, document building) therefore run with the parent context, so their spans are not children of the BuildIndex span and the BuildIndex trace is missing all its nested work. It should be `ctx, span := ...` like the other fixed call sites.

Constructor leaks context and goroutines when Init fails

NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) and returns nil on error, but never calls the cancel() created for the server's internal context. If init fails partway (e.g. search.init succeeded and started its watch goroutine, then initWatcher failed), the cancellable context is leaked and the search watch goroutine - which runs on a detached context.Background() - is never cleaned up. The error path should invoke s.cancel() (and ideally s.Stop) before returning.

Postgres integration test skipped with an unexplained failure instead of being fixed

The PR adds a permanent skip for postgres ('test not working with postgres in Drone. Works locally.') to the only integration test covering the storage-server target. This removes CI coverage for a supported database exactly when the initialization model changes from lazy per-request to blocking at construction - a change that could plausibly behave differently on postgres (e.g. timing/migration ordering during InitTestDB). The root cause should be diagnosed and fixed, or at least an issue linked, rather than silently dropping postgres coverage; otherwise a real postgres regression from this change will go undetected.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() permanently kills the shared queue pool, causing silent message loss after any Kafka rebalance

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and shuts down every queue.Queue. But the FixedQueuePool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. Arroyo's StreamProcessor rebuilds the processing strategy on every rebalance (it calls close() on the old strategy, then create_with_partitions again on the same factory). After the first rebalance, the new strategy is constructed around the already-shut-down pool: queue_pool.submit() calls work_queue.put() which raises queue.ShutDown, that exception is caught by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325), which marks the offset as completed. The commit loop then advances the committed offsets past those messages. Result: after any routine consumer-group rebalance (deploys, consumer joins/leaves), every subsequent message on that consumer is silently dropped while offsets are committed as if processed. The strategy must not tear down factory-scoped resources (e.g. the pool shutdown should only happen from ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or the pool should be recreated per strategy).

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure and memory grows without limit under backlog

FixedQueuePool creates each queue via queue.Queue() with no maxsize, so submit() never blocks. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately to Arroyo, which keeps polling and handing over messages, so if the worker threads fall behind, both the in-memory queues and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound (offsets can't be pruned until they're committed, and commits can't advance past the backlog). This is a memory leak / OOM risk exactly in the slow-consumer scenario this PR is meant to address. It also contradicts the class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') — no backpressure exists. Pass maxsize to queue.Queue (or bound the number of in-flight messages) so put() blocks the Arroyo thread when queues fill.

A sentry_sdk transaction is started per message in each worker, nested inside ResultProcessor's own transaction

OrderedQueueWorker.run() wraps every single work item in sentry_sdk.start_transaction(). This creates one Sentry transaction per consumed message (per worker), which at uptime-results throughput means a very large transaction ingestion volume and per-message tracing overhead. It is also redundant: ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 48) already starts its own transaction per result, so every message now produces nested/duplicate transactions. Existing modes (serial/parallel) only instrument the processor, not one transaction per message. The per-item transaction should be removed or sampled.

Claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is false: failures are still marked complete and committed

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 254) guarantees offsets are only committed after successful processing, but OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises (lines 144-149), and ResultProcessor.__call__ additionally swallows all exceptions itself. A message whose processing fails is therefore treated as done, its offset becomes committable, and after the commit it is permanently skipped — a silent drop of failed messages with no retry and no DLQ. This is the opposite of what the docstring (and the PR's own error-handling test, see separate finding) states. Either the guarantee should be implemented (e.g. don't complete the offset, or route to a DLQ/retry) or the docstring must be corrected to state that failed messages are skipped.

queue_depth gauge is missing a worker/queue tag, so workers overwrite each other's values

OrderedQueueWorker emits metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize()) with only an 'identifier' tag — no worker_id or queue index. Every worker reports the same metric name and tags with a different value (its own queue's depth), so the last writer wins and the gauge reflects an arbitrary single queue rather than per-queue depths. Since it's emitted after every processed item, the value is also effectively random. Add a worker_id/queue tag or drop this gauge in favor of the aggregate total_queued gauge emitted in poll().

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown before draining, so queued messages are abandoned

In shutdown(), worker.shutdown = True is set for all workers before q.shutdown(immediate=False). A worker that is mid-item will check `while not self.shutdown` after finishing and exit, leaving any remaining items in its queue unprocessed; queue.shutdown(immediate=False) does not block until the queue is drained in this construction (and task_done() is never called anyway). The docstring says 'Gracefully shutdown all workers', but in-flight backlog is discarded. Because those offsets were added but never completed they won't be committed, so the messages are replayed on restart (at-least-once), but the shutdown is not actually graceful: to drain, only the queue shutdown should signal termination and workers should keep processing until get() raises ShutDown.

test_stats_reporting asserts total_items > 0 immediately after submit, racing the workers

The test submits 10 items and immediately asserts stats['total_items'] > 0. The three worker threads can process all items within microseconds (the result processor just appends to a list), so by the time get_stats() is called the queues may already be empty, making the assertion flaky. The assertion should either be removed, or the pool should be paused/verified deterministically (e.g. block the result processor on an event until stats are captured).

Code requires Python 3.13+ (queue.Queue.shutdown / queue.ShutDown) with no guard

The implementation uses queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception, both of which were only added in Python 3.13. On any earlier interpreter, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError (breaking close()/terminate() and therefore consumer shutdown), and queue.ShutDown does not exist so the except clauses in the worker would themselves fail. If the repository still supports Python < 3.13 in CI or deployment targets, this breaks at runtime; if 3.13 is now the minimum, this is fine, but it's worth confirming since nothing in the PR documents or enforces the requirement.

Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError

When `enable_advanced_features` is on and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySet slicing explicitly rejects negative indices ("AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported"), so this path raises instead of paginating. The inline comments ("The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level") are factually wrong: negative slicing does not work on querysets, and permissions have nothing to do with slicing. true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes on datetime sort keys

OptimizedCursorPaginator copies Paginator.get_item_key, which does `int(math.floor(value))` on the item's sort-key attribute. The only caller of this class (organization_auditlogs.py) paginates with order_by="-datetime", so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises TypeError. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes to epoch-ms; the optimized class also lacks DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor's ms-to-datetime conversion, so a page-2 cursor would compare a timestamp column against a raw float in SQL. Net effect: any request with `optimized_pagination=true` will 500 (page 1 in get_item_key via build_cursor, page 2+ in the where clause).

false_positives.candidate:
enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`, but `Endpoint.paginate` in sentry/api/base.py has a fixed keyword signature (paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, max_limit, desc, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits) and constructs the paginator with only those arguments — it does not forward arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`. Unless the base method was also changed (it is not in this PR), this call raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, 500-ing every request that passes `optimized_pagination=true` with the required privileges. Even if the intent is for the flag to reach the paginator, `BasePaginator.__init__` would then need to receive it.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds ~100 lines of new paginator code (OptimizedCursorPaginator), modifies BasePaginator.get_result's offset handling for every existing paginator, and adds a new request-driven code path to the audit logs endpoint, yet includes zero tests: no unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator (including its negative-offset branch), no tests that BasePaginator behavior is unchanged for existing paginators, and no endpoint tests for the `optimized_pagination` parameter (including the authorization gate). Any of the crash modes described in the other findings would have been caught by a single basic test invoking the new code path.

Unrelated audit-log pagination feature mixed into a span-buffer PR with no rationale

This PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and its description is just "Test 2", yet roughly half the diff introduces an unrelated, undocumented API behavior (`optimized_pagination=true` query param enabling a different paginator for superusers/global-access members) to the audit logs endpoint. This makes the change unreviewable as a unit and unrollbackable independently: a revert of the span-buffer work would either take the API change with it or require manual surgery. The audit-log changes should be split into their own PR with a real description, and if kept, the new query param should be documented/validated rather than read ad-hoc from request.GET.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, splitting deep segments

The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a trace's redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:*` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop now exits without resolving the root, `set_span_id` stays at the 1000th intermediate node, and the span is buffered under a partial key — silently splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments. This is a 10x reduction in the supported chain depth with no accompanying metric, log, or test, so the failure mode is invisible in production.

zpopmin eviction can drop the root span, producing segments with no is_segment span

Eviction removes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. Nothing protects the root/segment span from eviction: if the root span's end timestamp is among the 1000 smallest (possible for out-of-order or async spans), its payload is popped while the `span-buf:hrs:*` flag is still set and the segment is still flushed under the root's key. The flushed segment then contains no span with `is_segment=true`, and every remaining span is stamped with a `segment_id` referring to a span that isn't in the payload — breaking the segment contract for downstream consumers. Evicted spans are also silently dropped with no metric, so the data loss is unobservable.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit

The Python-side enforcement of `max_segment_spans` (the check in `_load_segment_data` with its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log) was removed in favor of eviction inside the Lua script, but the `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` constructor parameter was left in place and is now never read. Meanwhile the Lua script hardcodes its own limit of 1000. Consequence: any deployment that configures `max_segment_spans` via options gets silently ignored behavior, and the off-by-one (1001 vs 1000) plus the dead parameter will confuse future readers. The limit should be passed to the script (e.g., as an ARGV) or the parameter removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The new factory helper wraps its logic in two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks, so any structural problem with `contexts` (or an invalid sample rate value) is silently ignored and the event is stored without a sample rate, making downstream upsampled-count assertions pass or fail for the wrong reason. false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count() is only registered in DiscoverDataset but is enabled for the errors dataset

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to DiscoverDataset's function_converter, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in error_upsampling.py returns True whenever the request's dataset is `sentry.snuba.errors`, causing `_get_event_stats` to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` for errors-dataset requests. If the errors dataset's query builder does not include `upsampled_count` in its own function converter (the errors dataset is a separate dataset class and only discover.py was modified), those requests will fail with an invalid/unknown function error for every allowlisted project. This path is also untested — all new endpoint tests exercise the default (discover) dataset.

Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` filters as error-focused queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A discover query like `!event.type:error` (excluding errors, i.e. returning transactions/other events) contains the substring, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True and `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. For non-error events `sample_weight` is not populated (the helper itself documents that sample_weight doesn't exist for transactions), so the returned count will be wrong (typically 0) instead of the real event count. The check needs to parse the query's filter conditions rather than substring-match, or at least reject negated terms.

Endpoint tests don't isolate the 60s eligibility cache, making them order-dependent

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches its result under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds in the shared cache, and nothing in the new test class clears it. Django test transactions roll back org/project id sequences, so consecutive test methods in this class reuse the same org id and project ids. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches `True` for that key; if `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` (which mocks a partial allowlist and asserts un-upsampled counts of 1) runs afterwards in the same process with a real (non-dummy) cache backend, it reads the cached `True`, applies upsampling, and asserts against counts of 10 — failing. setUp should delete the cache keys (or the helper should be patched), and there are no tests at all for `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself, its caching, or `invalidate_upsampling_cache`.

The docstring of `invalidate_upsampling_cache` says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but no code in this PR (option update handler, signal, or task) invokes it. In practice the only consistency mechanism is the 60-second TTL, so the function is misleading dead code; either wire it into the option-change path or remove it and document that only the TTL bounds staleness.

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites y-axis columns; `equations=self.get_equation_list(organization, request)` is passed through untouched. A widget using yAxis `count()` plus an equation such as `equation(count() / count_unique(user))` on an allowlisted error query will get an upsampled `count()` series next to an equation computed from the raw sampled `count()`, producing internally inconsistent numbers (e.g. an "events per user" ratio computed from a count 10x smaller than the displayed count). Either rewrite count() inside equations or reject/skip upsampling when equations are present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenates components with '_' without escaping, allowing key collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with single underscores and no delimiter escaping. Two different requests can therefore map to the same cache entry, e.g. name="a_b" with parent="c" produces the same key as name="a" with parent="b_c". Today Grafana UIDs are alphanumeric so this is unlikely to trigger, but user/service-account identifiers and future actions are not guaranteed to be underscore-free, and a collision produces a wrong deny verdict for a different resource. Use a separator that cannot appear in the components (or length-prefix/hash the components).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: `userPermDenialCacheKey` constructs cache keys by joining components with underscores without escaping, which can cause key collisions and incorrect permission denial cache hits if any of the components contain underscores.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denial entries block the DB fallback and override newer grants, reintroducing the bug this PR fixes

Once a Check is denied, the result is written to permDenialCache with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) and every subsequent Check for the same (user, action, resource, parent) returns deny immediately, without consulting permCache or the database. This defeats the PR's own fix in two ways: (1) if a Check for a newly created dashboard races the permission insert (or hits a lagging read replica, which is the normal deployment for legacysql in cloud), the denial is pinned for 30s and the creator is locked out of the dashboard they just created — the exact symptom the PR claims to fix; (2) when permissions are granted after a denial was recorded (admin grants access, folder moved), the user stays denied for up to 30s even though the database now allows it. Additionally, the denial cache is consulted *before* the positive permCache, so a denial entry written at time T wins over a permCache entry refreshed at T+20 with allowing scopes. There is also no invalidation of denial entries when permissions change. Consider checking the denial cache only after a positive permCache/DB lookup fails, or deleting the denial entry whenever a fresh DB query allows.

Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous:0 and render:0 share entries

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, UserUID, action, name and parent — but not the identity type. The subject "anonymous:0" (TypeAnonymous) and "render:0" (TypeRenderService) both parse to UserUID "0", so they produce identical denial keys. Because the denial cache is checked before any identity-type handling, an anonymous user's denial for e.g. dashboards:read on dashboard X (anonymous users can lack read scope on specific dashboards) will cause the render service to be denied rendering of X for up to 30s, even though getRendererPermissions unconditionally grants wildcard read to renderers — and vice versa, a renderer denial of a write action can deny an anonymous user who has that action via a custom Viewer-role permission. Include the identity type in the denial key.

Denial cache has unbounded cardinality (one entry per user×action×resource×parent)

Unlike permCache, which is bounded per (namespace, user, action), the denial cache creates a distinct entry for every denied (user, action, resource, parent-folder) combination. In the standalone server deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the underlying cache may be a shared external cache (e.g. Redis). A user — or an attacker — enumerating resource names via Check requests will write one denial entry per unknown/unauthorized resource per user, each held for 30s. With batch/Check-heavy clients this can flood the shared cache with garbage entries and cause memory/eviction pressure on the cache cluster. Consider bounding the denial cache (e.g. only caching denials for resources known to exist, using an LRU, or per-user entry limits).

No test covering access after a permission is granted post-denial (the issue this PR fixes)

TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, DB fallback on miss, DB fallback on stale cache, and deny-from-denial-cache, but there is no test for the critical ordering: a denial entry written before a permission was granted (or before the resource existed) versus a later DB/permCache state that allows. Given that the PR's stated purpose is 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created', a test should pin down the expected behavior when a Check for the not-yet-permitted resource precedes the creation/grant — currently that test would fail (deny wins), which suggests the intended semantics are not covered anywhere.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth 'state' is a static per-provider value, so the CSRF/state check provides no real protection

OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` and validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic value derived from the pipeline/provider name (the tests hard-code the same state, `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, across different users, organizations, and sessions), so it is identical for every user of the deployment. Any user who starts their own GitHub install flow sees this value in the authorize redirect URL and can therefore forge a valid callback for any other user's pipeline. Concretely: an attacker obtains their own OAuth `code` (authenticating as themselves), then gets a victim's browser to hit the setup URL with that code plus the known state; the token exchange succeeds in the victim's pipeline and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, after which the installer-identity check passes and the integration is linked. The state must be a per-pipeline/per-session random nonce (stored in pipeline state and compared on callback), not a shared constant, for the check described in the PR description to be meaningful.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same vulnerability as the golden comment: that `pipeline.signature` is a static value being used as the OAuth `state`, whereas it should be a per-request/per-session random nonce to prevent CSRF.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata

GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. However, `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is set, so Integrations can legitimately exist without a "sender" key (e.g. created through the pipeline when the installation webhook never supplied a sender, or legacy rows). For such installations this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. The lookup should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: unconditionally accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` which raises a KeyError when the 'sender' key is missing from metadata.

false_positives.candidate:
Installer verification is skipped when the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration

The new user-identity check (comparing `github_authenticated_user` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs on the branch where the Integration row already exists. That row is created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; if the webhook is delayed or lost, `Integration.objects.get` raises DoesNotExist and dispatch calls `pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all, and `build_integration` later creates the Integration without a sender. This means the security control this PR is meant to add can be bypassed by simply racing the webhook (or by webhook delivery failure), which is a common condition in practice. The verification (or an explicit 'installation not yet registered, retry' failure) should also apply on the DoesNotExist path, or the pipeline should wait/retry until the webhook-created Integration is visible.

Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info and token exchange produce a 500 instead of the error page

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP call to GitHub's /user endpoint and raises ApiError on any non-2xx response (e.g. revoked token, GitHub 5xx, secondary rate limit); `safe_urlopen` for the token exchange can likewise raise on connection errors. These exceptions propagate out of the pipeline view and result in an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page shown for the other failure modes. The calls should be inside the try/except (or a separate one) that falls back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 / 'installation could not be found' path

The test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, i.e. that build_integration's IntegrationError on a GitHub 404 is surfaced. After the change it asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` because the second request uses a state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the flow fails at the state check and the `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for `/app/installations/<id>` is never exercised. The renamed test now effectively duplicates a state-mismatch test, and the 'installation could not be found' regression path (IntegrationError raised in build_integration on GitHub 404) has no coverage. A separate test with a valid state and a 404 stub should be added, along with a dedicated test for the state-mismatch case.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() skips invalidating the internalId cache entry when the alias key is not cached

In remove(alias), when the alias cache key is not in the session's invalidation set and there is no cached entry under the alias key, no invalidation is registered for the provider's internalId (the else-branch only calls registerIDPInvalidation when `cached != null`). An IDP can, however, be cached under its internalId via getById() without ever having been looked up by alias, so after remove() completes, a subsequent getById(internalId) can return the already-deleted identity provider from cache. This staleness matters even more now that getForLogin() and getByOrganization() resolve cached list entries through session.identityProviders().getById(id). The fix is to always invalidate the internalId (e.g. registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) in both branches, guarding for null). Note this hole pre-exists but the method was reworked in this PR and the new list caches depend on getById freshness.

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares an org-aware wrapped original against the raw updated model

In update(), the "original" model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns the anonymous wrapper whose isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled (createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel). The "updated" model is the raw caller-supplied model whose isEnabled() is the stored value. The skip decisions in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate therefore depend on the organization's runtime enablement state rather than only on stored IDP attributes. The fix is to re-read `entryPointAssetsCache` after taking the write lock (or before assigning at line 69) and return the cached value if it is now non-nil in non-Dev mode.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context, so they are canceled as soon as the request completes

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to LegacyStorage derives its context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The handler returns immediately after the unified-storage write, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the request finishes. Because the legacy write runs asynchronously, it will frequently observe an already-canceled parent context and fail with 'context canceled' (or the 10s timeout never even matters). The result is that the legacy store is silently not written for many (potentially most) operations, which defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use a detached context, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (plus the timeout), or a background context carrying only the logger.

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. This records a legacy-storage duration/latency observation for a failure that happened in the unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics: legacy dashboards will show errors and latencies that never touched legacy storage, and no storage-side failure is recorded for the failing call. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`, as done in Delete/DeleteCollection.

Update records storage failures under the legacy metric

Same defect as in Create: a unified-storage failure is attributed to the legacy store in the metrics (wrong metric name, wrong latency sample, wrong error count). It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

The previous implementation logged an error when the legacy write failed ('unable to create object in legacy storage', etc.). The new goroutines only record a Prometheus metric (`recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`) and discard the error entirely; nothing is ever written to the log. Operators investigating a divergence between unified and legacy storage will have no log evidence of when or why the legacy write failed (timeout, conflict, validation error). The goroutines should at minimum log the returned error, e.g. `if err != nil { log.Error(err, "legacy write failed") }` (using a detached context for the logger).

In Create, the goroutine passes the caller's `obj` (the same runtime.Object that `d.Storage.Create` was called with and whose result the handler serializes to the client) to `d.Legacy.Create`. Storage Create implementations commonly mutate the passed object in place (setting UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, generation). While the apiserver is serializing the response from the unified write, the legacy write goroutine can be mutating the same object concurrently — a data race that can produce corrupted response bodies or runtime panics under `-race`. The object passed to the legacy goroutine should be a deep copy, and the same consideration applies to `objInfo` in Update (the legacy Update runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against shared state while the handler may still be using it).

Mode 3's defining behavior is that writes go to unified storage synchronously and to legacy storage asynchronously. None of the new tests assert that Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection were invoked (e.g. via m.AssertExpectations or eventually-style waiting), so a regression that drops the legacy write entirely would still pass. The tests should wait for the async write (e.g. a channel/signaled mock or polling on mock call counts) and then assert the legacy call happened.

Pagination math is off by one, producing an empty phantom last page

`totalPages` is computed as `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1`. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (e.g. 100 members, limit 50), totalPages becomes 3 even though there are only 2 pages, so `showingLast` never becomes true on the real last page. Combined with the `next` action clamping `offset` to `user_count` (line 33: `Math.min(offset + limit, user_count)`), clicking next on the last real page sets offset to 100 and fetches an empty third page (currentPage 3/3 with no members). totalPages should use Math.ceil and offset should be clamped to the largest valid page start, not to user_count.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: clamping the `offset` to `user_count` in the `next` action (combined with the off-by-one pagination calculation when `user_count` is a multiple of `limit`) results in an empty phantom last page when `offset` equals `user_count`.
