false_positives.candidate:
PUT /admin/groups/:id silently drops membership updates from existing API consumers

The old `update_put` action processed `params[:group][:usernames]` to replace group membership, and `update_patch` handled `params[:changes]` add/delete deltas (the PATCH route is also removed from config/routes.rb). The new `update` action only handles name/alias_level/visible, yet still returns success_json for a PUT containing a `group[usernames]` payload. Any existing API client, plugin, or script that manages memberships via PUT /admin/groups/:id will now get a 200 success while the membership change is silently ignored, with no error and no deprecation warning. Membership mutations should either still be accepted or rejected explicitly so consumers notice.

create action ignores the alias_level parameter sent by the client

The frontend Group#create (app/assets/javascripts/discourse/models/group.js) posts `asJSON()` which includes `alias_level`, but the server's create action only assigns `name` and `visible`. When an admin creates a new group with an alias level other than the default selected in the form, that setting is silently discarded and the group is created with alias_level 0; the admin only sees the correct value if they notice and save again. `group.alias_level = params[:alias_level].to_i if params[:alias_level].present?` (as done in update) is missing from create.

Public group members page now truncated to 50 members with no pagination UI

Previously the public members endpoint returned all members for non-automatic groups (limit was only applied, with a default of 200, to automatic groups). Now `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` caps every group at 50 members, and the public group page (app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs) has no pagination controls, so the members list is silently cut off at 50 for larger groups. This is a user-visible regression: members 51+ are unreachable on the public group page. Either the template needs pagination like the admin page, or the default limit for the public route must not truncate.

Unvalidated limit/offset parameters on the public members endpoint

`limit` and `offset` are taken directly from params with no bounds validation. A client can request `/groups/<name>/members.json?limit=1000000` forcing serialization of the entire membership in one response (a cheap enumeration/DoS vector on large groups), and negative values (e.g. `limit=-1` or `offset=-5`) are passed straight into `.limit()/.offset()` which produces invalid SQL and a 500 error on PostgreSQL. The values should be clamped (e.g. limit between 1 and a max cap, offset >= 0).

Save error handler crashes on non-JSON error responses

In the `save` action's rejection handler, `$.parseJSON(e.responseText).errors` assumes the error body is always JSON containing an `errors` key. If the server returns a non-JSON body (e.g. a 500 HTML error page, a proxy timeout page, or an empty response), `$.parseJSON` throws and the user sees neither the real error message nor any feedback — the button just re-enables via .finally with no alert. The handler should fall back to a generic message when parsing fails or `errors` is absent.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
should_block? performs a DB write inside model validation and double-counts attempts

BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and saves the record, and it is invoked from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. from inside User's validation. In UsersController#create, `user.valid?` is called at line 168 and then `user.save` runs the same validations again, so every blocked signup attempt increments match_count twice (or more if valid? is called elsewhere, e.g. change_username also calls valid?). Side-effectful writes during validation are also surprising: any code calling valid? on a user with a changed email mutates the blocked_emails table. The statistics update should happen once, outside the validation path (e.g. in the controller when the error is actually returned), or use a guard so it only runs once per attempt.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same core problem: the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (or `should_block_email?`) predicate method has unexpected side effects because it mutates the database (updating statistics/match_count) during a read/validation check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and can be bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with the raw email string, and there is a unique index on the email column as-is. User emails are not normalized to lowercase on assignment (UsersController#create passes params[:email] straight into the model, and mixed-case emails can exist since email uniqueness is also case-sensitive here). A user whose address was blocked as 'spammer@example.com' can register as 'Spammer@Example.com' and the lookup returns no row, completely bypassing the block. The lookup (and the unique index) should compare downcased emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is case-sensitive, which allows blocked users to bypass the restriction by altering the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
change_email flow bypasses the blocked-email check entirely

The new EmailValidator only runs on the User model when `email_changed?`. The change_email action never assigns user.email; it creates an email_token with the new address (`user.email_tokens.create(email: lower_email)`) and the address is later attached to the user when the token is confirmed (EmailToken.confirm), which typically uses update_attribute/save paths that skip validations. As a result, an existing user can switch their account email to any blocked address and receive mail there, defeating the purpose of the blocked-email feature. The blocked/whitelist/blacklist check must also be applied in change_email (and at token creation/confirmation), not only in the model's email-changed validation.

Read-modify-write race on match_count loses increments under concurrency

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the counter in Ruby and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same value and both write value+1, losing one increment (and clobbering last_match_at updates with a stale AR object). Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` instead.

Any server-side email error permanently marks the email invalid with the wrong message

On a failed account creation, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into rejectedEmails whenever the response contains any `errors.email` key. That includes errors unrelated to the email being unacceptable, e.g. 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist 'not allowed' error. The emailValidation computed property then shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') ('invalid email address') for that address, which is misleading for a taken or blocked address (the server message is 'is not allowed.' / 'has already been taken'). The client should key off the specific error type, or at least surface a message matching the server's reason. The email also stays rejected for the lifetime of the controller even if the underlying condition changes.

Validator spec stubs out the behavior under test; no integration coverage for users or the controller contract

The only spec for EmailValidator stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the actual model wiring (User's `validates :email, email: true`, the migration, and the BlockedEmail lookup) is never exercised end-to-end: nothing proves that a user with a blocked email fails validation and cannot be created. There is also no spec for the new UsersController#create failure payload (`errors` hash and `values` hash) that the new frontend code in create_account_controller.js depends on, so a rename or shape change of that JSON would not be caught. Add a spec that fabricates a blocked email, builds/creates a User with it, and asserts the validation error, plus a controller spec asserting the errors/values keys on failed create.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
-ms-align-items is not a real vendor-prefixed property

The new `align-items` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's flexbox prefixes are `-ms-flex-align` (already emitted on the line above) and, for the modern syntax, the unprefixed `align-items` (also already emitted). This declaration is always invalid and silently dropped, adding dead code to the generated stylesheet for every flex-aligned rule. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the exact same problem as the golden comment: that `-ms-align-items` is not a real property and that `-ms-flex-align` is the correct Microsoft prefix for flexbox alignment.

false_positives.candidate:
.small-action button { float: right } is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container

This change makes `.small-action` a flex container (`@include flexbox()` at the top of the rule), but the nested `button { float: right; }` at line 309 was left unchanged. Floats on flex items are ignored by the flexbox spec, so the float has no effect. Previously the button (e.g. the small-action buttons in the topic stream) was pushed to the far right edge of the row; now it will sit immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text with default spacing, since no `margin-left: auto` was added to replace the float. The trailing `clear: both` on `.small-action` (line 312) is likewise dead. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right-edge alignment.

margin-left: auto on .panel does not right-align in the legacy flexbox implementations the mixins target

The new `flexbox()` mixin deliberately emits the 2009 syntax (`display: -webkit-box`, `display: -moz-box`) and the IE10 syntax (`display: -ms-flexbox`), but the right-alignment of the header panel relies solely on `margin-left: auto` on `.panel`. Auto-margin packing in flex containers is a feature of the final flexbox spec: IE10's `-ms-flexbox` implementation notoriously ignores auto margins for alignment, and the 2009 `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` spec provides `box-pack` instead. So in exactly the older browsers these prefixes were added for, the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge and will sit next to the site title, breaking the header layout. Either add a `box-pack: end`-based fallback or accept dropping the ancient-prefix output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing question mark, so the include guard is never called by AMS

ActiveModel::Serializers only invokes the conditional-include hook named `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark) — every other guard in this file follows that convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, `include_card_image_badge?`). The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no `?`), so it is dead code: the serializer never calls it. Consequently, when a user has no website, the JSON still contains `"website_name": null` instead of omitting the key, and the intended `website.present?` guard has no effect. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main problem in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` suffix required by ActiveModel::Serializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue regarding string mutation (`'.' << website_host`), the core bug is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 users' website info to anonymous visitors

The serializer lists `website` in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor). The new `website_name` attribute is not added to that list, so for those same users the API still serializes `website_name`, which now includes not just the host but the full URL path (e.g. `example.com/private-page`). This defeats the purpose of hiding `website` for untrusted profiles and leaks information the site explicitly intends to hide. `website_name` must be added to `untrusted_attributes` alongside `website`.

Untrusted-attributes spec list was not updated to cover website_name

The `untrusted_attributes` list in the 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' context still contains only `bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background`. Since this PR adds a new attribute derived directly from `website`, `:website_name` should be added to that list so the spec verifies it is suppressed for restricted users. As written, the existing test suite would not catch the leak of `website_name` (host plus full path) for TL0 profiles viewed anonymously — adding it would make the spec fail today and force the fix.

URI(website.to_s) is re-parsed up to three times per serialization

The `website_name` method calls `URI(website.to_s)` once for the host (line 138) and again for the path (lines 143, 146, 149), meaning the URL string is parsed up to three times for every user serialized. This runs for every user in any payload using UserSerializer (user pages, staff lists, etc.). Parse the URI once into a local variable and reuse it for both `host` and `path`.

Query string and fragment are silently dropped from the displayed path

`website_name` builds the display string as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding the query string and fragment. A user whose website is `http://example.com/profile?user=42` on a same-domain instance will see `example.com/profile` in their profile, which links correctly (the href uses the full `website`) but displays a URL that does not correspond to the link target. If showing the complete URL is the goal, the query/fragment should be preserved (or this limitation acknowledged).

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check via `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` is a weak substring match

The postMessage handler validates the sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it accepts any message whose origin string appears anywhere in the configured discourseUrl. Because it is a substring (not prefix/exact) match, an origin that happens to be contained in the URL string passes; e.g. a discourseUrl of `http://discourse.example.com` accepts an event from origin `http://d` (host `d`) or any origin that is a substring of the URL. The consequence is limited to setting the iframe height today, but the correct check is an exact/parsed comparison (e.g. compare `e.origin` against the URL's `protocol + '//' + host`), since future message types would inherit the flaw.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same vulnerability: the origin validation using `indexOf` is a weak substring match that can be bypassed by an attacker.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer-based authorization is trivially spoofable, allowing unbounded job enqueueing and forced fetching

Access control for /embed/best relies solely on the Referer header matching SiteSetting.embeddable_host. Any non-browser client can set an arbitrary Referer header, so anyone on the internet can hit the endpoint and cause `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` for arbitrary embed_url values. The TopicRetriever throttle is only 60 seconds per exact URL string, so an attacker can vary the URL (query strings, paths) to enqueue an unbounded number of jobs, each of which causes the Discourse server to make an HTTP request to the embeddable host (a limited but real SSRF/abuse vector) and, when feed polling is enabled, synchronously executes the entire Jobs::PollFeed run inside the job. Rate limiting at the controller level and/or a global cap on retrieve jobs is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the same core security vulnerability: relying on the `Referer` header for access control/validation is flawed because `Referer` headers can be easily spoofed. While the golden comment also mentions `X-Frame-Options` and the candidate elaborates on the downstream impact (unbounded job enqueueing), they point to the exact same underlying access control flaw in the code.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: URL interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute in the 'imported from' footer `contents << "...#{url}..."` interpolates the embed URL directly into HTML that is later stored via the raw_html cook method and rendered with `raw`. The `^https?://` regex check on line 11 does not exclude single quotes, `>` or other markup characters that can appear in a URL's path/query (e.g. `http://embeddable-host/?x='>`). This allows attribute breakout and markup injection into the stored post. The URL should be HTML-escaped (and the href properly quoted) before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment mentions two issues: a potential NoMethodError if contents is nil, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML. The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact XSS vulnerability from the unescaped URL interpolation in `TopicEmbed.import`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view fails to render

Line 6 closes the header if/else with `<%- end if %>`, which ERB compiles to the Ruby fragment `end if ` — a modifier `if` with no condition, a syntax error. Every render of the embed view (the success path when a topic exists) will raise ActionView::Template::Error / SyntaxError and return a 500 to the embedding site, making the whole feature non-functional in the topic-found case. It should be `<%- end %>`. The controller specs don't catch this because `TopicView` is stubbed with a mock, so the template never renders against a real topic view.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: using `end if` instead of `end` in an ERB template, which causes a Ruby syntax error at render time.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil `i.content` (or a feed error) crashes the whole poll, and retry is disabled

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has `content`; RSS feeds that only provide `description` (or ATOM entries with only a summary) will raise NoMethodError on nil, aborting the entire `poll_feed` run partway through — items after the offending one are never imported. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until the next hourly run, which will fail at the same item. `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is likewise unguarded, so a transient network error kills the run. Guard for missing content (fall back to `i.description`) and rescue per-item/feed-level errors.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue directly identifies the exact same bug as the golden comment: `i.content.scrub` assumes `i.content` is present, which will raise a NoMethodError on nil for RSS feeds that only provide `description`, and suggests falling back to `i.description`.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript allows XSS on the Discourse origin

The embed layout renders `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` with the raw Referer header inserted into a JavaScript string literal without escape_javascript/html escaping. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter only validates that the referer's *host* equals SiteSetting.embeddable_host, so an attacker making a direct HTTP request (where the Referer header is fully attacker-controlled, e.g. `http://<embeddable_host>/', alert(document.cookie), '`) can break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary script in a page served from the Discourse origin. This is a reflected XSS; the value must be escaped with `j()`/escape_javascript before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: the unescaped interpolation of `request.referer` into JavaScript, which leads to a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported RSS content is stored as raw HTML with skip_validations and rendered with `raw`, enabling stored XSS

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`, which makes `Post#cook` return the raw content verbatim (no markdown/sanitization pipeline). The RSS path in `Jobs::PollFeed` passes `i.content` (fully controlled by whatever the feed at feed_polling_url contains) straight into import — unlike `import_remote`, which at least runs the content through ruby-readability's tag/attribute whitelist. `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` then renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. A compromised or malicious feed entry containing `<script>` or `onerror=` handlers is stored and executed on the Discourse forum and on every page that embeds the comments iframe. The feed content needs sanitization (e.g., Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw HTML.

Discussion replies rendered with `raw post.cooked` include any HTML users managed to post

The embed view renders each post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. While normal posts go through the cooking/sanitization pipeline, this view bypasses all of the markup filtering Discourse normally applies when displaying cooked content (e.g., the whitelist applied elsewhere), so any HTML that survives into `cooked` for any post in the topic — including raw_html posts created by other import paths or plugins — is executed verbatim in a frame that is served from the Discourse origin with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL`. Combined with the raw_html import path this widens the XSS surface; cooked output should be passed through the same sanitization used by the main topic renderer.

Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can leave the throttle key without a TTL, permanently blocking retrieval

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key exists with no TTL and never expires, so that embed_url is throttled forever — the topic is never retrieved and the embed shows the loading page indefinitely. Use a single atomic command (e.g., `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` available via the redis gem, or a Lua script) so the expiry is always set.

PostCreator jobs are enqueued inside the wrapping transaction, before the TopicEmbed row commits

`TopicEmbed.import` wraps `creator.create` in `Topic.transaction` and only creates the `TopicEmbed` record *after* the post is created. PostCreator's `enqueue_jobs` (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs while still inside this outer transaction. If the subsequent `TopicEmbed.create!` fails — most plausibly in the race where two concurrent retrieve jobs for the same embed_url both pass the `where(embed_url: url).first` check and the second hits the unique index — the whole transaction rolls back, but the already-enqueued Sidekiq jobs referencing the rolled-back post/topic are not un-enqueued, and `TopicTrackingState.publish_new` messages have already been published on MessageBus for a topic that never committed. The unique-index race should also be handled (rescue RecordNotUnique / create the embed first or use find-or-create).

`feed_key` is dead code — the modified/ETag check it hints at was never implemented

The `feed_key` method builds a Redis key (`feed-modified:<sha1 of feed url>`) but nothing in the class ever reads or writes it. Either the conditional-fetch logic was dropped accidentally, in which case the key is misleading dead code, or the intent was to skip polling when the feed is unchanged — either way it should be removed or wired up. As it stands every poll re-parses and re-imports the full feed each hour.

`force: true` added to an already-shipped migration can silently drop the top_topics table

This PR modifies the existing CreateTopTopics migration (2013-12-23) to add `force: true`, which makes `create_table` DROP the table if it exists. For any database that already ran this migration and then re-runs it (e.g., `rake db:migrate:redo`, or environments that replay migrations), all top_topics data would be destroyed. Editing historical migrations also means schema state diverges between deployments that ran the old version and the new one. The `force: true` should be reverted here (it belongs only in brand-new migrations, if anywhere).

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

false_positives.candidate:
Animated GIFs are flattened to a single frame when downsized because the extension check never matches tempfile paths

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) pipeline only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the paths passed from `create_upload` are Rack multipart tempfiles or `FileHelper.download` tempfiles, whose names have no `.gif` extension. Consequently any animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is processed by ImageMagick `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame: the user's animated upload is silently converted to a still image even when `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation-detection should be based on the original filename/content, not the tempfile path.

413 error message always claims the limit is 10 MB

`displayErrorForUpload` reports a hard-coded "10 MB" maximum when the server returns 413, but the actual limit is `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb`, which the admin can set to anything. On sites with a different limit the message shown to users is factually wrong and confusing. The previous code read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` here.

API URL download cap hard-coded to 10MB regresses sites with higher max_image_size_kb

The remote-download size limit for API uploads was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hard-coded `10.megabytes`. Sites that configured `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer pull images via URL larger than 10MB (they now silently fail with `rescue nil`, producing a confusing `tempfile`-nil path), while the client-facing intent of the PR is to allow large images that are then downsized. The cap should be derived from the setting (or at least max(setting, 10MB)).

Downsizing loop runs up to 5 full ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload and can still not converge

Each iteration applies `-resize 80%`, which reduces area to ~64%, so five iterations shrink the image at most ~10x; an image far above the limit (e.g. 50MB against a 1MB setting) still exceeds it after the loop and then fails in `Upload.create_for` with a generic error. Additionally, when `downsize` returns false (convert failure), the return value is ignored, so the loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing on the same file. Each pass also invokes ImageOptim, making this expensive CPU work on the request path for synchronous API uploads. The loop should stop early on failure and compute a resize percentage that reaches the target in one pass.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash

A TopicUser row is only created once a user has visited/interacted with a topic, yet the unsubscribe link is included in every notification email — e.g. a user who was mentioned or invited to a topic but never opened it will have no row. Clicking the emailed 'stop receiving notifications' link then raises NoMethodError on nil and returns a 500 instead of unsubscribing them. The code should fall back to TopicUser.change(...)/create the row with the desired level.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `TopicUser.find_by(...)` can return `nil` if no record exists, and subsequently calling methods on `tu` will raise a nil pointer exception (NoMethodError).

false_positives.candidate: Notification state is mutated by an unauthenticated-CSRF-able GET request, and refresh re-toggles it The `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route is a GET that flips the user's notification_level (watching/tracking -> regular, regular/muted -> muted) with no CSRF token or confirmation. Because it is a plain GET with session cookies, any logged-in user can have their topic notification settings silently changed just by loading a URL — e.g. an attacker can embed `` in a post or external page and the victim's browser will hit the endpoint and mute/unwatch the topic. Additionally, since the same GET both performs the toggle and renders the unsubscribe page, every page refresh or link re-visit toggles the level again (watching -> regular -> muted), so the user's final state depends on how many times the URL was loaded. State changes should not happen on GET (or should be idempotent, e.g. always mute).

Email copy promises to stop notifications but the endpoint only downgrades to regular

The new unsubscribe_link text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here', but TopicsController#unsubscribe only sets watching/tracking users to `regular` — a level that still emails the user when someone replies to them or @mentions them. A user who clicks the link believing they will no longer receive emails for that topic will keep getting reply/mention notifications, which is a trust/warranty problem for the feature. Either the endpoint should set the level to muted, or the message should accurately describe what will still be received.

Unsubscribe link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} and raises for callers that don't supply it

The `unsubscribe_link` locale now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, and both `html_part` (line 67) and `body` (line 90) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`. I18n raises `MissingInterpolationArgument` when an interpolation key in the translation has no value, so any caller that builds an email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now fail to render and the email send will blow up. The only in-repo caller was updated (and the message_builder spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url`), but MessageBuilder is a reusable API used by plugins and mailers that set `add_unsubscribe_link` on its own; the builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. to the user preferences URL) or use `I18n.t(..., unsubscribe_url: ... )` with a fallback so missing values degrade gracefully.

No request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The TopicsController#unsubscribe action introduces new routing, access control (ensure_logged_in), a toggle rule based on the current notification level, and a 301 redirect for slug mismatch, but no controller/request specs were added for it — the only test change in the PR is unrelated (adding unsubscribe_url to a message_builder spec). Notably, the nil-TopicUser case and the watching->regular vs regular->muted toggle behavior are completely untested, which is how the nil crash above ships unnoticed.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache throws generic Error instead of TRPCError

When the credential lookup fails, the handler throws `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In a tRPC procedure this surfaces to the client as an INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with the message potentially logged as an unexpected server error, rather than a typed TRPCError (e.g. UNAUTHORIZED/NOT_FOUND) like the other handlers in this router use. The client cannot distinguish authorization failure from a real server fault, and the message conflates two different conditions ('not found' vs 'access denied'). true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: throwing a generic `Error` in a tRPC procedure results in an internal server error (500), and recommend replacing it with a structured `TRPCError` using an appropriate status code.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status never resolves for delegated (in-memory) credentials

The cache status is looked up with `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds(connectedCalendars.map(cal => cal.credentialId))`, but for delegated Google Calendar connections the connectedCalendar.credentialId is a synthetic negative in-memory id (see `isInMemoryDelegationCredential` in the cache repository, and the userId+key based lookup in `getCachedAvailability`). CalendarCache rows for delegated users are stored/retrieved keyed by userId, not by that credentialId, so the groupBy on these ids returns nothing and `cacheUpdatedAt` will always be null. Since calendar cache is primarily a team/organization (delegation) feature, the new cache status and delete-cache UI will silently never appear for the main audience of this feature. The status query needs a userId-based path (mirroring `getCachedAvailability`) to cover delegated credentials.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars, leaving stale cache status

After a successful `trpc.viewer.calendars.deleteCache` call, only `onSuccess?.()` (the parent's `onChanged`) is invoked. Unlike the sibling `disconnectMutation`, which explicitly invalidates `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`, the deleteCache mutation never invalidates that query. `onChanged` in `SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper` is the caller's callback and does not refetch the tRPC `connectedCalendars` query, so after deleting the cache the 'Cache Status' row and 'Last updated' timestamp remain visible until a manual page refresh, contradicting the success toast.

Cache status includes expired cache rows

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups CalendarCache rows by credentialId with no `expiresAt` filter. `getCachedAvailability` only serves rows where `expiresAt >= now`, so a cache that expired over a month ago (and is no longer used for availability lookups) will still report a `updatedAt` value. The UI will then show a 'Cache Status' with a stale 'Last updated' time and a 'Delete cached data' action for data that is effectively already gone, telling the user they have an active cache when they don't. The where clause should include `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to match what the cache actually serves.

No tests for the new cache-status and delete-cache code paths

This PR adds a new tRPC mutation (`deleteCache`), a new repository method (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`), a new repository method (`updateManyByCredentialId`), a Prisma schema change, and a new UI component, but includes no tests at all: no test for the authorization check in `deleteCacheHandler` (e.g. that a user cannot delete another user's cache by passing an arbitrary credentialId), no test that `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` returns the max updatedAt per credential, and no test for `updateManyByCredentialId`. The `dev:cron` script was changed from `ts-node cron-tester.ts` to `npx tsx cron-tester.ts`, but `tsx` is not present in devDependencies (only `ts-node` is). If tsx is the intended runner it should be added to devDependencies with a pinned version; also this change is unrelated to the calendar cache feature and shouldn't ride along in this PR.

This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` is a duplicate of `start`, so slots overrunning the host's working hours are not rejected

In the new working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start` and never accounts for the event length (it should be derived from slotEndTime). As a result the condition `end > workingHour.endTime` only rejects slots that *start* after the working hours end; a slot that starts before closing but extends past it (e.g. a 60-minute event starting 30 minutes before the fixed host's end of day) passes the check and is offered even though the host is not available for the full duration. This is precisely the class of bug (fixed hosts bookable when unavailable in round-robin) that this PR claims to fix, so the fix is undermined for end-of-day slots.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies that `end` is calculated using `slotStartTime` instead of `slotEndTime`, which is the exact same bug described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === , so the equal-start/end override branch is dead code

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two Dayjs object references, which is always false regardless of the underlying times. The intended check — detecting overrides where start equals end (the "unavailable" full-day marker) — never executes, and such overrides instead fall through to the window comparisons, where a slot starting exactly at the override timestamp is returned as available. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `.valueOf()`/`.getTime()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: using the `===` operator to compare two Dayjs objects (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` and `dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')`), which compares object references rather than values and always evaluates to false. Both suggest using `.isSame()` to fix the issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override bypass the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot's date matches a date override and the slot falls inside the override window, the code hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` and returns before evaluating the `busy` array. That means for any host that has a date override on a given day, existing ACCEPTED bookings and external calendar events that fall inside the override window are completely ignored, and those slots are returned as available. An attendee can then book over an existing booking (double booking / data integrity). The busy check must still run for slots that lie within a date override; only the working-hours check should be skipped for override days.

Working-hours check treats days outside the host's schedule as available

The new working-hours filter uses `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { if (workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())) { ... } })`. If the slot's weekday is not included in any of the host's working-hours entries (e.g. a Saturday slot for a Mon-Fri host), the callback returns undefined for every entry, `find` returns undefined, and the code falls through to the busy-only check — i.e. the slot is considered available. For round-robin events the aggregate availability is the union of hosts, so slots generated from another host's Saturday availability will pass this fixed-host check even though the fixed host never works that day. A day with no matching working-hours entry must be treated as unavailable, not available.

Override date is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared against a UTC date

The date gate compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` (UTC mode), but `dayjs(date.start)` is in the server's local timezone, so its `.format()` renders the date in the server's timezone. On any deployment where the process timezone is not UTC, the two dates disagree for times near midnight, causing date overrides to fail to match (slots wrongly unavailable via the fall-through, or wrongly available). The left side should be built with `dayjs.utc(date.start)` so both dates are rendered in UTC.

Optional override.timeZone silently falls back to the server's local timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` uses the new optional `timeZone` field of TimeRange. If a caller supplies date overrides without `timeZone` (the type explicitly allows this), `dayjs.tz(..., undefined)` falls back to the server's local timezone, and the computed organizer UTC offset — and therefore every converted override start/end — will be wrong with no error. getSlots already receives `organizerTimeZone` as a parameter; that should be the fallback (or the field should be required) so a missing value cannot silently corrupt slot times.

Overrides shifted across midnight by the timezone conversion are applied to the wrong invitee day

activeOverrides is selected by checking `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (the raw stored wall-clock-UTC value) against the invitee's day window, but the override times are then converted to invitee-local minutes-of-day. When the offset shift moves the override across a midnight boundary, those minutes belong to a different calendar day than the one being built. Example: an organizer in UTC+13 with an override stored at 23:00–23:30 UTC and an invitee in UTC-11 yields an offset of -1440 minutes; the invitee-local times are 23:00–23:30 on the *previous* day, but the filter attaches the override to the invitee day containing the stored 23:00 UTC, so availability is added on the wrong day (and the user's normal working hours for the wrong day are removed).

No test for the headline fix: round-robin with a fixed host having a date override

The PR description states the primary fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected in round-robin events (issue #8207), but no test covers that scenario: all team-event tests use empty `hosts` or non-fixed configurations, and the only new test added is the timezone variant of a single-user personal event (which also only differs by 30 minutes of offset, both on the same side of the override window). Additionally, there is no test combining a date override with an existing booking, which is exactly the interaction that the new `dateOverrideExist` short-circuit in checkIfIsAvailable gets wrong (slots inside an override are never checked against busy times). Both scenarios should be covered before merging.

Database update inside the catch block can itself throw, aborting the entire cron run

The new code in the catch block performs `prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` before the console.log. If that update throws (e.g., the reminder was concurrently deleted by the deleteMany of an overlapping cron run, or a transient DB error), the exception propagates out of the catch and out of the for-loop, so the handler never sends a response (the caller gets a 500) and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are not processed in this run. Comment no longer matches what the deleteMany does

A maintainer reading the comment will misunderstand the destructive scope of this query; update the comment to reflect both conditions.

Reminders dropped after two failures with no logging or record of the loss

When the deleteMany removes reminders because retryCount > 1, nothing is logged and no record is kept of which bookings lost their reminders. The per-attempt failures only `console.log` the raw error with no reminder id, so after the row is deleted there is no way to audit that an attendee stopped receiving an SMS reminder. New retryCount predicate in deleteMany cannot use any existing index

An empty array is not rejected by the schema and instead surfaces later as the misleading `emails_must_be_unique_valid` BAD_REQUEST error, while an unbounded array lets one request create hundreds of attendee rows and trigger hundreds of outbound emails (each existing attendee gets an email per call), which is an email-bombing / resource-exhaustion vector even for an authenticated attendee. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write; codes can be replayed or burned

The backup code is consumed by reading `user.backupCodes`, decrypting, nulling the matched index, and writing the whole array back with an unconditional `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction or conditional update, so two concurrent login requests presenting the same code can both pass `indexOf` and both succeed — the code is effectively reusable within the race window. Additionally, the code is burned inside authorize() before the rest of the sign-in pipeline completes; if anything fails downstream or the client never receives the success response (network drop), the user's code is permanently consumed and their retry with the same code returns IncorrectBackupCode. Consumption should be atomic (e.g. a conditional update filtered on the code being present, or a transaction with a re-check) and ideally only committed once sign-in is assured.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly describes the exact same race condition where backup codes are read, decrypted, mutated in memory, and written back without atomicity, allowing concurrent requests with the same code to both succeed.

false_positives.candidate:
Valid backup code alone can authenticate without the account password

In the credentials authorize() the password check is guarded by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)` (line 121), i.e. the password is skipped whenever any non-empty totpCode is supplied. The new backup-code branch at line 131 then runs when `credentials.backupCode` is set, without ever verifying the password. So a request containing email, an arbitrary junk totpCode (e.g. "000000"), and a valid backupCode signs the user in with no password knowledge. Backup codes are single-use 40-bit hex strings typically saved in plaintext files or on paper; they are intended as a second factor, not a password substitute. The server should require a verified password (or otherwise ensure the first-factor step actually happened) before accepting a backup code.

"Generate backup codes in your settings" is impossible — no regeneration path exists, and pre-PR 2FA users have none

The new `missing_backup_codes` message says "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.", but this PR adds no endpoint or UI to generate/regenerate backup codes — they are only created once, during initial 2FA setup (setup.ts), and only shown once. Users who enabled 2FA before this PR have `backupCodes = null`, so if they lose their authenticator the "Lost access" flow is a dead end, and users who dismiss the backup-codes dialog without saving can never retrieve their codes again. The error message instructs them to do something that cannot be done, on both the login page and the disable-2FA modal.

resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step, but never resets the react-hook-form `totpCode` field. After a completed (or abandoned) setup, the form still holds the previously entered 6-digit code. When the user later re-opens the modal and reaches the EnterTotpCode step, the registered hidden `totpCode` input still contains the old value while the digit boxes render empty; submitting (or any change that retriggers the auto-submit effect watching `totpCode`) can send the stale, now-invalid code, producing a confusing "code is incorrect" error before the user has typed anything. resetState should also call form.setValue("totpCode", "").

onEnable is only fired from the "Close" button; dismissing the dialog via X/Escape skips it and resetState

The prop contract says onEnable is "Called when the user enables two-factor auth", and previously it was invoked as soon as enable succeeded. Now it is only called from the backup-codes "Close" button click handler. If the user dismisses the dialog through the built-in close affordances (X button, Escape key, overlay click — all routed to onOpenChange), onEnable never fires, so any parent that refreshes its state in onEnable (e.g. the two-factor switch on the security settings page) will keep showing 2FA as disabled even though it is enabled. resetState is also skipped, leaving the modal on the DisplayBackupCodes step with the codes still in memory if reopened.

Backup codes are persisted as AES-encrypted plaintext (`symmetricEncrypt(JSON.stringify(backupCodes))`) using the shared CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and returned in plaintext in the API response. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be recoverable to validate codes), backup codes can be validated by hashing the user input and comparing digests, which is the industry standard (GitHub, Google, etc.). As stored, anyone with database access plus the encryption key — a key already used for many other secrets — recovers all unused backup codes, which per the finding above can even be replayed as a standalone credential.

The PR's headline feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The updated e2e tests only exercise the backup-codes screen's download/copy/close buttons; the TODO at the top of the file ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") acknowledges this. Neither the happy path (correct code logs in and is consumed), nor wrong-code rejection, nor code-single-use behavior is verified anywhere, leaving the new authorize() and disable.ts branches untested.

The change adds `tabIndex={-1}` to the show/hide password button inside PasswordField. This makes the toggle unreachable via keyboard (Tab/Synth events), so keyboard-only and screen-reader users can no longer reveal their password on the login page, the 2FA setup modal, or anywhere else PasswordField is used. When a user arrives at /auth/login via a `totp` JWT (SSO/Google users with 2FA who were redirected by loginWithTotp), the footer rendered is ExternalTotpFooter, which only offers a "cancel" button — the "Lost access" button that switches to the BackupCode input exists only in TwoFactorFooter. Such users have backup codes generated by this feature but no UI to enter them, so if they lose their authenticator they are locked out despite the feature existing. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

Consequences: (1) `Reschedule` returns `true` and the reschedule email is sent before the external calendar events and video meetings are actually deleted; on a serverless platform the execution context can be frozen after the response, so the deletions may never run and stale events remain on users' calendars; (2) the surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from these async callbacks, so any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Eager import() calls mean all apps load at import time and failed chunks become unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal evaluates `import("./x")` for every app as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so all ~29 app chunks start loading immediately on any code path that touches appStore — the intended deferral is not achieved for cold starts. Worse, each of these promises is created without a rejection handler: if any app chunk fails to load (a common case on Next.js/Vercel when in-flight requests reference chunks invalidated by a new deploy), the promise for that app rejects before anything awaits it. Since Node 15+, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default, so one app's failed chunk can take down the whole server even though no request ever used that app. To be genuinely lazy and safe, the store should use getters (e.g. `get stripepayment() { return import("./stripepayment"); }`) so the import (and its promise) is only created when actually requested.

In a serverless environment the function can be suspended after the response, leaving the old calendar events permanently in place. Because forEach does not await the callbacks, the handler continues to line 652 (`await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`) while the forEach callbacks are still suspended at their awaits; the Promise.all therefore snapshots a `apiDeletes` array that may be empty or partial, and the cancellation API response is returned before the calendar deletion calls have even been started. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires

In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: breaking out of the process loop when the deadline expires skips termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources

In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract method getShortcut() on the pluggable OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI breaks existing custom grant implementations

`getShortcut()` was added as an abstract (non-default) method to the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` interface in `server-spi-private`. OAuth 2.0 grant types are a deployable extension point (factories are registered via META-INF/services), so any existing third-party grant-type provider will fail to load/compile after upgrade with "does not define getShortcut()". To preserve compatibility, the method should have a sensible `default` implementation (e.g., deriving from the ID or returning a marker that the encoder maps to the UNKNOWN shortcut) instead of forcing every existing implementation to be updated.

Public copy constructor OAuth2GrantType.Context(Context) was removed

The public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` of the public static class `OAuth2GrantType.Context` was deleted as part of this change. This class lives in the `server-spi-private` grants package that custom grant-type implementations compile against; any external code that used the copy constructor will break at compile time on upgrade. The removal is not required by the rest of the change (the new `grantType` field could be copied along), so it should either be kept (also copying `grantType`, which would arguably be more correct than re-reading form params) or the break should be explicitly acknowledged.

Decoder assumes fixed 2-character shortcuts but the SPI javadoc invites longer shortcuts, producing undecodable token IDs

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` hard-requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 characters (2 chars each for session type, token type and grant type) and throws `IllegalArgumentException` otherwise. However, `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` is documented as "usually like 3-letters shortcut" with no length constraint, and third parties can implement it. A custom grant whose shortcut is not exactly 2 characters will encode fine (`encodeTokenId` just concatenates), but the resulting token ID (e.g., 7-char prefix) will be rejected by `getTokenContextFromTokenId` with an exception — tokens minted by Keycloak itself become undecodable. Either enforce/validate the 2-char length when populating the factory maps in `postInit`, or make the decoding format length-agnostic (e.g., split on fixed delimiters as in the original longer `st.on_tt.rt_gt.ac:` format).

The decoder is lenient for legacy IDs without ':' (returns UNKNOWN context) but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for IDs that contain ':' with an unknown or wrong-length prefix. Since the token ID (`jti`) originates from externally presented tokens — e.g., tokens issued by another Keycloak deployment with a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider` (the SPI explicitly exists to allow alternate encodings), a future format change, or foreign IDPs whose `jti` happens to contain a colon — any consumer of this method (introspection, userInfo, the planned session-lookup optimization from #37662) can be made to fail with a runtime exception by presenting an otherwise perfectly valid, signature-verified token. Decoding of a descriptive prefix should degrade gracefully to UNKNOWN (as already done for the no-colon case) rather than throw, since the encoded info is an optimization hint, not a security invariant.

`postInit` validates shortcut/ID uniqueness once by comparing map sizes, and `getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` later add entries for grant factories not present at startup (comment: "in case new grant type was deployed") without re-checking for collisions. If a hot-deployed grant uses a shortcut (or ID) already mapped, `grantsByShortcuts.put(...)` silently overwrites the existing entry, so two distinct grant types map to the same shortcut and previously issued token IDs are misinterpreted (wrong grant type returned from `getTokenContextFromTokenId`). At minimum the lazy-population paths should detect the collision (e.g., refuse to overwrite an existing different mapping) instead of silently clobbering.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and can be reused indefinitely

When the recovery-authn-codes credential lives in a user storage (the scenario this PR enables), `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().isValid(...)` delegates to the storage provider's `CredentialInputValidator.isValid`. Unlike the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`, whose isValid() marks the matched code as used, there is no framework path that tells the storage to invalidate the used code, and the reference implementation added in this PR (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.isValid`, which does a plain `anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse()))`) demonstrates that the same recovery code passes validation again on every login. One-time use is a core security property of recovery codes. Either the framework needs a consumption/update callback for storages, or the storage SPI contract (and the test provider plus a reuse-rejection test) must require storages to invalidate used codes; as merged, a federated user's recovery code is effectively a permanent credential.

removeStoredCredentialById() is called with a user-storage credential ID it cannot delete

After successful validation, when `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` returns a federated credential and `allCodesUsed()` is true, the code calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`. That ID belongs to the user storage, not Keycloak's local credential store (for the test provider it is even regenerated fresh on every `getCredentials()` call via `createFromValues`, and may be null), and `CredentialInputUpdater` offers no delete-by-id for storages (`BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.disableCredentialType` ignores recovery-authn-codes entirely). Consequence: an exhausted federated recovery-code credential is never removed, the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is re-added on every login while the dead credential keeps `configuredFor` true, and passing an unresolvable/null ID risks an exception from the credential store inside the authentication flow.

Regenerating recovery codes does not remove a pre-existing credential in the other store

`createRecoveryCodesCredential` either stores the new codes in the user storage (`userStorageCreated == true`) or in Keycloak's local DB, but never removes an existing recovery-authn-codes credential from the store it did not write to. A user who previously had recovery codes in the local DB (e.g. created before federation or while the storage did not support the type) keeps that old credential fully valid after regenerating: `credentialManager().isValid()` can still accept the old local codes, so regeneration fails to invalidate the previous code set. Additionally `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` prefers the federated credential while validation may succeed against the local one, so the UI can prompt with a code number from a different credential than the one actually consumed. Both stores should be reconciled (old credential deleted) when new codes are created.

Extending the frozen 4.8.3 backwards-compatibility provider undermines the test's purpose

The class javadoc states this provider was created with Keycloak 4.8.3 and that "Future Keycloak versions should work fine without a need to change the code of this provider" — its whole point is to verify current Keycloak against an unchanged, old provider. This PR substantially modifies it (adds recovery-authn-codes support to supportsCredentialType/updateCredential/isValid/isConfiguredFor, adds getCredentials), so the suite no longer exercises a genuinely legacy provider. Also, `getCredentials()` can NPE via `getMyUser(user)` returning null (the sibling methods `getDisableableCredentialTypesStream` and `isConfiguredFor` guard against this), and on deserialization failure it silently drops the credential from the stream, making `getCredentials()` and `isConfiguredFor()` inconsistent for the same user.

This PR introduces a new preview feature, ROLLING_UPDATES (key 'rolling-updates'), but the server documentation page that enumerates supported/preview/experimental features (docs/guides/server/features.adoc, the 'Enabling and disabling features' guide) is not updated. Users looking up what `--features=rolling-updates` enables, or which preview features exist, will find no mention of it, even though other guides in this same PR instruct users to enable it. The feature table should be updated in the same change that adds the enum entry.

Feature-disabled path only tested for 'metadata' and without asserting the new exit code 4

The new testFeatureNotEnabled only launches the `metadata` subcommand and only asserts the error message text. The documentation added in this PR promises a specific exit code 4 ('The feature rolling-updates is disabled') and the same gate is implemented in both UpdateCompatibilityCheck and UpdateCompatibilityMetadata, but neither the exit code nor the `check` subcommand's disabled path is verified. If the gate is accidentally removed, the exit code changes, or the check command crashes (e.g., NPE from Profile not being initialized) instead of exiting 4, no test would catch it. The test should assert exitCode() == 4 and cover `check` as well.
