true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission includes the aggregate 'Clients' resource name in the returned client-id set

getClientsWithPermission iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...). The aggregate 'Clients' resource created in AdminPermissionsSchema.init() also carries type 'Clients', so it is included in the callback. When a blanket permission on it is granted, the method adds the literal string "Clients" to the returned set of names. Callers that treat the result as the set of client IDs the admin may access get a bogus entry that matches no client, and more importantly a blanket all-clients grant is represented as a single meaningless ID rather than 'all clients', so a filtering caller would show the admin an empty client list despite the grant. The aggregate resource (name equal to CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) should be excluded, and a grant on it should be surfaced as a wildcard/all-clients result.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that getClientsWithPermission queries typed resources and returns the aggregate 'Clients' resource name as though it were a client ID, producing invalid IDs for callers expecting actual clients. The candidate omits the specific role-mapping caller and the fact that per-client resources lack a type, but identifies the same underlying resource-selection and ID mismatch bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission(client, scope) can pass a null Resource to PolicyStore.findByResource and NPE

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no resource exists for the specific client, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE). That method returns null when the schema is not supported for this resource server (e.g. realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled() is false while the admin permissions client still exists) or when the aggregate 'Clients' resource was never created (realms whose admin permissions client was initialized before this change, since init() only creates resources on first setup). The null is then passed directly to authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource), which throws a NullPointerException (store implementations dereference resource.getId()) instead of cleanly denying access. A null check on the result of getResourceTypeResource is needed before querying the policy store.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same null-handling bug: getResourceTypeResource can return null in ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, which is passed to findByResource and causes a NullPointerException. Both recommend a defensive null check.

false_positives.candidate:
Client removal listener throws UnsupportedOperationException under V2 because guard checks the V1 feature flag

In registerListener, the event handling is now guarded by Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) (the V1 flag), but the handler calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). When the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 feature is enabled (which depends on the V1 feature being enabled), management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2, whose setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean) unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). The ClientRemovedEvent listener therefore throws on every client deletion on a server with V2 enabled, breaking client deletion even in realms that do not use fine-grained admin permissions. The guard should also exclude the V2 feature (or the V2 implementation should be a no-op instead of throwing).

canExchangeTo/isPermissionsEnabled/getPermissions throw UnsupportedOperationException from live request paths

ClientPermissionsV2.canExchangeTo (line 149), isPermissionsEnabled (line 189), getPermissions (line 204) and setPermissionsEnabled (line 194) all throw UnsupportedOperationException. These are not dead code: the token exchange flow invokes canExchangeTo on the admin permission evaluator (AdminPermissions.evaluator returns MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever the V2 feature is enabled), and the admin REST 'management/permissions' endpoints for a client invoke isPermissionsEnabled/getPermissions/setPermissionsEnabled. With the V2 feature enabled, those requests will fail with a 500 error instead of being denied or handled. These overrides should return a safe default (e.g. false/null) rather than throwing, or the calling code must be updated to handle V2.

init() does not migrate existing admin permissions clients: 'Clients' resource and new scopes are never created

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null (lines 226-228), so realms that already enabled admin permissions under V2 before this change (Users resource type only) will never get the new 'Clients' aggregate resource or the new scopes 'configure', 'map-roles-client-scope' and 'map-roles-composite'. On such realms, creating a Clients permission referencing those scopes fails ('Scope [configure] does not exist' / 'No scopes found' ModelException from getOrCreateResource line 108), and ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(String scope) at line 244 silently returns false because findByName for 'Clients' yields nothing — admins appear to have no client permissions at all with no diagnostic. A migration step is needed to add the new scopes and the 'Clients' resource to existing admin permissions clients.

Javadoc for requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() incorrectly describes them as boolean getters

The newly added javadoc on requireView() (lines 95-98) reads "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}" — but requireView() is a void method that throws ForbiddenException based on canView(), not canViewClientScopes(). Likewise the javadoc for requireViewClientScopes() (lines 100-103) says "Returns {@code true} if ..." for a void require-method. The docs contradict the method signatures and reference the wrong predicate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() (no-arg) grants manage rights for a view-only permission on Groups

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() (the global, no-argument variant) falls back to hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), i.e. a caller granted only the 'view' scope on the Groups type resource passes the manage check. requireManage() (no-arg) guards POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups (GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup), which both creates top-level groups and, when the representation carries an existing group id, moves that group to the top level via realm.moveGroup. So an admin explicitly granted only 'view' on Groups can create groups and move arbitrary existing groups. The per-group variant canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE only, as does UserPermissions.canManage() for the Users resource; the no-arg variant should not accept VIEW. The javadoc added in GroupPermissionEvaluator matches this code, but the behavior contradicts the method's contract and the per-group semantics.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the no-argument GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() accepts VIEW or MANAGE permissions, allowing view-only users to pass a manage check. It correctly states that this fallback should require MANAGE only.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission mixes resource IDs with group IDs and cannot find per-group resources

GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission enumerates resources with resourceStore.findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and then both looks up permissions with hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the result set. This is wrong on two counts: (1) per-group resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, clientId) with the group id as the resource NAME and a store-generated ID, and without setting the resource type, so findByType("Groups") never returns them; (2) hasPermission resolves resources with findByName(...), so passing a resource's generated ID as a 'group id' finds nothing and falls through to the all-groups type resource. Consequences: an admin holding only per-group view-members/manage-members grants gets an empty set, so the UserModel.GROUPS filter used by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource user search and getUsersCount is never applied at the DB level — searches scan all realm users and rely on the in-memory canView filter, which breaks pagination (first/max are applied before filtering) and returns wrong counts. Worse, an admin holding a view-members/manage-members grant on the type-level 'Groups' resource gets that resource's UUID added as a bogus 'group id', so user search and getUsersCount return zero users even though canView(user) evaluates to true. The existing tests pass only because the in-memory usersEvaluator::canView filter compensates; nothing covers the all-groups or paginated cases.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core mismatch: getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes and returns resource IDs rather than underlying group IDs stored as resource names, while hasPermission resolves by name and downstream user filters/counts require group IDs. Its additional claims about resource types, pagination, and tests go beyond the golden comment but do not change the shared underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
UnsupportedOperationException thrown on live code paths (group deletion, management-permissions endpoints)

GroupPermissionsV2 overrides setPermissionsEnabled, isPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions, viewPermission, etc. to throw UnsupportedOperationException, but these methods are still invoked on real paths when the V2 feature is active. AdminPermissions.registerListener (guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ flag, which can be enabled together with — or implied by — ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) calls management(...).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false) on every GroupRemovedEvent, so deleting any group in a V2 realm throws UnsupportedOperationException and the DELETE fails with a 500. Similarly GroupResource.getManagementPermissions/setManagementPermissionsEnabled call isPermissionsEnabled(group)/getPermissions(group) after ProfileHelper.requireFeature(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), which now returns 500 instead of the previous working V1 behavior (before this change MgmtPermissionsV2 fell back to the functional V1 GroupPermissions implementation). Either these paths must be guarded/disabled for V2 realms or the V2 implementation must handle them instead of throwing.

Existing admin-permissions realms never get the Groups resource or the new group scopes (no migration)

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null. Realms where the admin permissions client was already created (e.g., with the earlier Clients resource type support) will therefore never receive the new 'Groups' type-level resource or the new group scopes (manage-membership, manage-members, view-members) that init() creates from the schema. In such realms, creating any group scope permission fails: getOrCreateResource does scopeStore.findByName(...) for each schema scope and throws ModelException("No scopes found.") when a scope is missing, and getScope rejects the request with "Scope [...] does not exist". Additionally getResourceTypeResource(session, server, "Groups") returns null because the type resource was never created, which makes GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission fall into the null-resource path. A migration (or lazy creation of missing type resources/scopes for existing admin-permissions clients) is needed; otherwise upgraded realms cannot use the new Groups resource type at all.

hasPermission can NPE when the 'Groups' type resource cannot be resolved

In GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission, when the per-group resource is not found the code assigns resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE) without a null check, then calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) and later resource.getScopes(). getResourceTypeResource returns null whenever supportsAuthorizationSchema is false — e.g., the realm's admin permissions flag is disabled while the admin permissions client (and its resource server) still exists, or the 'Groups' type resource is missing in a pre-existing realm (see the init()/migration issue). In those states, any group permission evaluation (canView(group), requireView(group) on GET /groups/{id}, etc.) throws a NullPointerException instead of denying access. A null check returning false is needed. The same pattern exists in UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission, but GroupPermissionsV2 is newly added by this PR.

No test covers user search/count with a type-level (all-groups) permission or pagination under group-scoped permissions

The new tests only exercise user search for admins holding per-group view-members/manage-members grants on a single group in a realm with two users, where the in-memory usersEvaluator::canView filter masks any problem in getGroupIdsWithViewPermission. There is no test for: (a) an admin holding view-members on the type-level 'Groups' resource performing user search/getUsersCount (this currently returns zero users because the resource UUID is used as a group id); (b) pagination/first/max correctness when the DB-level group filter is absent or wrong (currently searches scan all users and filter in memory); (c) getUsersCount with group-scoped admins. Adding these would catch the broken group-id enumeration in GroupPermissionsV2.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, violating the interface contract

The CryptoProvider contract for `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) security provider. This implementation instead returns the provider of `KeyStore.getDefaultType()` (typically the SUN provider). Any shared code path in keycloak-common/keycloak-core that obtains the provider via this method and relies on BC-specific services (algorithms, keystore types like BCFKS/PKCS12 via BC, etc.) will get a provider that does not provide them, resulting in confusing NoSuchAlgorithmException/KeyStoreException failures rather than a clear 'not supported' signal, or worse, subtly different cryptographic behavior. Unlike the other methods that clearly throw UnsupportedOperationException, this one silently returns something that does not match the documented contract.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider instead of the expected BouncyCastle provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead code in concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates and discards two ASN1 encoders

Lines 114-115 (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) create two encoders, write the integers into them, and throw the results away; only the `writeDerSeq(...)` chain on lines 117-121 contributes to the returned value. The statements have no effect, allocate objects unnecessarily on every signature conversion (a hot path during JWT signature verification), and look like leftover debugging code that will confuse future readers.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unused ASN1Encoder instances that are written to and discarded, while separate encoders in the return statement perform the actual encoding.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Adding abstract method order() to the CryptoProvider SPI breaks existing implementations

The new `int order();` method is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI interface without a default implementation. CryptoProvider is a published extension point loaded via ServiceLoader (documented Keycloak crypto SPI), so any third-party or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will (a) no longer compile and (b) at runtime fail with AbstractMethodError as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the comparator while sorting the loaded providers. Previously-working custom crypto providers are therefore completely broken by this change, not just the new ordering feature. The method should be declared as `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) to preserve source and binary compatibility of the SPI.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility issue: adding abstract order() to CryptoProvider breaks existing implementations. The candidate elaborates on compilation and runtime failures and suggests a default implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Silent, order-tied provider selection removes the FIPS misconfiguration safeguard

detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which acted as a hard safety check against misconfigured deployments (most importantly a classpath accidentally containing both the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider). Now it silently picks one and only logs ignored providers at debug level. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order() == 200, so in a deployment that accidentally contains both, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration order (classpath order), which can silently select the non-FIPS-approved provider in an environment intended to run in FIPS mode, with no warning at any noticeable log level. At minimum, equal-order providers should produce a warning, and the FIPS/non-FIPS collision should be handled deterministically or fail loudly as before.

ECDSA tests use a single P-256 keypair for ES384/ES512 and never verify the DER signature

The test generates one keypair with the JVM default curve (P-256) and reuses it for all three algorithms. For ES384/ES512 the concatenated r/s halves are zero-padded 32-byte values, so the tests never exercise values whose most significant byte within the target length is set, nor the truncation branch of integerToBytes for real 48/66-byte r/s values. Additionally, the test only checks the concat→DER→concat round trip; it never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a valid ECDSA signature via Signature.verify with the public key, which is the actual purpose of the conversion. A bug producing a well-formed but value-incorrect DER encoding would only be caught indirectly. The tests should generate curve-appropriate keypairs (P-384, P-521) and assert Signature.verify(convertedSignature). There is also no test at all for the core mechanism of this PR: the ServiceLoader registration of AuthzClientCryptoProvider and the CryptoIntegration order()-based provider selection/priority logic.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getSubGroupsCount() silently returns null for a deleted group, inconsistent with the adapter's contract elsewhere

When the underlying group has been deleted concurrently, `getSubGroupsCount()` now returns null instead of throwing. Every other path in GroupAdapter that fails to load the delegate (`getDelegateForUpdate()` at line 61 and `isUpdated()` at line 74) throws `IllegalStateException("Not found in database")`, so this change introduces a third, silent behavior for the same condition. Returning a null Long is risky: GroupModel.getSubGroupsCount() is not documented to return null, and any caller that unboxes it (e.g. `== 0` comparisons) will now get an NPE at a distance from the real cause. In GroupUtils.populateSubGroupCount it results in `representation.setSubGroupCount(null)`, leaking a null count into the admin REST response rather than signaling the group is gone. Returning 0L or throwing the same IllegalStateException used by the rest of the class would keep the contract consistent.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that getSubGroupsCount() returns null in violation of its non-null contract and can cause NPEs in callers. The candidate adds context about deleted groups and inconsistent error handling but describes the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the race being tested can be missed or exceptions lost

In `createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti`, after `deletedAll.set(true)` the test immediately asserts `caughtExceptions` is empty, without joining the reader thread. Two consequences: (1) an HTTP request that is in flight when the flag is set can still fail after the assertion has already run, so a real regression can pass the test; (2) the thread is left running (it is not a daemon thread), leaking it and its admin-client connections for the remainder of the JVM/test-suite run. The test should signal completion, then `thread.join()` (with a timeout) before asserting. Additionally, since the thread is only started and never synchronized before deletions begin, it may not execute at all before all groups are deleted, in which case the test passes vacuously without ever exercising the concurrent read/delete path it was written to cover.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing reader-thread synchronization: after setting deletedAll, the test asserts before the reader finishes, allowing late exceptions to be missed. Its additional concerns do not change this core match.

false_positives.candidate:
NPE on concurrent group deletion still possible in the paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads

The PR fixes the NPE only in `getSubGroupsCount()`, but the sibling methods at lines 256, 262, and 268 (`getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer)`, `getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer)`, `getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer)`) still call `modelSupplier.get().getSubGroupsStream(...)` with no null check. `modelSupplier` wraps `getGroupModel()`, which returns null when the group has been deleted, so the exact same concurrent-delete scenario that produced issue #40368 (a cached group being read while another thread removes it) will still produce an NPE on these paths. The fix should apply the same null handling (whatever is chosen for getSubGroupsCount) to all delegating methods that dereference `modelSupplier.get()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation

UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but after this change no zero-argument method with that name exists anywhere in the class hierarchy: UsernamePasswordForm (the only superclass that defines anything similar) only defines isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at line 160, and neither AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator nor AbstractFormAuthenticator provides a no-arg version. The services module therefore fails to compile. Either a no-arg overload must be added to UsernamePasswordForm, or the call must be changed to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing required UserModel argument in the call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() within UsernameForm.authenticate(). The candidate additionally explains the resulting compilation failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Requiring an identified user drops WebAuthn conditional-UI setup on the initial login page

In authenticate() (line 115) and challenge(context, error, field) (line 137), the WebAuthn setup is now gated on isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), which (lines 160-162) additionally requires user != null. On a normal initial login no user is set yet, so webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) is never invoked: the login page never receives the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID or enableWebAuthnConditionalUI attributes, the hidden form //form[@id='webauth'] is not rendered, and passkey autofill / automatic discoverable-key login cannot work. The base code this PR removes explicitly set up the webauthn data "when the user is not already selected". The PR's own tests contradict the new behavior: PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey and webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication assert the webauthn form and the 'username webauthn' autocomplete on the initial page before any user is identified, PasskeysUsernameFormTest.passwordLoginWithNonDiscoverableKey asserts the same after a failed username, and the webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey tests expect the user to be logged in automatically straight from oauth.openLoginForm(). The fill must also happen when context.getUser() == null (i.e. the condition must not require an identified user), otherwise passkey login on the standard first login page is broken.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: requiring a non-null user prevents authenticate() from calling webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page, breaking conditional UI and ID-less passkey authentication before a user is selected.

false_positives.candidate:
Broad catch (Exception) can make the 'no webauthn button' check pass spuriously

In reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey (and the identical block around line 312), the absence of the webauthn form is verified with: try { assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button"); } catch (Exception nsee) { }. Two problems: (1) driver.findElement never returns null, so assertThat(..., nullValue()) can never succeed and the fail() line is dead code; (2) catching Exception rather than NoSuchElementException means any unrelated driver/page error (timeout, stale element, page not loaded) is silently swallowed and the test passes without actually verifying the webauthn form is absent. If the webauthn form is present the AssertionError correctly propagates, but the check should use Assert.assertThrows(NoSuchElementException.class, ...) as done in the other test classes to avoid false passes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing of a Django QuerySet raises AssertionError; the 'advanced feature' can never work

The negative-offset path in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 877-882) slices the queryset as queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — the ORM raises "AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported" — so this branch always errors instead of returning results. The code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually wrong. Since the cursor string ("value:offset:is_prev") is client-controlled and Cursor.from_string happily parses negative offsets, any client hitting this endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a crafted cursor such as "0:-5:0" triggers an unhandled exception / 500. There is no valid input for which this feature works.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses negative slice offsets on Django QuerySets, which do not support negative slicing and raise AssertionError. The candidate's additional trigger details do not change the underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the endpoint's datetime sort key and will 500

The endpoint orders by "-datetime" but OptimizedCursorPaginator inherits Paginator's key handling: get_item_key (src/sentry/api/paginator.py:838-840) computes int(math.floor(value)) on a datetime, which raises TypeError, and value_from_cursor (line 842) returns the raw millisecond integer from the cursor and passes it into a WHERE clause comparing a timestamp column to a bigint ("datetime <= 1234567890123"), which Postgres rejects with an operator-does-not-exist error. Unlike DateTimePaginator, this class never converts between datetimes and the ms-epoch cursor representation. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all worker threads and shuts down every queue.Queue. But the FixedQueuePool is owned by the ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. Arroyo's StreamProcessor rebuilds the processing strategy on every rebalance (it calls close() on the old strategy, then create_with_partitions again on the same factory). After the first rebalance, the new strategy is constructed around the already-shut-down pool: queue_pool.submit() calls work_queue.put() which raises queue.ShutDown, that exception is caught by the except block in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (lines 317-325), which marks the offset as completed. The commit loop then advances the committed offsets past those messages. Result: after any routine consumer-group rebalance (deploys, consumer joins/leaves), every subsequent message on that consumer is silently dropped while offsets are committed as if processed. The strategy must not tear down factory-scoped resources (e.g. the pool shutdown should only happen from ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown(), or the pool should be recreated per strategy).

FixedQueuePool creates each queue via queue.Queue() with no maxsize, so submit() never blocks. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns immediately to Arroyo, which keeps polling and handing over messages, so if the worker threads fall behind, both the in-memory queues and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets grow without bound (offsets can't be pruned until they're committed, and commits can't advance past the backlog). This is a memory leak / OOM risk exactly in the slow-consumer scenario this PR is meant to address. It also contradicts the class docstring at line 253 ('Natural backpressure when queues fill up') — no backpressure exists. Pass maxsize to queue.Queue (or bound the number of in-flight messages) so put() blocks the Arroyo thread when queues fill.

This creates one Sentry transaction per consumed message (per worker), which at uptime-results throughput means a very large transaction ingestion volume and per-message tracing overhead. It is also redundant: ResultProcessor.__call__ (result_consumer.py line 48) already starts its own transaction per result, so every message now produces nested/duplicate transactions. Existing modes (serial/parallel) only instrument the processor, not one transaction per message. The per-item transaction should be removed or sampled.

Claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is false: failures are still marked complete and committed

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring (line 254) guarantees offsets are only committed after successful processing, but OrderedQueueWorker.run() completes the offset in a finally block even when result_processor raises (lines 144-149), and ResultProcessor.__call__ additionally swallows all exceptions itself. A message whose processing fails is therefore treated as done, its offset becomes committable, and after the commit it is permanently skipped — a silent drop of failed messages with no retry and no DLQ. This is the opposite of what the docstring (and the PR's own error-handling test, see separate finding) states. Either the guarantee should be implemented (e.g. don't complete the offset, or route to a DLQ/retry) or the docstring must be corrected to state that failed messages are skipped.

But the implementation completes offsets even when result_processor raises (the worker's finally block), so once both messages finish the commit loop will commit offset 102 for the partition on its next 1-second tick. The test only passes because it breaks out of its wait loop as soon as queues are empty (within ~0.3s) and asserts before the commit thread's 1.0s wait elapses; on a slow CI machine or if the commit interval fires earlier, the assertion fails. The test should either assert the real behavior (failed messages' offsets are committed) or the implementation should be changed to match the intended behavior.

OrderedQueueWorker emits metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', self.work_queue.qsize()) with only an 'identifier' tag — no worker_id or queue index. Every worker reports the same metric name and tags with a different value (its own queue's depth), so the last writer wins and the gauge reflects an arbitrary single queue rather than per-queue depths. Since it's emitted after every processed item, the value is also effectively random. Add a worker_id/queue tag or drop this gauge in favor of the aggregate total_queued gauge emitted in poll().

Because those offsets were added but never completed they won't be committed, so the messages are replayed on restart (at-least-once), but the shutdown is not actually graceful: to drain, only the queue shutdown should signal termination and workers should keep processing until get() raises ShutDown.

The assertion should either be removed, or the pool should be paused/verified deterministically (e.g. block the result processor on an event until stats are captured).

The implementation uses queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception, both of which were only added in Python 3.13. false_positives.candidate:
enable_advanced_features kwarg is not accepted by Endpoint.paginate

The endpoint calls `self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True)`, but `Endpoint.paginate` in sentry/api/base.py has a fixed keyword signature (paginator_cls, order_by, on_results, max_limit, desc, count_hits, known_hits, max_hits) and constructs the paginator with only those arguments — it does not forward arbitrary kwargs to `paginator_cls`. Unless the base method was also changed (it is not in this PR), this call raises `TypeError: paginate() got an unexpected keyword argument 'enable_advanced_features'`, 500-ing every request that passes `optimized_pagination=true` with the required privileges. Even if the intent is for the flag to reach the paginator, `BasePaginator.__init__` would then need to receive it.

No tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds ~100 lines of new paginator code (OptimizedCursorPaginator), modifies BasePaginator.get_result's offset handling for every existing paginator, and adds a new request-driven code path to the audit logs endpoint, yet includes zero tests: no unit tests for OptimizedCursorPaginator (including its negative-offset branch), no tests that BasePaginator behavior is unchanged for existing paginators, and no endpoint tests for the `optimized_pagination` parameter (including the authorization gate). Any of the crash modes described in the other findings would have been caught by a single basic test invoking the new code path.

Unrelated audit-log pagination feature mixed into a span-buffer PR with no rationale

This PR is titled "Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert" and its description is just "Test 2", yet roughly half the diff introduces an unrelated, undocumented API behavior (`optimized_pagination=true` query param enabling a different paginator for superusers/global-access members) to the audit logs endpoint. This makes the change unreviewable as a unit and unrollbackable independently: a revert of the span-buffer work would either take the API change with it or require manual surgery. The audit-log changes should be split into their own PR with a real description, and if kept, the new query param should be documented/validated rather than read ad-hoc from request.GET.

Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, splitting deep segments

The redirect-following loop was reduced from 10000 to 1000 iterations, and the comment explaining the tradeoff ("theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. If a trace's redirect chain in `span-buf:sr:*` exceeds 1000 hops, the loop now exits without resolving the root, `set_span_id` stays at the 1000th intermediate node, and the span is buffered under a partial key — silently splitting one segment into multiple flushed segments. This is a 10x reduction in the supported chain depth with no accompanying metric, log, or test, so the failure mode is invisible in production.

zpopmin eviction can drop the root span, producing segments with no is_segment span

Eviction removes the spans with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores whenever a set exceeds 1000 members. Nothing protects the root/segment span from eviction: if the root span's end timestamp is among the 1000 smallest (possible for out-of-order or async spans), its payload is popped while the `span-buf:hrs:*` flag is still set and the segment is still flushed under the root's key. The flushed segment then contains no span with `is_segment=true`, and every remaining span is stamped with a `segment_id` referring to a span that isn't in the payload — breaking the segment contract for downstream consumers. Evicted spans are also silently dropped with no metric, so the data loss is unobservable.

max_segment_spans parameter is now dead and disagrees with the hardcoded Lua limit

The Python-side enforcement of `max_segment_spans` (the check in `_load_segment_data` with its `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log) was removed in favor of eviction inside the Lua script, but the `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` constructor parameter was left in place and is now never read. Meanwhile the Lua script hardcodes its own limit of 1000. Consequence: any deployment that configures `max_segment_spans` via options gets silently ignored behavior, and the off-by-one (1001 vs 1000) plus the dead parameter will confuse future readers. The limit should be passed to the script (e.g., as an ARGV) or the parameter removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows all errors and drops client_sample_rate of 0

The new factory helper wraps its logic in two bare `except Exception: pass` blocks, so any structural problem with `contexts` (or an invalid sample rate value) is silently ignored and the event is stored without a sample rate, making downstream upsampled-count assertions pass or fail for the wrong reason. Additionally, `if client_sample_rate:` treats a legitimate value of `0` as absent, so a client_sample_rate of 0 never sets sample_rate. At minimum, narrow the exception handling and compare against None explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same bug: `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0 as falsy, preventing a sample rate of 0.0 from being set. Its additional exception-handling concern does not negate this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is computed against the closure `dataset` and original request query, not the scoped dataset/query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, ...)`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer `dataset` variable and the raw `request.GET["query"]`, ignoring the `scoped_dataset` and `query` arguments. In the dashboard widget discover-split flow (`get_event_stats_factory`), `_get_event_stats` is invoked with `scoped_dataset=discover` and a rewritten query such as `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` (errors-only). When the outer dataset is e.g. metrics_enhanced_performance, or the original query string lacks `event.type:error`, the transform is skipped even though the executed query is an error-only discover query that should be upsampled — dashboards on allowlisted projects will show under-sampled counts. The decision must be made from `scoped_dataset` and the actual `query` string passed in.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core bug: the upsampling eligibility check uses the outer dataset rather than scoped_dataset, causing discover dashboard-split queries originating from a metrics dataset to skip upsampling. Its additional concern about the original query does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
upsampled_count() is only registered in DiscoverDataset but is enabled for the errors dataset

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to DiscoverDataset's function_converter, yet `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` in error_upsampling.py returns True whenever the request's dataset is `sentry.snuba.errors`, causing `_get_event_stats` to rewrite `count()` into `upsampled_count() as count` for errors-dataset requests. If the errors dataset's query builder does not include `upsampled_count` in its own function converter (the errors dataset is a separate dataset class and only discover.py was modified), those requests will fail with an invalid/unknown function error for every allowlisted project. Either register the function in the errors dataset's converter as well, or restrict the transform to datasets where the function is actually defined. This path is also untested — all new endpoint tests exercise the default (discover) dataset.

Substring check treats negated `!event.type:error` filters as error-focused queries

`_is_error_focused_query` does a raw substring test `"event.type:error" in query`. A discover query like `!event.type:error` (excluding errors, i.e. returning transactions/other events) contains the substring, so `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True and `count()` is rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`. For non-error events `sample_weight` is not populated (the helper itself documents that sample_weight doesn't exist for transactions), so the returned count will be wrong (typically 0) instead of the real event count. The check needs to parse the query's filter conditions rather than substring-match, or at least reject negated terms.

Endpoint tests don't isolate the 60s eligibility cache, making them order-dependent

`is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` caches its result under `error_upsampling_eligible:{org_id}:{hash(project_ids)}` for 60 seconds in the shared cache, and nothing in the new test class clears it. Django test transactions roll back org/project id sequences, so consecutive test methods in this class reuse the same org id and project ids. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caches `True` for that key; if `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist` (which mocks a partial allowlist and asserts un-upsampled counts of 1) runs afterwards in the same process with a real (non-dummy) cache backend, it reads the cached `True`, applies upsampling, and asserts against counts of 10 — failing. setUp should delete the cache keys (or the helper should be patched), and there are no tests at all for `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` itself, its caching, or `invalidate_upsampling_cache`.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code — nothing calls it when the allowlist option changes

The docstring of `invalidate_upsampling_cache` says it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes to ensure cache consistency across the system", but no code in this PR (option update handler, signal, or task) invokes it. In practice the only consistency mechanism is the 60-second TTL, so the function is misleading dead code; either wire it into the option-change path or remove it and document that only the TTL bounds staleness.

Equations referencing count() are not transformed, mixing sampled and upsampled values in one response

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` only rewrites y-axis columns; `equations=self.get_equation_list(organization, request)` is passed through untouched. A widget using yAxis `count()` plus an equation such as `equation(count() / count_unique(user))` on an allowlisted error query will get an upsampled `count()` series next to an equation computed from the raw sampled `count()`, producing internally inconsistent numbers (e.g. an "events per user" ratio computed from a count 10x smaller than the displayed count). Either rewrite count() inside equations or reject/skip upsampling when equations are present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenates components with '_' without escaping, allowing key collisions

userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with single underscores and no delimiter escaping. Two different requests can therefore map to the same cache entry, e.g. name="a_b" with parent="c" produces the same key as name="a" with parent="b_c". Today Grafana UIDs are alphanumeric so this is unlikely to trigger, but user/service-account identifiers and future actions are not guaranteed to be underscore-free, and a collision produces a wrong deny verdict for a different resource. Use a separator that cannot appear in the components (or length-prefix/hash the components).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify ambiguous underscore concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey as causing key collisions and incorrect denial cache hits for different permission requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denial entries block the DB fallback and override newer grants, reintroducing the bug this PR fixes

Once a Check is denied, the result is written to permDenialCache with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) and every subsequent Check for the same (user, action, resource, parent) returns deny immediately, without consulting permCache or the database. This defeats the PR's own fix in two ways: (1) if a Check for a newly created dashboard races the permission insert (or hits a lagging read replica, which is the normal deployment for legacysql in cloud), the denial is pinned for 30s and the creator is locked out of the dashboard they just created — the exact symptom the PR claims to fix; (2) when permissions are granted after a denial was recorded (admin grants access, folder moved), the user stays denied for up to 30s even though the database now allows it. Additionally, the denial cache is consulted *before* the positive permCache, so a denial entry written at time T wins over a permCache entry refreshed at T+20 with allowing scopes. There is also no invalidation of denial entries when permissions change. Consider checking the denial cache only after a positive permCache/DB lookup fails, or deleting the denial entry whenever a fresh DB query allows.

Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous:0 and render:0 share entries

userPermDenialCacheKey is built from namespace, UserUID, action, name and parent — but not the identity type. The subject "anonymous:0" (TypeAnonymous) and "render:0" (TypeRenderService) both parse to UserUID "0", so they produce identical denial keys. Because the denial cache is checked before any identity-type handling, an anonymous user's denial for e.g. dashboards:read on dashboard X (anonymous users can lack read scope on specific dashboards) will cause the render service to be denied rendering of X for up to 30s, even though getRendererPermissions unconditionally grants wildcard read to renderers — and vice versa, a renderer denial of a write action can deny an anonymous user who has that action via a custom Viewer-role permission. Include the identity type in the denial key.

Denial cache has unbounded cardinality (one entry per user×action×resource×parent)

Unlike permCache, which is bounded per (namespace, user, action), the denial cache creates a distinct entry for every denied (user, action, resource, parent-folder) combination. In the standalone server deployment (RegisterRBACAuthZService) the underlying cache may be a shared external cache (e.g. Redis). A user — or an attacker — enumerating resource names via Check requests will write one denial entry per unknown/unauthorized resource per user, each held for 30s. With batch/Check-heavy clients this can flood the shared cache with garbage entries and cause memory/eviction pressure on the cache cluster. Consider bounding the denial cache (e.g. only caching denials for resources known to exist, using an LRU, or per-user entry limits).

No test covering access after a permission is granted post-denial (the issue this PR fixes)

TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, DB fallback on miss, DB fallback on stale cache, and deny-from-denial-cache, but there is no test for the critical ordering: a denial entry written before a permission was granted (or before the resource existed) versus a later DB/permCache state that allows. Given that the PR's stated purpose is 'creator can't access the dashboard they just created', a test should pin down the expected behavior when a Check for the not-yet-permitted resource precedes the creation/grant — currently that test would fail (deny wins), which suggests the intended semantics are not covered anywhere.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth 'state' is a static per-provider value, so the CSRF/state check provides no real protection

OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth2 `state` and validates the callback with `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. `Pipeline.signature` is a deterministic value derived from the pipeline/provider name (the tests hard-code the same state, `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`, across different users, organizations, and sessions), so it is identical for every user of the deployment. Any user who starts their own GitHub install flow sees this value in the authorize redirect URL and can therefore forge a valid callback for any other user's pipeline. Concretely: an attacker obtains their own OAuth `code` (authenticating as themselves), then gets a victim's browser to hit the setup URL with that code plus the known state; the token exchange succeeds in the victim's pipeline and binds the attacker's GitHub login as `github_authenticated_user`, after which the installer-identity check passes and the integration is linked. The state must be a per-pipeline/per-session random nonce (stored in pipeline state and compared on callback), not a shared constant, for the check described in the PR description to be meaningful.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: OAuth state is set to the static pipeline.signature instead of a per-request random nonce, undermining CSRF protection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError/500 when existing Integration has no 'sender' in metadata

GitHubInstallation.dispatch accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` unconditionally when an Integration exists but no OrganizationIntegration does. However, `build_integration` only stores `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is set, so Integrations can legitimately exist without a "sender" key (e.g. created through the pipeline when the installation webhook never supplied a sender, or legacy rows). For such installations this line raises KeyError and the user gets a 500 instead of a graceful error page. The lookup should use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a failed verification.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify an unchecked access to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] that raises a KeyError when sender metadata was not set during integration creation.

false_positives.candidate:
Installer verification is skipped when the installation webhook has not yet created the Integration

The new user-identity check (comparing `github_authenticated_user` against `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`) only runs on the branch where the Integration row already exists. That row is created by the GitHub `installation` webhook; if the webhook is delayed or lost, `Integration.objects.get` raises DoesNotExist and dispatch calls `pipeline.next_step()` with no verification at all, and `build_integration` later creates the Integration without a sender. This means the security control this PR is meant to add can be bypassed by simply racing the webhook (or by webhook delivery failure), which is a common condition in practice. The verification (or an explicit 'installation not yet registered, retry' failure) should also apply on the DoesNotExist path, or the pipeline should wait/retry until the webhook-created Integration is visible.

Unhandled exceptions from get_user_info and token exchange produce a 500 instead of the error page

In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is not wrapped in error handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP call to GitHub's /user endpoint and raises ApiError on any non-2xx response (e.g. revoked token, GitHub 5xx, secondary rate limit); `safe_urlopen` for the token exchange can likewise raise on connection errors. These exceptions propagate out of the pipeline view and result in an unhandled 500 error rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` error page shown for the other failure modes. The calls should be inside the try/except (or a separate one) that falls back to `error(request, self.active_organization)`.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 / 'installation could not be found' path

The test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, i.e. that build_integration's IntegrationError on a GitHub 404 is surfaced. After the change it asserts `b"Invalid installation request."` because the second request uses a state (`ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`) that does not match the pipeline signature, so the flow fails at the state check and the `responses.replace(..., status=404)` stub for `/app/installations/<id>` is never exercised. The renamed test now effectively duplicates a state-mismatch test, and the 'installation could not be found' regression path (IntegrationError raised in build_integration on GitHub 404) has no coverage. A separate test with a valid state and a 404 stub should be added, along with a dedicated test for the state-mismatch case.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers removal of literal "alias" instead of the created IDP aliases

In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup is registered as `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (lines 381 and 425), using the literal string "alias" rather than the actual alias of the created provider ("idp-alias-" + i / "idp-alias-20"). As a result, none of the 21 identity providers created by the test are registered for cleanup, and cleanup instead issues DELETE requests for a non-existent "alias" provider (likely 404, which can fail the cleanup phase). The leaked providers include 10 IDPs that remain linked to organization "orga", so if testCacheIDPForLogin runs before testCacheIDPByOrg (JUnit method order is not guaranteed), testCacheIDPByOrg's assertion of exactly 6 IDPs for orga (orga-identity-provider + 5 linked) will fail. The same copy-paste bug exists at line 381 inside the creation loop and at line 425 for idp-alias-20 (and pre-exists at line 303 in testCacheIDPByOrg).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same cleanup alias bug: removal targets the literal "alias" instead of the created provider alias, "idp-alias-" + i. Its additional discussion of consequences does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() skips invalidating the internalId cache entry when the alias key is not cached

In remove(alias), when the alias cache key is not in the session's invalidation set and there is no cached entry under the alias key, no invalidation is registered for the provider's internalId (the else-branch only calls registerIDPInvalidation when `cached != null`). An IDP can, however, be cached under its internalId via getById() without ever having been looked up by alias, so after remove() completes, a subsequent getById(internalId) can return the already-deleted identity provider from cache. This staleness matters even more now that getForLogin() and getByOrganization() resolve cached list entries through session.identityProviders().getById(id). The fix is to always invalidate the internalId (e.g. registerIDPInvalidation(storedIdp) in both branches, guarding for null). Note this hole pre-exists but the method was reworked in this PR and the new list caches depend on getById freshness.

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares an org-aware wrapped original against the raw updated model

In update(), the "original" model passed to registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate comes from getById(), which returns the anonymous wrapper whose isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled (createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel). The "updated" model is the raw caller-supplied model whose isEnabled() is the stored value. The skip decisions in registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate therefore depend on the organization's runtime enablement state rather than only on stored IDP attributes. Concrete scenario: an org-linked, public, enabled IDP whose organization is disabled appears in the cached getForLogin lists (the JPA query is config-based); if an admin then disables that IDP, both predicate tests evaluate to false and the login caches are NOT invalidated, leaving a disabled IDP in the cached getForLogin() stream. Correctness then relies entirely on every consumer re-checking isEnabled() — only the two OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean paths patched in this PR do so. Using the raw delegate model (idpDelegate.getById) as "original" would make the invalidation decision deterministic and independent of org state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions contains inverted, dead feature-flag logic that invites accidental re-enabling

The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` reads `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns `false` in both branches, so the function always returns false regardless of the flag. Besides being dead code, the logic is inverted relative to its name (when the flag is ON, `enabled` is false; when the flag is OFF, `enabled` is true), and the result is never used. A future maintainer 'fixing' the seemingly-wrong inversion (e.g. changing the first branch to `return true`) would silently re-enable the SQL expression code path that this PR deliberately disables for CVE-2024-9264. Since the intent is to unconditionally reject SQL expressions, the flag lookup and helper should be removed entirely and the case body should just return an error directly, making the security intent explicit and unambiguous.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that enableSqlExpressions returns false in both branches regardless of the feature flag, unconditionally disabling SQL expressions—the same underlying issue as the golden comment. Its additional security context and proposed fix do not change that match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB methods keep unreachable code paths in SQLCommand.Execute alive with silent failure semantics

The new `DB` stub makes every method return `errors.New("not implemented")`. Because `NewSQLCommand` calls `sql.TablesList` (which now always fails) the command can never be constructed, so `SQLCommand.Execute` is dead code — yet it still contains a live call to `db.QueryFramesInto` whose error is swallowed into `rsp.Error` and returned as a successful (nil-error) result. If the construction-time guard is ever relaxed (e.g. by re-enabling the flag), queries would fail at execute time with a generic 'not implemented' error surfaced as query data rather than a clear server-side rejection. Consider deleting or clearly deprecating the unreachable Execute body, or failing fast, so the disabled state is enforced in one place only.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the DB methods as stubs returning hardcoded 'not implemented' errors, including TablesList and QueryFramesInto. Although it emphasizes downstream command-construction and error-handling consequences, it identifies the same underlying issue as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" misleads users about why the query was rejected

When a user submits a SQL expression query, they now get `"sqlExpressions is not implemented"`. The feature is implemented but intentionally disabled for security reasons; additionally, the message references the internal feature-toggle name (`sqlExpressions`) which still exists in featuremgmt and can be enabled by admins, yet enabling it has no effect. An admin who enables the `sqlExpressions` feature toggle per the existing documented behavior will still get this error with no indication that the flag is now a no-op. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled/unavailable (and ideally the flag should be removed or documented as non-functional).

No tests verify that SQL expression queries are rejected, and existing SQL tests are not updated

This PR changes the behavior of the SQL expression query type from executing (behind the `sqlExpressions` feature flag) to always failing, but adds no test asserting the new behavior (e.g. that ReadQuery with QueryTypeSQL returns an error, and that the go-duck-backed TablesList/QueryFramesInto paths are never reachable). Existing tests covering SQL expressions in pkg/expr (e.g. tests constructing SQLCommand or calling sql.TablesList) would now fail against the 'not implemented' stubs if they exercise the removed functionality, and no updated tests are included in the changed files. A regression test is needed so that a future refactor cannot silently re-enable this path without a test failure.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is incomplete: no re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock

GetWebAssets reads the cache under RLock, and if empty, acquires the write lock and unconditionally re-reads the manifest without re-checking whether another goroutine already populated the cache in the meantime. Two consequences in non-Dev mode: (1) redundant duplicate file reads on a cold start, and more importantly (2) goroutine A succeeds and caches a valid *dtos.EntryPointAssets; goroutine B, waiting behind A, then re-reads the file and if that read fails transiently, line 69 (`entryPointAssetsCache = result`) overwrites the good cached value with nil and B returns an error — a user-visible failure even though a valid cached result existed. The fix is to re-read `entryPointAssetsCache` after taking the write lock (or before assigning at line 69) and return the cached value if it is now non-nil in non-Dev mode.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incomplete double-checked locking bug in GetWebAssets: after finding the cache empty under a read lock, the function acquires a write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine populated the cache. The candidate adds potential consequences and a fix but matches the underlying issue exactly.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

The fix is to re-read `entryPointAssetsCache` after taking the write lock (or before assigning at line 69) and return the cached value if it is now non-nil in non-Dev mode.

Although framed around incomplete double-checked locking, it describes the same error-handling flaw as the golden comment.

Write lock is held across file/network I/O, serializing all GetWebAssets callers

To fully close the race, the cached value must be treated as immutable after publication (and any mutation, such as SetContentDeliveryURL, must happen before it is stored), or a copy returned per call.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

Changing `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run increases the run frequency of every job in `clean()` (expired snapshots, dashboard version deletion, expired image deletion, user invite expiry, short URL deletion, query history row-limit enforcement) by 10x, not just the annotation cleanup this PR targets. A user who configures `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above those limits (the test itself uses 32,767, which would exceed SQL Server's 2100 limit) will get hard failures from the DELETE on every cleanup cycle. The old single-statement DELETE with a subquery had no such parameter count. The guard should key off the actual dialect's parameter limit (or the actual len(ids)) rather than only SQLite's 999.

In the SQLite large-batch branch of deleteByIDs, the ID list is built with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop, which copies the accumulated string on every iteration. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes use the request context, so they are canceled as soon as the request completes

In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to LegacyStorage derives its context from the incoming request context (`ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`). The handler returns immediately after the unified-storage write, and the apiserver cancels the request context when the request finishes. Because the legacy write runs asynchronously, it will frequently observe an already-canceled parent context and fail with 'context canceled' (or the 10s timeout never even matters). The result is that the legacy store is silently not written for many (potentially most) operations, which defeats the stated purpose of mode 3 ('write to legacy as a safe measure') and leaves the two stores divergent. The goroutines should use a detached context, e.g. `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (plus the timeout), or a background context carrying only the logger.

Create records storage failures under the legacy metric

In DualWriterMode3.Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. This records a legacy-storage duration/latency observation for a failure that happened in the unified storage, corrupting the dual-writer metrics: legacy dashboards will show errors and latencies that never touched legacy storage, and no storage-side failure is recorded for the failing call. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`, as done in Delete/DeleteCollection.

Update records storage failures under the legacy metric

In DualWriterMode3.Update, the error path after `d.Storage.Update` fails calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Same defect as in Create: a unified-storage failure is attributed to the legacy store in the metrics (wrong metric name, wrong latency sample, wrong error count). It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection records the async legacy write under the storage metric

In the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. The legacy write outcome is attributed to the unified-storage metric instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, so legacy delete-collection failures/errors never show up in legacy metrics and pollute storage metrics. Compare with Delete (line 113) and Update (line 140), which correctly use recordLegacyDuration.

Failures of the asynchronous legacy writes are never logged

The previous implementation logged an error when the legacy write failed ('unable to create object in legacy storage', etc.). The new goroutines only record a Prometheus metric (`recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`) and discard the error entirely; nothing is ever written to the log. Operators investigating a divergence between unified and legacy storage will have no log evidence of when or why the legacy write failed (timeout, conflict, validation error). The goroutines should at minimum log the returned error, e.g. `if err != nil { log.Error(err, "legacy write failed") }` (using a detached context for the logger).

Async legacy Create mutates the request object concurrently with response serialization

In Create, the goroutine passes the caller's `obj` (the same runtime.Object that `d.Storage.Create` was called with and whose result the handler serializes to the client) to `d.Legacy.Create`. Storage Create implementations commonly mutate the passed object in place (setting UID, resourceVersion, creation timestamp, generation). While the apiserver is serializing the response from the unified write, the legacy write goroutine can be mutating the same object concurrently — a data race that can produce corrupted response bodies or runtime panics under `-race`. The object passed to the legacy goroutine should be a deep copy, and the same consideration applies to `objInfo` in Update (the legacy Update runs objInfo.UpdatedObject against shared state while the handler may still be using it).

Create error test never mocks Storage.Create, so the test exercises a mock panic instead of the error path

The test case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' (input failingObj) only sets up a legacy `Create` expectation via setupLegacyFn and leaves setupStorageFn nil. Mode3's Create calls `d.Storage.Create` first; the storageMock has no expectation for it, so the mock will panic ('mock: I don't know what to return because the method call was unexpected') rather than return an error. The test therefore does not verify the intended error path (and looks like the legacy/storage mock setups were swapped relative to the other tests, e.g. TestMode3_Delete which mocks storage only).

Tests never assert that the asynchronous legacy write actually happens, and the shared mock is used from untracked goroutines

Mode 3's defining behavior is that writes go to unified storage synchronously and to legacy storage asynchronously. None of the new tests assert that Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection were invoked (e.g. via m.AssertExpectations or eventually-style waiting), so a regression that drops the legacy write entirely would still pass. Additionally, the legacy calls happen in fire-and-forget goroutines sharing the same non-thread-safe testify `mock.Mock` with the test goroutine, and the test returns without waiting for them — this is both a potential data race under -race and a source of flaky panics when the goroutine calls the mock after the test has finished. The tests should wait for the async write (e.g. a channel/signaled mock or polling on mock call counts) and then assert the legacy call happened.
