TestMode3_Get declares `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` locally, shadowing the package-level `p` used by all other tests in the file (the PR even removed exactly this pattern from dualwriter_mode1_test.go). This is inconsistent and means the metrics registered for this test are silently different from every other mode-3 test; if the intent was to share one registry, this test diverges from it and a future reader can't tell whether it is intentional.

Stale JSDoc and props comment reference the removed Ruler fetch

The component JSDoc still says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints" (line 25) and the `expectedRulesCount` prop comment (lines 16-21) still says "Ruler response might contain different number of rules", but this PR removed the `useGetGrafanaRulerGroupQuery` call and all ruler handling from GrafanaGroupLoader. In `useGrafanaGroupsGenerator`, the comment at line 81 ("This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load...") and the variable name `cacheAndRulerPreload` (line 84) describe the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` call that this PR deleted. Only the prometheusApi cache upsert remains, so both the comment and the name are now wrong and should be updated.

Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting() disables the $__range guard, causing wrong results for range-variable queries

Queries are now mapped through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 299) before the split/no-split decision at line 300. querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) to detect `$__range`, `$__from`, `$__to`, etc. in the raw expression, but after template interpolation those variables have already been substituted with the full dashboard range, so the check never matches. The code comment at line 285-287 explicitly says such queries must not be split because the range variable becomes incorrect per sub-request. Consequence: a query like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` now gets split into 1-day chunks with the full range (e.g. `[2d]`) baked in, and each sub-request's start/end truncates the lookback window, so the returned counts differ from the unsplit query — a silent data-correctness regression. The range-variable check must be evaluated against the pre-interpolation expression (or such queries must otherwise stay unsplit). There is also no test covering queries containing $__range after this change, so nothing would catch this.

Template variables are applied twice in the shard-splitting path

runShardSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (line 52), and then splitQueriesByStreamShard() delegates each sub-request to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which — after this same PR — applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again to those already-interpolated targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). So every query is interpolated at least twice, and once more per additional shard group cycle. A second interpolation pass is not idempotent in general: if a variable's value, a label value, or a log-line filter regex legitimately contains `$` or `${...}` sequences (common in log content), the second pass will re-expand them against template variables, corrupting the query sent to Loki. The updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' shows applyTemplateVariables being called 5 times for a single query, but the test mock's replace is trivially idempotent, so this corruption is not covered. The interpolation should happen in exactly one layer, or runSplitQuery should skip interpolation for targets that were already interpolated by the caller.

The new tests only cover happy-path interpolation of `$__auto` and `$step`. There is no test asserting that a query containing `$__range` (or `$__from`/`$__to`) is still routed to the non-splitting path now that interpolation happens before the querySupportsSplitting() check. Since interpolation substitutes these variables, the existing guard silently stops matching, and without a regression test this data-correctness behavior (documented in the comment on querySupportsSplitting) can break unnoticed — as it appears to in this PR.

This is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race: two concurrent requests from different new devices can both observe count < limit and both perform the upsert insert path, inserting two devices even when the limit allows one. The same applies across multiple Grafana instances sharing a database. There is no mapping to a dedicated status code or user-facing message, no error wrapping with context, and no logging at this site. Translation cache key ignores fallback locales, so cached fallback strings go stale when default_locale changes

However, the LRU cache key in I18n.translate is built as "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}", which does not include the fallback locales. SiteSetting.default_locale is a runtime-changeable setting (admins can change it from the site settings UI without a restart or I18n.reload!), so after such a change, requests for a key missing in the user's locale will keep serving the previously cached string from the OLD default locale until the cache is cleared. When the Fallbacks backend resolves a miss by looking up the key in the default locale or :en, those locales' YAML files are never loaded by that code path. The PR compensates for this by calling I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale, but that before_filter only runs for web requests. In background jobs and mailers (e.g. user-targeted emails where I18n.locale is set to the recipient's locale), the fallback locale files are not loaded, so fallback lookups will miss and produce 'translation missing' strings (or the raw missing-translation marker) instead of falling back to the default/English text. This PR introduces a nontrivial behavior: a custom FallbackLocaleList whose [] computes [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en] on every lookup, a per-request ensure_loaded! in ApplicationController#set_locale, and interaction between fallbacks and the caching/lazy-loading translate accelerator. None of this is covered by tests. At minimum there should be specs verifying that (a) a key missing in the user's locale is served from the site default locale and then :en, (b) the fallback order is correct when locales coincide, and (c) the accelerator still caches correctly across locales. Without these, regressions in translation resolution (e.g. from future i18n gem upgrades or changes to the accelerator) will ship silently.

Fallbacks are now enabled in development and test, masking missing-translation errors

BlockedEmail.should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with the raw email string, and there is a unique index on the email column as-is. User emails are not normalized to lowercase on assignment (UsersController#create passes params[:email] straight into the model, and mixed-case emails can exist since email uniqueness is also case-sensitive here). A user whose address was blocked as 'spammer@example.com' can register as 'Spammer@Example.com' and the lookup returns no row, completely bypassing the block. The lookup (and the unique index) should compare downcased emails.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, which allows a blocked user to bypass the block by changing the capitalization of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
change_email flow bypasses the blocked-email check entirely

The new EmailValidator only runs on the User model when `email_changed?`. The change_email action never assigns user.email; it creates an email_token with the new address (`user.email_tokens.create(email: lower_email)`) and the address is later attached to the user when the token is confirmed (EmailToken.confirm), which typically uses update_attribute/save paths that skip validations. As a result, an existing user can switch their account email to any blocked address and receive mail there, defeating the purpose of the blocked-email feature. The blocked/whitelist/blacklist check must also be applied in change_email (and at token creation/confirmation), not only in the model's email-changed validation.

Read-modify-write race on match_count loses increments under concurrency

`record.match_count += 1; record.save` reads the counter in Ruby and writes it back. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email will both read the same value and both write value+1, losing one increment (and clobbering last_match_at updates with a stale AR object). Use an atomic update such as `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` instead.

Any server-side email error permanently marks the email invalid with the wrong message

On a failed account creation, the controller pushes `result.values.email` into rejectedEmails whenever the response contains any `errors.email` key. That includes errors unrelated to the email being unacceptable, e.g. 'Email has already been taken' or the whitelist 'not allowed' error. The emailValidation computed property then shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') ('invalid email address') for that address, which is misleading for a taken or blocked address (the server message is 'is not allowed.' / 'has already been taken'). The client should key off the specific error type, or at least surface a message matching the server's reason. The email also stays rejected for the lifetime of the controller even if the underlying condition changes.

Validator spec stubs out the behavior under test; no integration coverage for users or the controller contract

The only spec for EmailValidator stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, so the actual model wiring (User's `validates :email, email: true`, the migration, and the BlockedEmail lookup) is never exercised end-to-end: nothing proves that a user with a blocked email fails validation and cannot be created. There is also no spec for the new UsersController#create failure payload (`errors` hash and `values` hash) that the new frontend code in create_account_controller.js depends on, so a rename or shape change of that JSON would not be caught. Add a spec that fabricates a blocked email, builds/creates a User with it, and asserts the validation error, plus a controller spec asserting the errors/values keys on failed create.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
-ms-align-items is not a real vendor-prefixed property

The new `align-items` mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`. No browser has ever implemented a property with that name; Microsoft's flexbox prefixes are `-ms-flex-align` (already emitted on the line above) and, for the modern syntax, the unprefixed `align-items` (also already emitted). This declaration is always invalid and silently dropped, adding dead code to the generated stylesheet for every flex-aligned rule. It should be removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify -ms-align-items as a nonexistent property and -ms-flex-align as the correct legacy Microsoft flexbox property.

false_positives.candidate:
.small-action button { float: right } is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container

This change makes `.small-action` a flex container (`@include flexbox()` at the top of the rule), but the nested `button { float: right; }` at line 309 was left unchanged. Floats on flex items are ignored by the flexbox spec, so the float has no effect. Previously the button (e.g. the small-action buttons in the topic stream) was pushed to the far right edge of the row; now it will sit immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text with default spacing, since no `margin-left: auto` was added to replace the float. The trailing `clear: both` on `.small-action` (line 312) is likewise dead. The button needs `margin-left: auto` (or the container needs `justify-content: space-between`) to restore right-edge alignment.

margin-left: auto on .panel does not right-align in the legacy flexbox implementations the mixins target

The new `flexbox()` mixin deliberately emits the 2009 syntax (`display: -webkit-box`, `display: -moz-box`) and the IE10 syntax (`display: -ms-flexbox`), but the right-alignment of the header panel relies solely on `margin-left: auto` on `.panel`. Auto-margin packing in flex containers is a feature of the final flexbox spec: IE10's `-ms-flexbox` implementation notoriously ignores auto margins for alignment, and the 2009 `-webkit-box`/`-moz-box` spec provides `box-pack` instead. So in exactly the older browsers these prefixes were added for, the search/hamburger/user panel will not be pushed to the right edge and will sit next to the site title, breaking the header layout. Either add a `box-pack: end`-based fallback or accept dropping the ancient-prefix output.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing question mark, so the include guard is never called by AMS

ActiveModel::Serializers only invokes the conditional-include hook named `include_<attribute>?` (with a question mark) — every other guard in this file follows that convention (e.g. `include_email?`, `include_stats?`, `include_card_image_badge?`). The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no `?`), so it is dead code: the serializer never calls it. Consequently, when a user has no website, the JSON still contains `"website_name": null` instead of omitting the key, and the intended `website.present?` guard has no effect. Rename it to `include_website_name?`.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same missing '?' suffix on include_website_name and its effect on conditional attribute inclusion. It does not mention the additional string-literal mutation concern, but it matches the golden comment's primary issue.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name is not registered as an untrusted attribute, leaking TL0 users' website info to anonymous visitors

The serializer lists `website` in `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which suppresses it when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true (e.g. a TL0 user viewed by an anonymous visitor). The new `website_name` attribute is not added to that list, so for those same users the API still serializes `website_name`, which now includes not just the host but the full URL path (e.g. `example.com/private-page`). This defeats the purpose of hiding `website` for untrusted profiles and leaks information the site explicitly intends to hide. `website_name` must be added to `untrusted_attributes` alongside `website`.

Untrusted-attributes spec list was not updated to cover website_name

The `untrusted_attributes` list in the 'TL0 user seen as anonymous' context still contains only `bio_raw bio_cooked bio_excerpt location website profile_background card_background`. Since this PR adds a new attribute derived directly from `website`, `:website_name` should be added to that list so the spec verifies it is suppressed for restricted users. As written, the existing test suite would not catch the leak of `website_name` (host plus full path) for TL0 profiles viewed anonymously — adding it would make the spec fail today and force the fix.

URI(website.to_s) is re-parsed up to three times per serialization

The `website_name` method calls `URI(website.to_s)` once for the host (line 138) and again for the path (lines 143, 146, 149), meaning the URL string is parsed up to three times for every user serialized. This runs for every user in any payload using UserSerializer (user pages, staff lists, etc.). Parse the URI once into a local variable and reuse it for both `host` and `path`.

Query string and fragment are silently dropped from the displayed path

`website_name` builds the display string as `website_host + URI(website.to_s).path`, discarding the query string and fragment. A user whose website is `http://example.com/profile?user=42` on a same-domain instance will see `example.com/profile` in their profile, which links correctly (the href uses the full `website`) but displays a URL that does not correspond to the link target. If showing the complete URL is the goal, the query/fragment should be preserved (or this limitation acknowledged).

true_positives.golden_comment: The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Origin check via `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` is a weak substring match

The postMessage handler validates the sender with `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin) === -1`, i.e. it accepts any message whose origin string appears anywhere in the configured discourseUrl. Because it is a substring (not prefix/exact) match, an origin that happens to be contained in the URL string passes; e.g. a discourseUrl of `http://discourse.example.com` accepts an event from origin `http://d` (host `d`) or any origin that is a substring of the URL. The consequence is limited to setting the iframe height today, but the correct check is an exact/parsed comparison (e.g. compare `e.origin` against the URL's `protocol + '//' + host`), since future message types would inherit the flaw.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same underlying vulnerability: origin validation using indexOf performs a substring match rather than an exact origin comparison, allowing unauthorized origins to pass. The differing bypass examples do not change the core issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: URL interpolated unescaped into an HTML attribute in the 'imported from' footer `contents << "...#{url}..."` interpolates the embed URL directly into HTML that is later stored via the raw_html cook method and rendered with `raw`. The `^https?://` regex check on line 11 does not exclude single quotes, `>` or other markup characters that can appear in a URL's path/query (e.g. `http://embeddable-host/?x='>`). This allows attribute breakout and markup injection into the stored post. The URL should be HTML-escaped (and the href properly quoted) before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unescaped URL interpolation and resulting XSS vulnerability described in the golden comment, though it does not mention the separate nil-contents NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`<%- end if %>` is a Ruby syntax error; the embed view fails to render

Line 6 closes the header if/else with `<%- end if %>`, which ERB compiles to the Ruby fragment `end if ` — a modifier `if` with no condition, a syntax error. Every render of the embed view (the success path when a topic exists) will raise ActionView::Template::Error / SyntaxError and return a 500 to the embedding site, making the whole feature non-functional in the topic-found case. It should be `<%- end %>`. The controller specs don't catch this because `TopicView` is stubbed with a mock, so the template never renders against a real topic view.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify `end if` as invalid Ruby/ERB syntax that causes rendering to fail and specify replacing it with `end` to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Nil `i.content` (or a feed error) crashes the whole poll, and retry is disabled

`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` assumes every feed item has `content`; RSS feeds that only provide `description` (or ATOM entries with only a summary) will raise NoMethodError on nil, aborting the entire `poll_feed` run partway through — items after the offending one are never imported. Since the job has `sidekiq_options retry: false`, the failure is silent until the next hourly run, which will fail at the same item. `open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url)` is likewise unguarded, so a transient network error kills the run. Guard for missing content (fall back to `i.description`) and rescue per-item/feed-level errors.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue: calling i.content.scrub when content is nil can crash processing, and it recommends falling back to i.description. The additional network-error and retry concerns do not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unescaped request.referer interpolated into inline JavaScript allows XSS on the Discourse origin

The embed layout renders `parent.postMessage({...}, '<%= request.referer %>')` with the raw Referer header inserted into a JavaScript string literal without escape_javascript/html escaping. The `ensure_embeddable` before_filter only validates that the referer's *host* equals SiteSetting.embeddable_host, so an attacker making a direct HTTP request (where the Referer header is fully attacker-controlled, e.g. `http://<embeddable_host>/', alert(document.cookie), '`) can break out of the string literal and execute arbitrary script in a page served from the Discourse origin. This is a reflected XSS; the value must be escaped with `j()`/escape_javascript before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious header content to break out of the string and execute arbitrary scripts.

false_positives.candidate:
Imported RSS content is stored as raw HTML with skip_validations and rendered with `raw`, enabling stored XSS

`TopicEmbed.import` creates posts with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` and `skip_validations: true`, which makes `Post#cook` return the raw content verbatim (no markdown/sanitization pipeline). The RSS path in `Jobs::PollFeed` passes `i.content` (fully controlled by whatever the feed at feed_polling_url contains) straight into import — unlike `import_remote`, which at least runs the content through ruby-readability's tag/attribute whitelist. `app/views/embed/best.html.erb` then renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. A compromised or malicious feed entry containing `<script>` or `onerror=` handlers is stored and executed on the Discourse forum and on every page that embeds the comments iframe. The feed content needs sanitization (e.g., Sanitize/Nokogiri whitelist) before being stored as raw HTML.

Referer-based authorization is trivially spoofable, allowing unbounded job enqueueing and forced fetching

Access control for /embed/best relies solely on the Referer header matching SiteSetting.embeddable_host. Any non-browser client can set an arbitrary Referer header, so anyone on the internet can hit the endpoint and cause `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` for arbitrary embed_url values. The TopicRetriever throttle is only 60 seconds per exact URL string, so an attacker can vary the URL (query strings, paths) to enqueue an unbounded number of jobs, each of which causes the Discourse server to make an HTTP request to the embeddable host (a limited but real SSRF/abuse vector) and, when feed polling is enabled, synchronously executes the entire Jobs::PollFeed run inside the job. Rate limiting at the controller level and/or a global cap on retrieve jobs is needed.

Discussion replies rendered with `raw post.cooked` include any HTML users managed to post

The embed view renders each post with `<%= raw post.cooked %>`. While normal posts go through the cooking/sanitization pipeline, this view bypasses all of the markup filtering Discourse normally applies when displaying cooked content (e.g., the whitelist applied elsewhere), so any HTML that survives into `cooked` for any post in the topic — including raw_html posts created by other import paths or plugins — is executed verbatim in a frame that is served from the Discourse origin with `X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL`. Combined with the raw_html import path this widens the XSS surface; cooked output should be passed through the same sanitization used by the main topic renderer.

Non-atomic SETNX/EXPIRE can leave the throttle key without a TTL, permanently blocking retrieval

`retrieved_recently?` does `$redis.setnx(key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(key, 60)`. If the process dies (or the Redis connection drops) between the two calls, the key exists with no TTL and never expires, so that embed_url is throttled forever — the topic is never retrieved and the embed shows the loading page indefinitely. Use a single atomic command (e.g., `SET key 1 EX 60 NX` available via the redis gem, or a Lua script) so the expiry is always set.

PostCreator jobs are enqueued inside the wrapping transaction, before the TopicEmbed row commits

`TopicEmbed.import` wraps `creator.create` in `Topic.transaction` and only creates the `TopicEmbed` record *after* the post is created. PostCreator's `enqueue_jobs` (process_post, feature_topic_users) runs while still inside this outer transaction. If the subsequent `TopicEmbed.create!` fails — most plausibly in the race where two concurrent retrieve jobs for the same embed_url both pass the `where(embed_url: url).first` check and the second hits the unique index — the whole transaction rolls back, but the already-enqueued Sidekiq jobs referencing the rolled-back post/topic are not un-enqueued, and `TopicTrackingState.publish_new` messages have already been published on MessageBus for a topic that never committed. The unique-index race should also be handled (rescue RecordNotUnique / create the embed first or use find-or-create).

`feed_key` is dead code — the modified/ETag check it hints at was never implemented

The `feed_key` method builds a Redis key (`feed-modified:<sha1 of feed url>`) but nothing in the class ever reads or writes it. Either the conditional-fetch logic was dropped accidentally, in which case the key is misleading dead code, or the intent was to skip polling when the feed is unchanged — either way it should be removed or wired up. As it stands every poll re-parses and re-imports the full feed each hour.

`force: true` added to an already-shipped migration can silently drop the top_topics table

This PR modifies the existing CreateTopTopics migration (2013-12-23) to add `force: true`, which makes `create_table` DROP the table if it exists. For any database that already ran this migration and then re-runs it (e.g., `rake db:migrate:redo`, or environments that replay migrations), all top_topics data would be destroyed. Editing historical migrations also means schema state diverges between deployments that ran the old version and the new one. The `force: true` should be reverted here (it belongs only in brand-new migrations, if anywhere).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize silently overrides the width/height variant

The file now defines `self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 and a second `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149. In Ruby the later definition wins, so any existing caller that passes width and height separately (the signature kept at line 145 implies such callers exist, e.g. avatar/import paths) will actually hit the second method: `dimensions` receives the width and `opts` receives the height (an Integer). Inside `optimize`, `opts[:allow_animation]` is then called on an Integer, which raises `TypeError: no implicit conversion of Symbol into Integer`, breaking every width/height-style downsize call at runtime. The first definition is dead code and the width/height calling convention is broken; either remove the old method and update all callers, or give the dimensions variant a different name.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions, with the later dimensions-string variant overriding the width/height variant and breaking existing calls that pass separate width and height arguments.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hard-coded 10MB client limit ignores max_image_size_kb and max_attachment_size_kb site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously enforced `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, i.e. the admin-configured per-type limit (images vs attachments). It now always allows 10MB. For attachments there is no server-side downsizing, so on sites where `max_attachment_size_kb` is set below 10MB the client-side guard no longer rejects oversized files with the friendly size message; the upload is sent in full and then fails server-side with a generic error. It also ignores admins who raised limits above 10MB. Only image downsizing was added server-side; the attachment check should keep reading the site setting.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: a hard-coded 10MB client limit replaces configurable per-type site settings, causing client-side validation to diverge from server limits. Not explicitly mentioning the 413 handler does not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Animated GIFs are flattened to a single frame when downsized because the extension check never matches tempfile paths

`OptimizedImage.optimize` selects the animated (gifsicle) pipeline only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but the paths passed from `create_upload` are Rack multipart tempfiles or `FileHelper.download` tempfiles, whose names have no `.gif` extension. Consequently any animated GIF larger than `max_image_size_kb` is processed by ImageMagick `convert from[0]`, which keeps only the first frame: the user's animated upload is silently converted to a still image even when `SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails` is enabled. The animation-detection should be based on the original filename/content, not the tempfile path.

413 error message always claims the limit is 10 MB

`displayErrorForUpload` reports a hard-coded "10 MB" maximum when the server returns 413, but the actual limit is `max_image_size_kb`/`max_attachment_size_kb`, which the admin can set to anything. On sites with a different limit the message shown to users is factually wrong and confusing. The previous code read `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb` here.

API URL download cap hard-coded to 10MB regresses sites with higher max_image_size_kb

The remote-download size limit for API uploads was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hard-coded `10.megabytes`. Sites that configured `max_image_size_kb` above 10MB can no longer pull images via URL larger than 10MB (they now silently fail with `rescue nil`, producing a confusing `tempfile`-nil path), while the client-facing intent of the PR is to allow large images that are then downsized. The cap should be derived from the setting (or at least max(setting, 10MB)).

Downsizing loop runs up to 5 full ImageMagick + ImageOptim passes per upload and can still not converge

Each iteration applies `-resize 80%`, which reduces area to ~64%, so five iterations shrink the image at most ~10x; an image far above the limit (e.g. 50MB against a 1MB setting) still exceeds it after the loop and then fails in `Upload.create_for` with a generic error. Additionally, when `downsize` returns false (convert failure), the return value is ignored, so the loop burns all 5 attempts doing nothing on the same file. Each pass also invokes ImageOptim, making this expensive CPU work on the request path for synchronous API uploads. The loop should stop early on failure and compute a resize percentage that reaches the target in one pass.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe action crashes when the user has no TopicUser record

In TopicsController#unsubscribe, `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil, and the next line immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. A TopicUser row is only created once a user has visited/interacted with a topic, yet the unsubscribe link is included in every notification email — e.g. a user who was mentioned or invited to a topic but never opened it will have no row. Clicking the emailed 'stop receiving notifications' link then raises NoMethodError on nil and returns a 500 instead of unsubscribing them. The code should fall back to TopicUser.change(...)/create the row with the desired level.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same nil dereference: when no TopicUser record exists, tu is nil and calling tu.notification_level causes a crash.

false_positives.candidate: Notification state is mutated by an unauthenticated-CSRF-able GET request, and refresh re-toggles it The `/t/:topic_id/unsubscribe` route is a GET that flips the user's notification_level (watching/tracking -> regular, regular/muted -> muted) with no CSRF token or confirmation. Because it is a plain GET with session cookies, any logged-in user can have their topic notification settings silently changed just by loading a URL — e.g. an attacker can embed `` in a post or external page and the victim's browser will hit the endpoint and mute/unwatch the topic. Additionally, since the same GET both performs the toggle and renders the unsubscribe page, every page refresh or link re-visit toggles the level again (watching -> regular -> muted), so the user's final state depends on how many times the URL was loaded. State changes should not happen on GET (or should be idempotent, e.g. always mute).

Email copy promises to stop notifications but the endpoint only downgrades to regular

The new unsubscribe_link text says 'To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, click here', but TopicsController#unsubscribe only sets watching/tracking users to `regular` — a level that still emails the user when someone replies to them or @mentions them. A user who clicks the link believing they will no longer receive emails for that topic will keep getting reply/mention notifications, which is a trust/warranty problem for the feature. Either the endpoint should set the level to muted, or the message should accurately describe what will still be received.

Unsubscribe link now requires %{unsubscribe_url} and raises for callers that don't supply it

The `unsubscribe_link` locale now contains `%{unsubscribe_url}`, and both `html_part` (line 67) and `body` (line 90) call `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)`. I18n raises `MissingInterpolationArgument` when an interpolation key in the translation has no value, so any caller that builds an email with `add_unsubscribe_link: true` but without passing `unsubscribe_url` will now fail to render and the email send will blow up. The only in-repo caller was updated (and the message_builder spec had to be amended to pass `unsubscribe_url`), but MessageBuilder is a reusable API used by plugins and mailers that set `add_unsubscribe_link` on its own; the builder should default `unsubscribe_url` (e.g. to the user preferences URL) or use `I18n.t(..., unsubscribe_url: ... )` with a fallback so missing values degrade gracefully.

No request specs for the new unsubscribe endpoint

The TopicsController#unsubscribe action introduces new routing, access control (ensure_logged_in), a toggle rule based on the current notification level, and a 301 redirect for slug mismatch, but no controller/request specs were added for it — the only test change in the PR is unrelated (adding unsubscribe_url to a message_builder spec). false_positives.candidate:

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a slot's date matches a date override and the slot falls inside the override window, the code hits `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` and returns before evaluating the `busy` array. That means for any host that has a date override on a given day, existing ACCEPTED bookings and external calendar events that fall inside the override window are completely ignored, and those slots are returned as available. An attendee can then book over an existing booking (double booking / data integrity). The busy check must still run for slots that lie within a date override; only the working-hours check should be skipped for override days.

Working-hours check treats days outside the host's schedule as available

The new working-hours filter uses `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { if (workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())) { ... } })`. If the slot's weekday is not included in any of the host's working-hours entries (e.g. a Saturday slot for a Mon-Fri host), the callback returns undefined for every entry, `find` returns undefined, and the code falls through to the busy-only check — i.e. the slot is considered available. For round-robin events the aggregate availability is the union of hosts, so slots generated from another host's Saturday availability will pass this fixed-host check even though the fixed host never works that day. A day with no matching working-hours entry must be treated as unavailable, not available.

Override date is formatted in the server's local timezone but compared against a UTC date

The date gate compares `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` with `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`. `slotStartTime` is `time.utc()` (UTC mode), but `dayjs(date.start)` is in the server's local timezone, so its `.format()` renders the date in the server's timezone. On any deployment where the process timezone is not UTC, the two dates disagree for times near midnight, causing date overrides to fail to match (slots wrongly unavailable via the fall-through, or wrongly available). The left side should be built with `dayjs.utc(date.start)` so both dates are rendered in UTC.

Optional override.timeZone silently falls back to the server's local timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` uses the new optional `timeZone` field of TimeRange. If a caller supplies date overrides without `timeZone` (the type explicitly allows this), `dayjs.tz(..., undefined)` falls back to the server's local timezone, and the computed organizer UTC offset — and therefore every converted override start/end — will be wrong with no error. getSlots already receives `organizerTimeZone` as a parameter; that should be the fallback (or the field should be required) so a missing value cannot silently corrupt slot times.

Overrides shifted across midnight by the timezone conversion are applied to the wrong invitee day

activeOverrides is selected by checking `dayjs.utc(override.start)` (the raw stored wall-clock-UTC value) against the invitee's day window, but the override times are then converted to invitee-local minutes-of-day. When the offset shift moves the override across a midnight boundary, those minutes belong to a different calendar day than the one being built. Example: an organizer in UTC+13 with an override stored at 23:00–23:30 UTC and an invitee in UTC-11 yields an offset of -1440 minutes; the invitee-local times are 23:00–23:30 on the *previous* day, but the filter attaches the override to the invitee day containing the stored 23:00 UTC, so availability is added on the wrong day (and the user's normal working hours for the wrong day are removed).

The PR description states the primary fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected in round-robin events (issue #8207), but no test covers that scenario: all team-event tests use empty `hosts` or non-fixed configurations, and the only new test added is the timezone variant of a single-user personal event (which also only differs by 30 minutes of offset, both on the same side of the override window). Additionally, there is no test combining a date override with an existing booking, which is exactly the interaction that the new `dateOverrideExist` short-circuit in checkIfIsAvailable gets wrong (slots inside an override are never checked against busy times). Both scenarios should be covered before merging.

Unlike Zoom/Office365, the Webex adapter wraps its refresh in `refreshOAuthTokens` but still validates the response with the full `webexRefreshedTokenSchema.safeParse`, which requires scope (exact literal), token_type, and refresh_token — none of which the credential-sync endpoint returns (it only returns access token + expiry). Every Webex token refresh under sync mode will reject with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned". It should use `parseRefreshTokenResponse` like the other adapted apps, or the schema needs to differ per mode.

Lark refresh incompatible with sync response shape

The refresh result is passed to `handleLarkError<RefreshTokenResp>(resp, this.log)`, which expects Lark's envelope `{code: 0, data: {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`. The credential-sync endpoint returns a plain `{access_token, expiry}` body with no `code`, so `handleLarkError` will treat it as an error (or `data.data.*` will be undefined), making Lark token refresh fail — or worse, persist credentials with undefined refresh_token/refresh_expires_date — whenever sync is enabled.

MS Teams credential key replaced wholesale, dropping refresh_token and email

In `refreshAccessToken`, `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: responseBody } })` replaces the entire stored key with the refresh response. In sync mode the response only contains access token + expiry, so the persisted credential loses `refresh_token` and `email`. Even though the parent app is the source of truth while sync is enabled, the local credential is silently destroyed: turning sync off, or any code path that hits the local refresh (e.g. a team credential where userId is null and `refreshOAuthTokens` falls back to the local refresh function) will then fail because the refresh token is gone.

Outbound credential sync request carries no authentication

The POST to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT sends only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` — no shared secret, signature, or header of any kind. The endpoint's response contains the user's third-party access token, so unless the self-hoster independently protects that URL, anyone who can reach it and guess/enumerate a user id can retrieve arbitrary users' OAuth access tokens. The webhook flow in the other direction is authenticated with CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET; this direction should send a comparable secret (e.g. the same webhook secret as a header).

Credential sync does not reset the `invalid` flag on update

When updating an existing credential the handler only sets `key`. If the credential was previously marked `invalid: true` (e.g. by the invalid_grant handling in Google/Zoom/Webex), pushing fresh valid keys through the webhook will not re-enable it — the app stays broken for that user even though the sync succeeded. The update should also set `invalid: false`.

Webhook secret compared with plain string inequality

`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is not constant-time. For a shared-secret check on an endpoint that can write OAuth credentials, use a timing-safe comparison (crypto.timingSafeEqual) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte to an attacker who can measure response times.

No tests for the webhook or the sync-mode refresh paths

The PR adds a new externally-callable endpoint that writes OAuth credentials and rewires token refresh for ~10 apps behind an env flag, with zero automated tests (the checklist explicitly says no tests were added). At minimum: webhook auth/validation/404/200 paths, and refresh behavior for each adapted app with sync both enabled and disabled. Given the number of adapters that break in sync mode (Google, HubSpot, Zoho, Webex, Lark, Zoom), tests would have caught most of these regressions before merge.

Although it adds retry concerns and does not explicitly flag the omitted SendGrid DELETE call, it clearly matches the underlying orphaned-record issue.

If the handler responds before these complete (serverless), the old booking's scheduled email/SMS is never cancelled in SendGrid/Twilio, and the reminder rows are never removed, so reminders for the superseded booking are still delivered. In the `update` mutation, `remindersToUpdate.forEach(async (reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` (and the same pattern at the removed-event-types loop around line 376 and the deleted-step loop around line 519) never awaits the async callbacks. These calls now perform DB writes (setting `cancelled: true`, deleting rows) and network calls (SendGrid/Twilio), so their outcome is nondeterministic relative to the rest of the mutation and the HTTP response; on serverless the pending work may be terminated before executing. This means reminders for edited steps / disabled event types can remain scheduled and still be sent. Collect and await the promises.

Cancellations are deferred to the next cron run, so reminders sending within ~15 minutes are still sent

When a booking is cancelled, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only sets `cancelled: true` and relies on this cron (running every 15 minutes) to actually cancel the SendGrid batch, and only for reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. If a reminder's `scheduledDate` (the SendGrid `send_at`) falls within the window between the cancellation request and the next cron execution (up to 15 minutes later), the cron runs after the email has already been sent, and the SendGrid cancel arrives too late. `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` should cancel immediately when `scheduledDate` is within the cron interval (or within the hour, matching the cron's own lookahead) instead of always deferring to the cron.

In the new cancellation block of the cron, the `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop awaits `client.request(...)` inside a single outer try/catch. If any single SendGrid cancellation request throws (invalid batch id, rate limit, network error), the loop aborts immediately: none of the remaining cancelled reminders are cancelled in SendGrid, and — because Prisma query builders are lazy and only execute when awaited — none of the already-collected `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` calls in `workflowRemindersToDelete` execute either. Since the failing reminder stays in the result set every run, it can permanently block cancellation of all reminders that come after it, causing their emails to be sent for cancelled bookings. No tests cover the new cancellation lifecycle

This PR changes the core cancellation semantics of workflow reminders (new `cancelled` flag, deferred cancellation via cron, changed signatures of `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` now taking `reminderId` and nullable `referenceId`), but adds no unit or integration tests. The reworked paths include several edge cases that are easy to regress: reminders with `referenceId === null`, the `immediateDelete` flag, SendGrid failure handling, and the cron's cancel-then-delete ordering. At minimum, tests for `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`'s three branches and the cron's cancellation query/loop would guard the fix for the issue this PR addresses.

Additionally, the code is burned inside authorize() before the rest of the sign-in pipeline completes; if anything fails downstream or the client never receives the success response (network drop), the user's code is permanently consumed and their retry with the same code returns IncorrectBackupCode. The error message instructs them to do something that cannot be done, on both the login page and the disable-2FA modal.

resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step, but never resets the react-hook-form `totpCode` field. After a completed (or abandoned) setup, the form still holds the previously entered 6-digit code. When the user later re-opens the modal and reaches the EnterTotpCode step, the registered hidden `totpCode` input still contains the old value while the digit boxes render empty; submitting (or any change that retriggers the auto-submit effect watching `totpCode`) can send the stale, now-invalid code, producing a confusing "code is incorrect" error before the user has typed anything. resetState should also call form.setValue("totpCode", "").

The PR's headline feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. Neither the happy path (correct code logs in and is consumed), nor wrong-code rejection, nor code-single-use behavior is verified anywhere, leaving the new authorize() and disable.ts branches untested.

In createEvent, the insert call uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar || "primary"`, but the follow-up `calendar.events.patch` that adds the hangout link to the description uses `calendarId: selectedCalendar` with no fallback. When no destination calendar matches the current `credentialId` (so `selectedCalendar` is undefined), the event is created on `primary` but the patch is sent with `calendarId: undefined` and fails, so meeting links never make it into the event description. The patch should use the same `selectedCalendar || "primary"` value as the insert.

Non-Google calendar services still only use the first destination calendar

Office365 (`const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []`), Lark (packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:128) and the CalDAV BaseCalendarService (packages/lib/CalendarService.ts:156) all read only the first element of the now-array `destinationCalendar`. Since EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents calls createEvent once per destination with each host's own credential, for a collective event with multiple hosts on these providers the second host's credential is used against the first host's `externalId`, creating the event in the wrong calendar or failing with an auth/404 error. Only the Google service was adapted (find by credentialId), so the multi-host fix this PR claims only works for Google Calendar. The same per-credential selection is needed in these services.

Team hosts' destination calendars dropped when organizer has none

For COLLECTIVE events the code does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. But `evt.destinationCalendar` is `null` when neither the event type nor the organizer user has a destination calendar (the ternary chain ends in `null`). Optional chaining makes the push a no-op in that case, so team members' destination calendars are silently discarded — precisely the collective scenario the PR is meant to fix — and no calendar events get created for those hosts. The code should assign `evt.destinationCalendar = teamDestinationCalendars` when it is null rather than relying on `?.push`.

organization select removed from dynamic-booking user query

The refactored `loadUsers` for the no-eventTypeId (dynamic link) branch drops `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` from the prisma.user.findMany select that the previous code included. Any downstream logic for dynamic bookings that reads `user.organization` (e.g. organization-aware routing/slug building for dynamic group bookings) will now see `undefined` and behave as if the user belongs to no organization. This removal is unrelated to the destinationCalendar change and looks accidental; the select should be restored.

Breaking change to webhook payload destinationCalendar shape

CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar is sent verbatim in BOOKING_* webhook payloads, and its shape changes from a single `DestinationCalendar` object (or null) to an array. External webhook subscribers that read `payload.destinationCalendar.externalId` etc. will break with no migration note, even though the PR is marked 'non-breaking'. Additionally the empty value is inconsistent across emitters: handleNewBooking emits `null` while confirm/cancel/payment handlers emit `[]` (see the e2e expectations at lines 119 `null` vs 249 `[]`), so consumers must handle both. This should be documented as a breaking webhook change and the empty representation unified.

Recurring cancellation deletes each booking event once per calendar reference

The recurring `allRemainingBookings` branch now lives inside a `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop over all calendar references, and for each reference it iterates ALL of the organizer's calendar credentials × ALL updated bookings, calling deleteEvent. With multiple calendar references (the multi-host case this PR introduces) the same booking's calendar event is deleted N times, and it is deleted with whichever credentials the organizer happens to have rather than the reference's own credential. At best this produces duplicate delete calls (only tolerated because Google treats 410/404 as success); other providers may error and surface as a failed cancellation.

No tests for the new multi-destination collective behavior

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The core change — destinationCalendar becoming an array, per-credential calendar selection in EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents, Google's find-by-credentialId, and the collective push of team calendars — is only covered by an updated e2e assertion for BOOKING_REJECTED. Unit tests for EventManager (create/reschedule/cancel with multiple destination calendars, empty destinationCalendar + Google Meet location, destination calendars without credentialId) are missing, which is how the crash at EventManager.ts:119 and the `?.push` no-op escaped review.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Eager import() calls mean all apps load at import time and failed chunks become unhandled rejections

The appStore object literal evaluates `import("./x")` for every app as soon as `@calcom/app-store` is first imported, so all ~29 app chunks start loading immediately on any code path that touches appStore — the intended deferral is not achieved for cold starts. Worse, each of these promises is created without a rejection handler: if any app chunk fails to load (a common case on Next.js/Vercel when in-flight requests reference chunks invalidated by a new deploy), the promise for that app rejects before anything awaits it. Since Node 15+, an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default, so one app's failed chunk can take down the whole server even though no request ever used that app. To be genuinely lazy and safe, the store should use getters (e.g. `get stripepayment() { return import("./stripepayment"); }`) so the import (and its promise) is only created when actually requested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

async forEach discards deletion promises; reschedule completes before calendar/video events are deleted

This PR changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})`. `Array.forEach` ignores the returned promises, so nothing waits for the `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls. Consequences: (1) `Reschedule` returns `true` and the reschedule email is sent before the external calendar events and video meetings are actually deleted; on a serverless platform the execution context can be frozen after the response, so the deletions may never run and stale events remain on users' calendars; (2) the surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from these async callbacks, so any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => ...))` instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: async callbacks passed to forEach produce unawaited promises, causing premature completion, incomplete cleanup, and unhandled rejections that surrounding try/catch cannot catch. Both recommend awaiting Promise.all with map as a fix.

false_positives.candidate:
requestReschedule fires-and-forgets calendar/video deletions via async forEach

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, this PR changes `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => ...)` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)`. forEach does not await the async callbacks, so the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule-request email and webhooks and returns the response while the old calendar events (`calendar?.deleteEvent`) and video meetings (`deleteMeeting`) are still being — or have not yet begun to be — processed. There is also no try/catch or `.catch()` on these promises, so any deletion failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. In a serverless environment the function can be suspended after the response, leaving the old calendar events permanently in place. Collect the promises with `.map()` and `await Promise.all(...)` before returning.

Recurring-cancellation branch pushes into apiDeletes after awaits, racing the final Promise.all

In the recurring-event cancellation branch (lines 458-470), the PR adds `await getCalendar(credential)` inside a `forEach(async (credential) => {...})` that pushes results into `apiDeletes`. Because forEach does not await the callbacks, the handler continues to line 652 (`await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`) while the forEach callbacks are still suspended at their awaits; the Promise.all therefore snapshots a `apiDeletes` array that may be empty or partial, and the cancellation API response is returned before the calendar deletion calls have even been started. The attendee/bookingReference DB deletes then complete while external calendar events are still pending, so a subsequent process freeze or crash leaves external calendars with events that no longer exist in Cal.com. Convert the forEach to an awaited `Promise.all(credentials.map(...))` and push the deletion promises before awaiting them.

`getCalendarCredentials` now stores the un-awaited `getCalendar(credential)` promise in the returned objects, and only `getConnectedCalendars` awaits `item.calendar`. Two problems: (1) `getCalendar(credential)` is called for every app credential before the `app.variant === "calendar"` filter, so for non-calendar variants a promise is created and immediately discarded — if the app's dynamic import rejects, this is an unhandled rejection (fatal by default on Node 15+); (2) the exported return type of `getCalendarCredentials` silently changed from `calendar: Calendar | null` to `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>`, a breaking contract change for any caller outside this file that accesses `.calendar` directly (they will now hold a Promise where they expect a service instance). Await the promise inside this function or only construct it for calendar-variant apps, and document/verify all callers.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not a promise, in the paid-booking branch

In the paid-booking cancellation path, line 617 does `await apiDeletes;`. `apiDeletes` is an array of promises (populated by `deleteMeeting`/`calendar?.deleteEvent` calls which this PR makes asynchronous), not a promise itself, so awaiting it resolves immediately without waiting for any of the contained deletions. The comment says the code deliberately deletes booking references, but the external calendar/video deletions should still be awaited before returning, e.g. `await Promise.all(apiDeletes)`. Since this PR touches the surrounding async deletion logic, this is the place to fix it.

This PR changes the timing semantics of core booking flows: getCalendar/getVideoAdappers/deleteMeeting became async, appStore lookups are now awaited dynamic imports, and several loops became async forEach. None of these paths (calendar event creation/update/deletion, booking cancellation, reschedule request, payment refund) have accompanying tests added or updated in the PR. Given the fire-and-forget issues this conversion introduces (deletion promises not awaited), at minimum regression tests for cancel/reschedule asserting that external deletions are awaited before the handler resolves should be added before merging.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires

In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: breaking out of the loop when the deadline elapses skips terminating the remaining flusher processes.

false_positives.candidate:
Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources

In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

Redis memory usage is summed across per-shard-group buffers, potentially double-counting clusters

submit() now computes Redis backpressure by extending memory_infos from every buffer in self.buffers and summing used/available across all entries. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

Per-process restart counters are never reset, so lifetime restarts eventually crash the consumer

self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

_create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code

The method _create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere; restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive() -> _create_process_for_shards() directly. Dead code with a misleading name that suggests per-shard restarts exist; it should be removed to avoid confusion.

Docstring says "one process per shard" but the shipped default is one process total

The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the new --flusher-processes CLI option in sentry/consumers/__init__.py defaults to 1, so the default (and typical) deployment runs a single process handling all shards in round-robin groups. The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

To preserve compatibility, the method should have a sensible `default` implementation (e.g., deriving from the ID or returning a marker that the encoder maps to the UNKNOWN shortcut) instead of forcing every existing implementation to be updated.

This class lives in the `server-spi-private` grants package that custom grant-type implementations compile against; any external code that used the copy constructor will break at compile time on upgrade. The removal is not required by the rest of the change (the new `grantType` field could be copied along), so it should either be kept (also copying `grantType`, which would arguably be more correct than re-reading form params) or the break should be explicitly acknowledged.

The decoder is lenient for legacy IDs without ':' (returns UNKNOWN context) but throws `IllegalArgumentException` for IDs that contain ':' with an unknown or wrong-length prefix. Since the token ID (`jti`) originates from externally presented tokens — e.g., tokens issued by another Keycloak deployment with a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider` (the SPI explicitly exists to allow alternate encodings), a future format change, or foreign IDPs whose `jti` happens to contain a colon — any consumer of this method (introspection, userInfo, the planned session-lookup optimization from #37662) can be made to fail with a runtime exception by presenting an otherwise perfectly valid, signature-verified token. Either the framework needs a consumption/update callback for storages, or the storage SPI contract (and the test provider plus a reuse-rejection test) must require storages to invalidate used codes; as merged, a federated user's recovery code is effectively a permanent credential.

Consequences: an admin holding only per-group view-members/manage-members grants gets an empty set, so the UserModel.GROUPS filter used by UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource user search and getUsersCount is never applied at the DB level — searches scan all realm users and rely on the in-memory canView filter, which breaks pagination (first/max are applied before filtering) and returns wrong counts. Worse, an admin holding a view-members/manage-members grant on the type-level 'Groups' resource gets that resource's UUID added as a bogus 'group id', so user search and getUsersCount return zero users even though canView(user) evaluates to true. The existing tests pass only because the in-memory usersEvaluator::canView filter compensates; nothing covers the all-groups or paginated cases.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission passes groupResource.getId() to hasPermission, which resolves resources by name, and it adds resource IDs rather than group IDs to the result. The returned set therefore doesn't fit how it is used for the user GROUPS filtering and counts. The candidate goes further than the golden comment but covers the same core problem.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The new `int order();` method is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI interface without a default implementation. CryptoProvider is a published extension point loaded via ServiceLoader (documented Keycloak crypto SPI), so any third-party or downstream implementation compiled against the previous interface will (a) no longer compile and (b) at runtime fail with AbstractMethodError as soon as `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` calls `CryptoProvider::order` in the comparator while sorting the loaded providers. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that adding an abstract order() method to the CryptoProvider interface breaks backward compatibility with existing implementations. The candidate adds detail on the compile failure, the runtime AbstractMethodError, and a default-method fix, but it is the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Silent, order-tied provider selection removes the FIPS misconfiguration safeguard

detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which acted as a hard safety check against misconfigured deployments (most importantly a classpath accidentally containing both the non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider). Now it silently picks one and only logs ignored providers at debug level. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order() == 200, so in a deployment that accidentally contains both, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader iteration order (classpath order), which can silently select the non-FIPS-approved provider in an environment intended to run in FIPS mode, with no warning at any noticeable log level. At minimum, equal-order providers should produce a warning, and the FIPS/non-FIPS collision should be handled deterministically or fail loudly as before.

ECDSA tests use a single P-256 keypair for ES384/ES512 and never verify the DER signature

The test generates one keypair with the JVM default curve (P-256) and reuses it for all three algorithms. For ES384/ES512 the concatenated r/s halves are zero-padded 32-byte values, so the tests never exercise values whose most significant byte within the target length is set, nor the truncation branch of integerToBytes for real 48/66-byte r/s values. Additionally, the test only checks the concat→DER→concat round trip; it never verifies that the DER produced by concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a valid ECDSA signature via Signature.verify with the public key, which is the actual purpose of the conversion. A bug producing a well-formed but value-incorrect DER encoding would only be caught indirectly. The tests should generate curve-appropriate keypairs (P-384, P-521) and assert Signature.verify(convertedSignature). There is also no test at all for the core mechanism of this PR: the ServiceLoader registration of AuthzClientCryptoProvider and the CryptoIntegration order()-based provider selection/priority logic.
